'''''Aquaria''''' is an [[action-adventure game]] designed by [[Alec Holowka]] and [[Derek Yu]], who [[video game publisher|published]] the game in 2007 as an [[indie game development|independent game company]] Bit Blot. The [[side-scrolling video game|side-scrolling]] game follows Naija, an aquatic [[humanoid]] woman, as she explores the underwater world of Aquaria. Along her journey, she learns about the history of the world she inhabits as well as her own past. The [[gameplay]] focuses on a combination of swimming, singing, and combat, through which Naija can interact with the world. Her songs can move items, affect plants and animals, and change her physical appearance into other forms that have different abilities, like firing projectiles at hostile creatures, or passing through barriers inaccessible to her in her natural form.

After more than two years of development, the game was released in late 2007 for [[Microsoft Windows|Windows]]. A [[porting|port]] of the game to [[Mac OS X]] was released in 2008 by [[Ambrosia Software]], and an updated version of the game was released on the [[Steam (service)|Steam]] service that same year. A [[Linux]] version of the game was released as part of the first [[Humble Bundle|Humble Indie Bundle]] collection in 2010, a version for the [[iPad]] was released in 2011, and an [[Android (operating system)|Android]] version debuted in 2013 alongside another Humble Bundle collection. In 2009, an album with the ''Aquaria'' soundtrack was released. It includes all of the music in the game, as well as a new nine-minute vocal track and a few remixes.

Reviews of the game were generally positive. Critics focused primarily on the visuals, music, and atmosphere as being particularly praiseworthy. The controls and gameplay were also lauded, while negative critiques more often centered on the map system and limited variety of [[glossary of video game terms#O|objectives]]. The game won the [[Seumas McNally Grand Prize]] at the [[Independent Games Festival]] in March 2007.

==Gameplay==
[[File:Aquaria - Screenshot 02.jpg|thumb|left|Naija in her default form riding a seahorse next to a sea dragon. Surrounding her is the eight-note ring through which the player can play songs.|alt=An aquatic humanoid woman swims to the left of the screen. A large seahorse floats behind her, while a larger green seahorse floats to the right. Plants and rock formations are seen around her and in the background in a faded green.]]
''Aquaria'' is an [[action-adventure game]], heavily focused on exploration and puzzle-solving, with a 2D [[side-scrolling video game|side-scrolling]] design and [[nonlinear gameplay|non-linear gameplay]]. The player controls Naija, a lone underwater dweller; although similar to a human woman, Naija also has several fish-like qualities, such as the ability to breathe underwater and propel herself quickly with webbed feet. The game, originally only available for [[personal computer]]s, was designed to be primarily controlled solely through the mouse, though it can also be controlled with a keyboard or [[Xbox 360]] controller.<ref name="GSint"/> The player directs Naija through an underwater world composed of several distinct regions, ranging from caves to underwater ruins to sunlit oases.<ref name="GCreview"/> These areas are filled with plant and animal life, which can be hostile, friendly, or neutral towards her. Hostile plants and animals can hurt Naija, reducing her [[Health (gaming)|health meter]], by touching her or firing projectiles at her.<ref name="IGNreview"/>

In general, Naija cannot interact directly with objects in the world. Instead, the majority of actions are accomplished through singing short tunes. The player does this by selecting a series of notes displayed in a circle of eight choices in the correct order. Each note corresponds with a different color.<ref name="EGreview"/> Singing notes affects plants and objects of the same color as the note, while singing the tunes, once learned through the plot, can lift objects, create a shield around Naija, or change Naija into different "forms" which have different appearances and unique abilities critical to overcoming the various challenges and obstacles found in the game.<ref name="IGNreview"/> The specific tones that are played when the player selects a note can subtly change in different regions, matching the background music.<ref name="GSmusicint"/> The default form, or "normal form", is the only one in which Naija can sing, and is the only one where her appearance is modifiable by the player by having Naija wear costumes found throughout the game.<ref name="MWreview"/>

{{listen|filename=Aquaria_-_Trailer_(Vorbis).ogg|title=''Aquaria'' trailer soundtrack|description= The soundtrack for the game's [[trailer (promotion)|trailer]], featuring music, voice acting, and sound effects from the game}}
Other forms, which can only be used once found in-game, are the "energy form", in which Naija can shoot projectiles to attack enemy creatures,<ref name="quote1"/> "beast form", which allows Naija to swim faster through the water and eat small fish to restore health,<ref name="quote2"/> and "nature form", in which Naija can shoot seeds that produce flowers and spiky plants that can harm other creatures.<ref name="quote3"/> In this form, Naija is not harmed by thorns on any plants. The player can also learn the "sun form", which allows Naija to give off light in dark regions,<ref name="quote4"/> "spirit form", which allows the player to move to specific locations marked by blue crystals without time passing,<ref name="quote5"/> "fish form", where Naija turns into a small, fast fish,<ref name="quote6"/> and "dual form", found at the end of the game, which allows Naija and another character named Li who is met late in the game's plot to merge, with actions taken by one affecting the other.<ref name="quote7"/><ref name="MLreview"/>

While exploring the world, Naija can collect various ingredients from interaction with plants and animals, mainly by combating her foes. These ingredients can be used to cook dishes, which have varying effects on Naija. The most common effects are healing and enhancing various characteristics such as speed and defense, but there are some more exotic dishes which grant her new abilities.<ref name="IGNreview"/> The player can learn new recipes by collecting new dishes directly, but can also learn them by combining ingredients without first knowing the recipe.<ref name="EGreview"/>

==Plot==
[[File:Aquaria - Screenshot 03.jpg|thumb|right|Naija in the "energy form" attacking sea creatures|alt=An aquatic humanoid woman surrounded by a light flare. Energy projectiles stream from her towards several small red creatures. Plants and rock formations are seen around her and in the background.]]
As the game opens, Naija has lost almost all of her memories, and is unaware of the world outside of her home as she "lives as a simple creature".<ref name="quote8"/> The player is told this in voice-over narrations in the form of a story told by a future Naija. These narrations serve as the primary source of information about Naija throughout the game, though there are occasional [[cutscene]]s. After being confronted by a shadowy figure and being shown a series of [[Flashback (narrative)|flashbacks]] she does not understand, Naija awakens. Feeling loneliness as the only member of her species, Naija decides to explore the world around her.<ref name="quote8"/><ref name="quote9"/> As the player explores, Naija discovers more and more about the history of the world, "Aquaria", and about her own past. The player is not forced to go through the plotline in a set sequence. The only limiting factor is physical barriers such as areas that can be accessed only by using a specific form. Combinations of these physical limitations place some plot elements later in the game.<ref name="IGNreview"/> The narrative for the majority of the game is centered on Naija's exploration of a series of ruined civilizations that she finds, each with a large monster in them. These civilizations make up the different regions of the game.

Towards the end of the game, Naija discovers that all of the ruined civilizations she has found throughout the game were destroyed by a god, "the Creator", who was jealous of the rising power of that civilization or of their gods. The powerful monsters she has found and defeated in each region were once the gods of that civilization. Each of these civilizations had a unique power, symbolized by the form that Naija learns after defeating their former gods. Along with Li, a human diver from the land she meets at the top of the ocean, Naija then descends to the bottom of the sea to confront the god. There she discovers that the Creator fell into the ocean as a child, and bonded with an ancient spirit to gain god-like powers. He then created Aquaria, threading a [[song structure#Verse|verse]] of a [[lullaby]] his mother had sung to him throughout, the only part of the song he remembers.<ref name="quote10"/> The [[melody]] of this song, the "verse", is what allows Naija to sing songs that affect the world around her; parts of the melody can be heard in different forms in the songs within the game's soundtrack.<ref name="GSmusicint"/>

The Creator, after creating Aquaria, created a series of civilizations, making a new one in turn when each one was destroyed. The Creator kidnaps Li, with whom Naija has fallen in love, and she attacks the Creator to get him back.<ref name="quote11"/> The player defeats the god as the final boss of the game, and returns home with Li. In the [[epilogue]], Naija is shown with Li and their child. If the player has found all of Naija's memories by discovering places she remembers, they reveal that the shadowy figure at the beginning of the game was her mother, Mia. Mia was made by the Creator and had the ability, like Naija, to use the different powers of all of the civilizations. She fled the Creator, and hid herself and Naija among several communities in succession; after the destruction of the last one she erased Naija's memory so that she would find out the history of Aquaria on her own and defeat the Creator. In the extended epilogue shown if the player has found all of the memories, Mia appears, telling Naija that the two of them can conquer the civilisations above the water. After Naija refuses, Mia kidnaps her, and vanishes; the extended epilogue ends with Lucien—Naija and Li's son—leaving to find her. If the player has not found all of the memories, the epilogue instead ends with Naija asking the player to find out about her past, and revealing that the narration of the game was intended to be heard by her son.<ref name="quote12"/>

==Development==
[[File:Aquaria - Naija.jpg|thumb|150px|right|Concept art of Naija|alt=An aquatic humanoid woman with green skin, large ears, and white hair. She is wearing a metal swimsuit, bracers and shin guards, and is raising her left hand to the viewer.]]
''Aquaria'' was developed by [[Derek Yu]] and [[Alec Holowka]] over the course of two years, off of a concept that Holowka had thought of a year prior.<ref name="GCint"/> Yu was the lead artist, and Holowka handled the programming and audio components. Both designers had previously worked in video games; Yu had made several freeware games, including ''[[I'm O.K – A Murder Simulator|I'm O.K]]'' with Holowka and others, while Holowka had worked for several video game start-ups, none of which had ever gotten a game published.<ref name="GSint"/> Some additional work on the game, including some level design and scripting for some enemies, was done by Brandon McCartin.<ref name="GSmusicint"/> Holowka and Yu officially formed the studio Bit Blot to back the game a week before submitting it to the 2007 [[Independent Games Festival]]. ''Aquaria'' was the studio's only game.<ref name="GSint"/> Both members of the team continued to make video games, but not as a partnership; Holowka went on to form a separate team called Infinite Ammo, and Yu went on to work on ''[[Spelunky]]''.<ref name="bitblotsingle"/>

The initial prototype of the game had styling similar to a text-based role-playing game, with a large [[open world]] and many sub-quests. After moving towards "multiple-choice text answers" and a complicated gameplay system, the team decided to simplify the game and set the 2007 Independent Games Festival as a deadline to complete everything. With this time pressure, they forced themselves to cut out a lot of what they felt was unneeded complexity, bringing the game to its core. After removing many of what they decided were extraneous elements they then added back in the cooking system, which they felt fit well with the rest of the game, as well as a map system.<ref name="GSIGSsummary"/> They then developed the game world and story in a roughly linear manner, creating basic designs of each region and then coming back to fill in details. They felt that this allowed them to create interesting ideas at the beginning of the game and then fill them out and resolve them at the end. One of these ideas was that of the "verse"; Holowka realized partway through development that he had been using the same twelve-note sequence transposed into different keys throughout the music, and realized that the idea of a pervasive musical theme to the world fit with the story.<ref name="GSmusicint"/> The game also includes a level and animation editor; several [[Mod (video gaming)|mods]] have been made for the game.<ref name="GCint"/>

The game was developed to be able to be controlled by the player with only the mouse, after it was suggested by Yu's father. The developers felt that this control scheme forced them to make the gameplay fluid and easy to grasp, though they also added the option to control the game with a keyboard or [[Xbox 360]] controller.<ref name="GSint"/> Yu and Holowka considered the "hallmark" of exploratory games to be a sense of loneliness, which they made a part of the narrative, but also wanted the player to get a sense of Naija's character. To that end, they used voice-overs to demonstrate to the player what Naija was feeling during key points of the game.<ref name="1UPint"/> The voice of Naija was performed by Jenna Sharpe, who was chosen after auditioning several other voice actresses.<ref name="GSint"/> She additionally sang the vocals for one song on the soundtrack, "Lost to the Waves".<ref name="GSmusicint"/> She also sang a nine-minute vocal piece, "Fear the Dark", for the release of the ''Aquaria'' soundtrack album, which was published by Bit Blot on November 14, 2009. The album features 50 tracks on two discs, including all of the music in the game as well as the new vocal track and a few remixes.<ref name="OSTRelease"/>

The game was released for Windows computers on December 7, 2007.<ref name="aquariarelease"/> A patch was later released which added new functionality to the in-game map, added widescreen support, and tweaked several game settings.<ref name="aquariapatch"/> A Macintosh port was released November 13, 2008, courtesy of [[Ambrosia Software]].<ref name="aquariamac"/> The game was released on [[Steam (service)|Steam]] on December 15, 2008; it included the addition of 27 Steam Achievements.<ref name="aquariasteam"/> A Linux version of the game was developed by [[Ryan C. Gordon]] in 2009; an open beta ran until February 6, 2010, and the Linux version of the game was released as part of the first [[Humble bundle|Humble Indie Bundle]].<ref name="aquarialinux"/> The source code for the game's engine was released under the [[GNU General Public License]] on June 3, 2010.<ref name="sourcecode"/><ref>[https://github.com/AquariaOSE/Aquaria Current repository]</ref> A modified version was released on the [[iPad]] on November 2, 2011. This version, which includes touchscreen support and changes to the way the map works, was created by Andrew Church, who was approached to do the port by Holowka after he did an unofficial [[PlayStation Portable]] [[source port]].<ref name="aquariaipad"/> The Humble Bundle with Android 6 collection, which was launched on June 18, 2013, debuted an [[Android (operating system)|Android]] version of ''Aquaria''.<ref name="aquariaandroid"/>

==Reception==
{{Video game reviews
| MC = PC: 82/100 <small>(7 reviews)</small><ref name="MCreviews"/><br />iOS: 84/100 <small>(8 reviews)</small><ref name="MCiosreviews"/>
| EuroG = 7/10<ref name="EGreview"/>
| IGN = 7.4/10<ref name="IGNreview"/>
| PCGUK = 8.1/10<ref name="PCGUreview"/>
| rev1 = ''GameCritics.com''
| rev1Score = 9/10<ref name="GCreview"/>
}}

''Aquaria'' was the [[Seumas McNally Grand Prize]] winner of the 2007 Independent Games Festival, and was also a finalist in the categories of Design Innovation, Excellence in Visual Art, and Excellence in Audio. The festival praised the game's "fluid controls, unique, non-linear gameplay, and vibrant hand-drawn storybook-style graphics".<ref name="IGFAward"/> The game received praise from many different reviewers; Cam Shea of ''[[IGN]]'' called it "a stunning effort from such a small team",<ref name="IGNreview"/> Richard Naik of ''GameCritics'' called it "an extremely high-quality product" and a fine example of the [[side-scrolling video game|side-scroller]] genre,<ref name="GCreview"/> while Chris Dahlen of ''[[The A.V. Club]]'' termed it "not so much a retro adventure as a fresh take on everything that made the old 2D adventures great".<ref name="AVreview"/> Praise for the game was centered primarily on its visuals and atmosphere. ''[[Hyper (magazine)|Hyper]]''{{'}}s Tim Henderson commended the game for "a rare and genuine sense of exploration, wonder and discovery".<ref name="Hyperreview"/> A review by Scott Colbourne from ''[[The Globe and Mail]]'' termed ''Aquaria'' "drop-dead beautiful" with a "deep and affecting story" and summarized it as "a game you can get comfortably lost in".<ref name="GAMreview"/>

[[File:Aquaria - IGF.jpg|thumb|left|Jenna Sharpe, [[Alec Holowka]] and [[Derek Yu]] accepting the grand prize at the 2007 [[Independent Games Festival]]|alt=Two men stand behind a podium marked Independent Games Festival, while a woman in a blue dress stands to the left.]]
Other reviewers, such as Tom Bramwell of ''[[Eurogamer]]'' and Chris Holt of [[Macworld]] echoed the praises for the graphics and atmosphere, while Craig Pearson of ''[[PC Gamer|PC Gamer UK]]'' added praises for the music and voiceovers and Suzie Ochs of ''[[MacLife]]'' praised the music and story.<ref name="EGreview"/><ref name="MWreview"/><ref name="MLreview"/><ref name="PCGUreview"/> Other praises for the game came for its control scheme and for the gameplay mechanics, with Holt calling out the cooking system as worthy of praise.<ref name="EGreview"/> Though noting that the visuals and presentation of the game would be the first thing players noticed, Nathan Cocks of ''[[PC PowerPlay]]'' claimed that "from a design standpoint, ''Aquaria'' is a triumph," with the right amount of complexity and level design that is "spot on".<ref name="PCPPreview"/>

Several reviewers, such as Bramwell and Holt, criticized the map system present in the initial version of the game as being confusing and difficult.<ref name="EGreview"/><ref name="MWreview"/> Other reviewers had different concerns, such as Henderson, who critiqued the initial release version for "lack of widescreen support and being occasionally fiddly",<ref name="Hyperreview"/> or Naik, who felt that the control scheme was not as intuitive when using an Xbox 360 controller.<ref name="GCreview"/> Shea and Pearson felt that the game could have used more puzzles or a wider variety of quests and objectives to balance out the exploration and combat.<ref name="IGNreview"/><ref name="PCGUreview"/> They did not feel, though, that these downsides compared to the game's positives, with Pearson saying that "the good far outweighs what are, essentially, niggles."<ref name="PCGUreview"/>

'''''Baldur's Gate''''' is a 1998 [[role-playing video game]] developed by [[BioWare]] and published by [[Interplay Entertainment]]. It is the first game in the ''[[Baldur's Gate (series)|Baldur's Gate]]'' series and takes place in the [[Forgotten Realms]], a high fantasy [[Dungeons & Dragons campaign settings|campaign setting]], using a modified version of the ''[[Dungeons & Dragons|Advanced Dungeons & Dragons]]'' (''AD&D'') [[Editions of Dungeons & Dragons|2nd edition]] rules. It was the first game to use the [[Infinity Engine]] for its graphics, with Interplay using the engine for other Forgotten Realms-licensed games, including the ''[[Icewind Dale (series)|Icewind Dale]]'' series and ''[[Planescape: Torment]]''. The game's story focuses on a player-made character who travels across the [[Sword Coast]] alongside a party of companions.

The game received critical acclaim and was credited for revitalizing computer role-playing games. An expansion pack was released titled ''[[Baldur's Gate: Tales of the Sword Coast|Tales of the Sword Coast]]'', as were two sequels, ''[[Baldur's Gate II: Shadows of Amn]]'' (2000) and ''[[Baldur's Gate 3]]'' (2023). An enhanced, remastered version of the Infinity Engine was later created as part of [[Beamdog]]'s ''[[Baldur's Gate: Enhanced Edition]]'', the first new release in the franchise in nearly nine years The original ''Baldur's Gate'' continues to be referenced as a point of inspiration in many modern role-playing games, and is often cited as [[List of video games considered the best|one of the best video games ever made]]. 

==Gameplay==
[[File:Duchal palace sarevok speaks BGI.png|right|thumb|A screenshot of ''Baldur's Gate'', showcasing the user interface designed by [[BioWare]] in order to provide relative ease in playing the game, with the UI template used in other Forgotten Realms-licensed games, such as ''Icewind Dale''. The game relies heavily on plot and dialogue as driving factors behind how it conveys the main story.]]

Players conduct the game from a [[Top-down perspective|top-down]] [[Isometric video game graphics|isometric]] [[Third-person (gaming)|third-person]] perspective, creating a character who travels across [[pre-rendered]] locations, taking on [[Quest (video games)|quests]], recruiting companions to aid them, and combating enemies, while working towards completing the game's main story. A user interface allows a player to move characters and give them actions to undertake, review information on on-going quests and the [[Statistic (role-playing games)|statistics]] of characters in their party, manage their inventories, and organize the formation of the party, though the screen does not need to be centered on the characters being controlled and can be moved around with the mouse and keyboard, the latter capable of accessing various player options through [[keyboard shortcut]]s. All of the gameplay mechanics were coded to conform to the [[Editions of Dungeons & Dragons#Advanced Dungeons & Dragons 2nd edition|''Advanced Dungeons & Dragons'' 2nd edition]] role-playing rules, with the game automatically computing rule intricacies, including tracking statistics and dice rolling.<ref name=schoffel>{{cite news |url= http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1G1-20497495.html |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20140611070950/http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1G1-20497495.html |url-status = usurped|archive-date= June 11, 2014 |author= Schoffel, Julian |title= RPG Revival |work=[[PCWorld (magazine)|PCWorld]] |date= April 1, 1998 |via= [[HighBeam Research]] |url-access= subscription |access-date= September 26, 2012}}</ref><ref name=tresca2010>{{citation |first1= Michael J. |last1=Tresca |title= The Evolution of Fantasy Role-Playing Games |publisher=McFarland |year=2010 |isbn= 978-0786458950 |page=144 |url= https://books.google.com/books?id=8H8bzqj6S4sC&pg=PA144}}</ref> Although the game is conducted in real-time, some elements of the rule set were modified to allow it to feature a [[pausable real-time]] mode. This allows players to pause at any time and prepare what actions a character would do, including the ability to set the game to automatically pause at preset points in combat.<ref name=schoffel/><ref name="jharris">{{cite web |first=John |last= Harris |work=Gamasutra |title=Game Design Essentials: 20 RPGs |url= https://www.gamedeveloper.com/design/game-design-essentials-20-rpgs |access-date= October 5, 2009 |url-status=live |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20091109154652/http://www.gamasutra.com/view/feature/4066/game_design_essentials_20_rpgs.php?page=10 |archive-date= November 9, 2009}}</ref><ref name="herald">{{cite news|date=March 14, 1999|title=Adventure Lives up to Hype|work=[[The Herald News]]|location=Joliet, Illinois|url=http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1N1-0EB096C2EDF69DCD.html|url-status=usurped|access-date=November 17, 2012|via=HighBeam Research|url-access=subscription|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150329145403/http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1N1-0EB096C2EDF69DCD.html|archive-date=March 29, 2015}}</ref>

For each new playthrough the player can either create a new character, or import one they exported from a previous playthrough. A new character requires the player to determine what their name, gender, [[Race (fantasy)|race]], [[class (Dungeons & Dragons)|class]], and [[alignment (Dungeons & Dragons)|alignment]] are, and what [[ability score]]s and weapon proficiencies they have. New characters can be [[Character class (Dungeons & Dragons)#Multi-classing|multi-class]], but must adhere to the restrictions that come from this, in accordance to the 2nd edition rules; for example, a character who is both a [[Cleric (Dungeons & Dragons)|cleric]] and a [[Fighter (Dungeons & Dragons)|fighter]], may only use weapons of the former class.<ref>{{cite web |url= http://clankiller.com/games/bg/dualclass/ |work= clankiller.com |title= Baldur's Gate Dual-Classing Guide |access-date= March 16, 2017}}</ref>

The game's main story is divided up into eight parts, featuring a prologue and seven chapters. Each section requires the player to complete a specific task in order to continue. Some areas of the map are not accessible until the player has advanced to a specific chapter.<ref name="schoffel" /> A player may have up to five companions travelling with them in their party, with the player free to decide whom to recruit or dismiss from the party.<ref name="schoffel" />

The main [[User interface|UI]] consists of three action bars surrounding the main screen. The first bar consists of a map, journal, character records, their inventories, spellbooks and a clock. The second bar consists of a portrait of each character in the party, their [[hit point|HP]], order, and any effects they are experiencing. The third bar provides specific actions per the number of characters being controlled: if a single character is selected, the player has the ability to switch between the weapons the character is wielding, use spells or items, or utilize a character's or piece of equipment's special abilities. If more than one character is selected, the bar displays options to allow them to converse with or attack [[non-player character]]s, stop what is being done, or change their formation.{{citation needed|date=January 2024}}

The inventory system allows each character to equip items categorized as: weapons, ammunition, armor, helmets, necklaces, rings, belts, cloaks, feet, or usable. The number of items a character can both equip and carry is affected by their weight limit, which is determined by their Strength ability score; going over this limit will encumber the character causing them to move slowly or prevent them moving altogether until they remove items from their inventory. The system also indicates what equipment a character may not use as defined by their class. This mechanic also determines how many weapon slots they have available; by default, all character have two weapon slots, with an off-hand slot for shields. Some classes allow characters additional weapon slots. Characters may equip three stacks of ammo for ranged weapons (bows, crossbows and slings), and use three different types of usable items (potions, scrolls and wands).{{citation needed|date=January 2024}}

Conversation can be initiated by players selecting a member of the party and clicking on a friendly or neutral NPC. Some conversations are initiated automatically when characters come close to them. Certain NPCs offer services the player can utilize, including buying and selling items and identifying enchanted items. Other useful places include inns where the party can rest in safety to recover lost hit points and memorize spells, as well as temples where characters can pay for healing services, such as resurrecting a dead party member.{{citation needed|date=January 2024}}

Other features that affect gameplay include:
* The ability to customize their character after creation, albeit with some restrictions.
* The ability to change the primary and minor colors used by each character.
* The ability to switch the game's [[Artificial intelligence in video games|AI]] on or off, and change what script a character uses.
* Most locations are hidden when first visited but are revealed as the character moves around them. A [[Fog of war#Simulations and games|fog of war]] effect hides explored areas when the player's characters move away from them.
* A [[reputation system]] that tracks the moral actions of the PC and affects how they are perceived, changing if they resolve a problem or commit a crime in the view of witnesses. Higher reputations cause shops to decrease prices, while lower reputations cause shops to increase prices. Lower reputations may also lead to the character being attacked when in town. Companions are also affected by reputation, with evil companions leaving the party, even attacking it, if it is high, and good and neutral companions leaving when it is low. Some side quests also require a minimum reputation to begin. Certain NPCs may also react negatively or positively depending on their alignment and the player's reputation.
* The ability to keep track of in-game time through the changes in lighting and the activity that is occurring. Characters become fatigued after spending a full in-game day, especially after travelling long distances between world map locations, and must rest to recover, either in an inn or camping out in the countryside/within a dungeon.
* Characters can be ambushed when camping out or travelling long distances between world map locations.<ref name=rollings_adams03/>
* Players can play either in [[single-player]] mode, or in [[multiplayer]] mode. The latter allows up to six players to work together online with their own created characters.

==Plot==
===Setting===
''Baldur's Gate'' takes place in the world of [[Ed Greenwood]]'s ''[[Forgotten Realms]]'' setting, during the year 1368 DR, along the western coast of the continent of [[Faerûn]] known as the [[Sword Coast]]. The game takes place during a regional iron shortage in which iron weapons and tools begin to corrode and break without explanation, threatening trade and stability throughout the region. The player's journey takes place across a variety of Sword Coast locations, including the library fortress of [[Candlekeep]], the mining town of Nashkel, the village of Beregost, the Cloakwood forest, and the city of [[Baldur's Gate]], one of the region's largest centres of commerce.

The conflict draws the player into the activities of several organisations from the Forgotten Realms setting, including the Iron Throne, a merchantile organization central to the iron crisis; the [[Flaming Fist]], the mercenary company responsible for maintaining order in Baldur's Gate; the [[Zhentarim]]; the [[Red Wizards of Thay]]; the [[Harper (Forgotten Realms)|Harpers]]; and the mercenary group known as the Chill.

===Characters===
The protagonist of ''Baldur's Gate'' is an orphan raised in the library fortress of Candlekeep by the mage Gorion, a member of the Harpers. The game has 25 characters who may join the player's [[party (role-playing games)|party]].<ref name="GB-companions">{{cite web |url=https://www.gamebanshee.com/baldursgate/companions.php |title=Companions |website=GameBanshee |access-date=13 September 2026}}</ref>  [[Imoen]], who also grew up in Candlekeep, is a childhood friend of the protagonist and the first party member to join.<ref name=carr_burn06>{{Cite book |author1=Carr, Diane |author2=Burn, Andrew |title=Computer Games: Text, Narrative and Play |chapter=Baldur's Gate |pages=31–33 |publisher=Polity |year=2006 |isbn=0-7456-3400-1}}</ref> Several are encountered in pairs: [[Jaheira]], a [[half-elf (Dungeons & Dragons)|half-elven]] warrior druid and [[Harper (Forgotten Realms)|Harper]] who was a friend of Gorion, travels with her husband Khalid, a nervous but capable fighter;<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.gamebanshee.com/baldursgate/companions/jaheira.php |title=Jaheira |website=GameBanshee |access-date=13 September 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.gamebanshee.com/baldursgate/companions/khalid.php |title=Khalid |website=GameBanshee |access-date=13 September 2026}}</ref> [[Minsc]], an eccentric Rashemi ranger who treats his hamster Boo as a "miniature giant space hamster", seeks to rescue Dynaheir, the Rashemi witch he is sworn to protect;<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.gamebanshee.com/baldursgate/companions/minsc.php |title=Minsc |website=GameBanshee |access-date=13 September 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite web Other recruitable companions include Ajantis Ilvastarr, a young paladin of the Order of the Most Radiant Heart sent to combat the increased bandit activity on the Sword Coast;<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.gamebanshee.com/baldursgate/companions/ajantis.php |title=Ajantis |website=GameBanshee |access-date=13 September 2026}}</ref> Alora, a cheerful halfling thief encountered while robbing Baldur's Gate's Hall of Wonders;<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.gamebanshee.com/baldursgate/companions/alora.php |title=Alora |website=GameBanshee |access-date=13 September 2026}}</ref> Branwen, a priest of the war god Tempus who may be freed after being turned to stone by the mage Tranzig;<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.gamebanshee.com/baldursgate/companions/branwen.php |title=Branwen |website=GameBanshee |access-date=13 September 2026}}</ref> Coran, an elven fighter and thief encountered hunting wyverns in the Cloakwood<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.gamebanshee.com/baldursgate/companions/coran.php |title=Coran |website=GameBanshee |access-date=13 September 2026}}</ref>; [[Edwin Odesseiron]], an arrogant Red Wizard of Thay who seeks the protagonist's help in killing Dynaheir<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.gamebanshee.com/baldursgate/companions/edwin.php |title=Edwin |website=GameBanshee |access-date=13 September 2026}}</ref>; Faldorn, a member of the militant Shadow Druids;<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.gamebanshee.com/baldursgate/companions/faldorn.php |title=Faldorn |website=GameBanshee |access-date=13 September 2026}}</ref> Garrick, a young bard and former member of a travelling troupe;<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.gamebanshee.com/baldursgate/companions/garrick.php |title=Garrick |website=GameBanshee |access-date=13 September 2026}}</ref> Kagain, a dwarven mercenary who operates a caravan escort business in Beregost;<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.gamebanshee.com/baldursgate/companions/kagain.php |title=Kagain |website=GameBanshee |access-date=13 September 2026}}</ref> Kivan, an elven ranger pursuing the bandit leader Tazok, who was responsible for the death of his partner Deheriana.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.gamebanshee.com/baldursgate/companions/kivan.php |title=Kivan |website=GameBanshee |access-date=13 September 2026}}</ref>; Quayle, an arrogant gnome cleric and illusionist who considers himself intellectually superior to those around him<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.gamebanshee.com/baldursgate/companions/quayle.php |title=Quayle |website=GameBanshee |access-date=13 September 2026}}</ref>; Safana, a thief and former pirate from Calimport;<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.gamebanshee.com/baldursgate/companions/safana.php |title=Safana |website=GameBanshee |access-date=13 September 2026}}</ref> Shar-Teel, an aggressive warrior with a particular hatred of the Flaming Fist<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.gamebanshee.com/baldursgate/companions/shar-teel.php |title=Shar-Teel |website=GameBanshee |access-date=13 September 2026}}</ref>; Tiax, a gnome cleric and thief devoted to the evil god Cyric who believes he is destined to rule the world<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.gamebanshee.com/baldursgate/companions/tiax.php |title=Tiax |website=GameBanshee |access-date=13 September 2026}}</ref>; Viconia deVir, a [[drow]] cleric of Shar who has fled the [[Underdark]] and is persecuted because of her race<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.gamebanshee.com/baldursgate/companions/viconia.php |title=Viconia |website=GameBanshee |access-date=13 September 2026}}</ref>; Xan, a pessimistic elven Greycloak mage from Evereska sent to investigate the iron shortage;<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.gamebanshee.com/baldursgate/companions/xan.php |title=Xan |website=GameBanshee |access-date=13 September 2026}}</ref> and Yeslick Orothiar, a dwarven fighter and cleric whose ancestral mine in the Cloakwood has been taken over by the Iron Throne after he was betrayed by Rieltar.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.gamebanshee.com/baldursgate/companions/yeslick.php |title=Yeslick |website=GameBanshee |access-date=13 September 2026}}</ref> 

The principal antagonist of ''Baldur's Gate'' is [[Sarevok]], the foster son of Rieltar Anchev, the leader the Iron Throne who is bent on monopolizing the iron and weapons trade in the Sword Coast.<ref name="History">{{cite web |url=https://www.pcgamer.com/the-history-of-baldurs-gate/2/ |title=The history of Baldur's Gate |date=March 1, 2020 |work=[[PC Gamer]] |access-date=March 7, 2020 |archive-date=March 8, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200308104610/https://www.pcgamer.com/the-history-of-baldurs-gate/2/ |url-status=live}}</ref> Other characters involved in the Iron Throne conspiracy include Mulahey, a priest of Cyric overseeing the sabotage of the Nashkel mines; the half-ogre Tazok, who commands the bandits disrupting trade on the Sword Coast; and Tamoko, Sarevok's lover, who later undermines him by supplying information to Gorion's Ward. The Flaming Fist is represented by its commander Eltan, one of the Dukes of Baldur's Gate, Eltan's lieutenant Scar, and Angelo Dosan, a corrupt officer who is Shar-Teel's father and is secretly allied with Sarevok.<Ref>{{cite video game |title=Baldur's Gate |developer=[[BioWare]] |publisher=[[Black Isle Studios]] |date=1998}}</ref> 

Several characters originated in the wider ''Forgotten Realms'' setting. These include [[Cadderly Bonaduce]], the priest and Chosen of Deneir; [[Drizzt Do'Urden]], who can be encountered in the wilderness; [[Elminster]], who periodically advises the protagonist; Thalantyr, a wizard who lives at High Hedge outside Beregost<ref>{{cite book |last=Greenwood |first=Ed |author-link=Ed Greenwood |title=Volo's Guide to the Sword Coast |publisher=TSR |year=1994 |pages=28, 225 |isbn=978-1-56076-904-0}}</ref>; Ardenor Crush, the hobgoblin commander of the Chill.<ref>{{cite book |last=Beach |first=Tim |title=Gold & Glory |publisher=TSR |year=1992 |page=19 |isbn=1-56076-334-5}}</ref>; and the traveller and author [[Volothamp Geddarm|Volothamp "Volo" Geddarm]].

Biff the Understudy is a fallback character created for the game's conversation system. If dialogue requires a character who is no longer present, Biff appears in the missing character's place and delivers the requisite lines, preventing the game from crashing and allowing critical dialogue to continue.<ref>{{cite web |title=Baldur's Gate Readme and Manual Addenda |url=https://pbg.bgforge.net/bg/media/files/patches/BGpatch4315.txt |publisher=[[Interplay Entertainment|Interplay Productions]] |date=1999 |access-date=13 September 2026}}</ref> Former BioWare developer Mark Darrah later explained that he created Biff as a backup for the game's dialogue system.<ref>{{cite web |last=Obedkov |first=Evgeny |title=Mark Darrah on lessons learned from Baldur's Gate: "If you look for perfection, you're never going to ship" |url=https://gameworldobserver.com/2023/05/25/baldurs-gate-mark-darrah-development-lessons-bioware |website=Game World Observer |date=25 May 2023 |access-date=13 September 2026}}</ref>

===Story===
The story of ''Baldur's Gate'' begins when Gorion abruptly instructs his Ward to leave Candlekeep without explanation. That night, the pair are ambushed by a mysterious armored warrior and his followers, who demand that Gorion surrender his Ward. Gorion refuses and is killed while allowing the Ward to escape. The Ward then begins investigating the iron shortage and increased bandit activity affecting the Sword Coast.

Travelling south to the mines of Nashkel, the party discovers that the region's iron ore is being deliberately contaminated. The saboteurs are connected to the bandits attacking caravans throughout the region, and both groups are working on behalf of the Iron Throne. The Ward traces the bandits to their camp and then to a mining operation in the Cloakwood, where the organisation is producing uncontaminated iron while rival supplies deteriorate. After disrupting the Cloakwood operation, the party travels to Baldur's Gate and investigates the Iron Throne's headquarters. They learn that several of its leaders have traveled to Candlekeep for an important meeting, prompting the Ward to return to their former home. While investigating the citadel, the Ward discovers a letter from Gorion revealing that they are one of the [[Bhaalspawn]], mortal offspring of the dead god [[Bhaal (Forgotten Realms)|Bhaal]]. The revelation corresponds with a prophecy by the seer Alaundo that Bhaal's children would spread chaos and ultimately destroy one another.

At Candlekeep, the Ward encounters a man calling himself Koveras, who offers assistance while encouraging suspicion of the Iron Throne's leaders. Soon afterwards, those leaders are murdered and the party is blamed for their deaths. Imprisoned beneath the fortress, they are helped to escape by Tethoril and travel through Candlekeep's catacombs, where they encounter doppelgangers who have infiltrated the citadel. During their escape, they learn that Koveras was Sarevok in disguise and that he was responsible for Gorion's death. Returning to Baldur's Gate, the party finds the city increasingly unstable. Duke Eltan has been poisoned, the Flaming Fist has fallen under Angelo Dosan's influence, and the Ward is wanted for the murders at Candlekeep. The party uncovers the true purpose of the iron crisis: the Iron Throne sabotaged competing supplies while stockpiling usable iron, intending to profit from shortages and tensions between Baldur's Gate and neighbouring Amn. Sarevok has manipulated the crisis further, seeking to escalate those tensions into open warfare.

Sarevok believes that the bloodshed from such a war will strengthen him and enable him to succeed Bhaal as the new God of Murder.  After eliminating members of the Iron Throne who threatened his plans, Sarevok moves to seize political power directly, arranging the poisoning of Eltan and an assassination attempt against another of Baldur's Gate's Dukes while positioning himself to join the Council of Four. The Ward and their companions enter the Ducal Palace during Sarevok's coronation and expose his conspiracy. Sarevok escapes into the ruins beneath Baldur's Gate, where the party pursues him to an ancient temple of Bhaal. After Sarevok and his remaining followers are defeated, his soul leaves his body and travels to an underground chamber containing statues representing the other Bhaalspawn, one of which crumbles following his death.

==Development and release==
''Baldur's Gate'' began development in 1995 by Canadian game developer BioWare, a company founded by [[Ray Muzyka]], [[Greg Zeschuk]], Trent Oster, his brother Brent, Zeschuk's cousin Marcel, and Augustine Yip.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.usgamer.net/articles/reflections-on-the-early-days-of-bioware-co-founder-trent-oster |title=Remembering the Early Days of BioWare with Co-Founder Trent Oster |first=Mike |last=Williams |date=20 August 2019 |access-date=June 19, 2022 |archive-date=May 20, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220520233657/https://www.usgamer.net/articles/reflections-on-the-early-days-of-bioware-co-founder-trent-oster |url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.eurogamer.net/how-bioware-revolutionised-the-rpg |title=How BioWare revolutionised the RPG |first=Graeme |last=Mason |newspaper=Eurogamer.net |date=30 September 2018}}</ref><ref name=gooddoctor>{{cite web | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20001207074200/http://gamecenter.com/News/Item/Textonly/0,78,0-2425,00.html | url=http://gamecenter.com/News/Item/Textonly/0,78,0-2425,00.html | title=The Good Doctor of ''Baldur's Gate'' | author=Asher, Mark | work=[[CNET Gamecenter]] | date=January 20, 1999 | archive-date=December 7, 2000 | url-status = dead}}</ref> The game was initially titled ''Forgotten Realms''.<ref name="NGen25">{{cite magazine |title=NG Alphas: Forgotten Realms|magazine=[[Next Generation (magazine)|Next Generation]]|issue=25 |publisher=[[Imagine Media]]|date=January 1997|pages=113–4}}</ref> The game had an estimated budget of $1 million.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/national-post/158411927/|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20241106095155/https://www.newspapers.com/article/national-post/158411927/|title=Untitled|newspaper=[[National Post]]|page=94|archivedate=November 6, 2024|date=October 23, 1999|accessdate=November 6, 2024|via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref> According to Muzyka, their head programmer read all Forgotten Realms books, including the short stories and the paperbacks, to immerse himself into that setting.<ref name="NGen25"/> The game required 90 man-years of development, which was spent simultaneously creating the game's content and the BioWare [[Infinity Engine]].<ref name=muzyka20010502/> The primary script engine for the game (used mainly as a debugging tool) was [[Lua (programming language)|Lua]].<ref name=gutschmidt2003/><ref>{{cite web|last=Tofer|first=Cameron|title=Re: lua and Baldur's gate|url=http://lua-users.org/lists/lua-l/1999-08/msg00056.html|website=lua-users mailing list archive}}<!-- author is one of bioware lead programmers, so it's a RS on a subject --></ref> [[DirectDraw]] was used for the graphics.<ref name="NGen25"/> ''[[Wasteland (video game)|Wasteland]]'' was a major influence on ''Baldur's Gate'', particularly its design philosophy of having more than one possible method to achieve each goal.<ref name="NGen25"/>

Unusually for the time, the graphics were not [[Tile-based video game|built from tiles]]; each background was individually rendered, which greatly extended the amount of time needed to create the game.<ref name="NGen25"/> At the time that the game was shipped, none of the sixty-member team had previously participated in the release of a video game.<ref name=carless2010816/> The time pressure to complete the game led to the use of simple areas and game design.<ref name=muzyka20010502/> Ray Muzyka said that the team held a "passion and a love of the art" and they developed a "collaborative design spirit". He believes that the game was successful because of the collaboration with Interplay.<ref name=carless2010816/>

According to writer Luke Kristjanson, the character of Imoen was a late addition to fill a "non-psychotic-thief gap in the early levels". Kristjanson assembled Imoen's lines by "editing voice-over" for a guard character named Pique from an unused demo, and explained that her lack of voiced dialogue or standalone interactions with other party members throughout the game was due to budgetary constraints.<ref name=Memories>{{cite web|url=http://rpgvault.ign.com/articles/940/940545p2.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090215085610/http://rpgvault.ign.com/articles/940/940545p2.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=2009-02-15 |title=RPG Vault: Baldur's Gate Memories |date=2009-02-15 |accessdate=2012-09-19}}</ref> The wife of Dean Anderson, a team member, was the basis for Imoen's facial features as depicted in her character portrait.<ref name=Frazer>{{cite web |url=https://www.gamespot.com/articles/mass-effect-andromeda-ian-frazier-interview/1100-6448748/ |title=Mass Effect: Andromeda Ian Frazier Interview |date= March 20, 2017 |author1= Lucy James |author2=Tamoor Hussain |work=[[GameSpot]] |access-date=August 28, 2021}}</ref>

''Baldur's Gate'' was released on December 21, 1998, and was published by Black Isle Studios, an internal division of Interplay.<ref name="releasedate"/><ref name="releasedate2"/> The Macintosh version was released by [[Graphsim Entertainment]] on July 17, 2000.<ref name=macdate>{{cite web|url=http://www.graphsim.com/_old_site/news.htm|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20000816225549/http://www.graphsim.com/_old_site/news.htm|url-status=dead |archive-date=2000-08-16 |title=GraphSim News|date=2000-07-17 |accessdate=2026-09-09}}</ref>

In 2009, a novelization of the game by [[Philip Athans]] was published.

In 2000 ''Baldur's Gate'' was re-released along with its expansion as ''Baldur's Gate Double Pack'', and again in 2002 as a three CD collection entitled ''Baldur's Gate: The Original Saga''. In 2002, the game and its expansion were released along with ''Icewind Dale'', ''[[Icewind Dale: Heart of Winter]]'' and ''Planescape: Torment'' as the ''Black Isle Compilation''. In 2004, it was re-released, this time along with ''Icewind Dale II'', in ''Part Two'' of the compilation. [[Atari]] published the ''Baldur's Gate 4 in 1 Boxset'' including all four games on a combination of DVDs and CDs.

''Baldur's Gate'' and its expansion were released digitally on [[Good Old Games]] (later GOG.com) on September 23, 2010.<ref>{{cite web |title= Baldur's Gate: The Original Saga |url= http://www.gog.com/en/gamecard/baldurs_gate_the_original_saga|work=[[Good Old Games]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Deleon |first= Nicholas |title= Good Old Games Not Shutting Down, Re-launches Tomorrow With Baldur's Gate Among New Games |url= https://techcrunch.com/2010/09/22/good-old-games-not-shutting-down-re-launches-tomorrow-with-baldurs-gate-among-new-games/ |work= [[TechCrunch]] |access-date= March 16, 2012 |date= September 22, 2010}}</ref> It has also been made available via GameStop App as part of the ''D&D Anthology: The Master Collection'', which also includes the expansion ''Baldur's Gate: Tales of the Sword Coast'', ''Baldur's Gate II: Shadows of Amn'', ''Baldur's Gate II: Throne of Bhaal'', ''Icewind Dale'', ''Icewind Dale: Heart of Winter'', ''[[Icewind Dale: Trials of the Luremaster]]'', ''Icewind Dale II'', ''Planescape: Torment'', and ''[[The Temple of Elemental Evil (video game)|The Temple of Elemental Evil]]''.<ref>{{cite web |title= D&D Anthology: The Master Collection |url= http://www.impulsedriven.com/products/ESD-IMP-W2574 |work= [[GameStop]] |access-date= December 12, 2012 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20140422032156/http://www.impulsedriven.com/products/ESD-IMP-W2574 |archive-date= April 22, 2014 |url-status= dead}}</ref>

A [[remaster]]ed and expanded edition of the original game, entitled ''[[Baldur's Gate: Enhanced Edition]]'', was released in 2012, developed by [[Overhaul Games]].<ref name="announcement"/><ref>{{cite web |url= http://www.baldursgate.com/news/2012/03/21/baldurs-gate-enhanced-edition-for-ipad-3/ |title= Baldur's Gate: Enhanced Edition for iPad |access-date= March 22, 2012 |date= March 20, 2012 |url-status = dead|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20120324030708/http://www.baldursgate.com/news/2012/03/21/baldurs-gate-enhanced-edition-for-ipad-3/ |archive-date= March 24, 2012}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url= http://forum.baldursgate.com/discussion/4796/ship-date-delay |author= Oster, Trent |title= Ship Date Delay |date= September 14, 2012 |access-date= September 26, 2012 |archive-date= September 16, 2012 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20120916230123/http://forum.baldursgate.com/discussion/4796/ship-date-delay |url-status= dead}}</ref> The game was released for Microsoft Windows, iOS, Mac OS X, Android and Linux.

Skybound Games, a division of [[Skybound Entertainment]], brought ''Baldur's Gate: Enhanced Edition'' to the [[PlayStation 4]], [[Xbox One]], and [[Nintendo Switch]] in 2019.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://venturebeat.com/2019/02/07/walking-dead-creator-skybound-games-will-publish-beamdogs-classic-rpgs-to-consoles/ | title = Walking Dead creator Skybound Games will publish Beamdog's classic RPGs to consoles | first=  Dean | last= Takahashi | date = February 7, 2019 | access-date = February 7, 2019 | work = [[Venture Beat]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.engadget.com/2019/05/31/bioware-baldurs-gate-neverwinter-nights-console-release-date/ | title = Six Bioware classics are coming to consoles this fall | first = AJ | last = Dellinger | date = May 30, 2019 | access-date = May 30, 2019 | work = [[Engadget]]}}</ref>

==Reception==
===Sales===
According to [[Feargus Urquhart]], Interplay's commercial forecasts for ''Baldur's Gate'' were "very low". He noted that the publisher's headquarters in Britain predicted zero sales in that region.<ref name=mattchat1>{{cite web |url= https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=72Q0E6bQ_i0 |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211222/72Q0E6bQ_i0 |archive-date=2021-12-22 |url-status=live|title= Matt Chat 255: Feargus Urquhart on ''Baldur's Gate'', ''Shattered Steel'', and ''Fallout'' |last= Barton |first= Matt |date= August 30, 2014 |work= [[YouTube]] |access-date= January 21, 2019}}{{cbignore}}</ref> Lifetime projections for the German market were "no more than 50,000" copies, as reported by Udo Hoffman of ''[[PC Player (German magazine)|PC Player]]''.<ref name=pcp>{{cite magazine | author=Hoffman, Udo | title=NachSpiel; ''Baldur's Gate'' | language=de | magazine=[[PC Player (German magazine)|PC Player]] | date=May 1999 | page=50}}</ref> Internally, BioWare's worldwide sales goal was 200,000 units, a number that ''[[PC Zone]]''{{'}}s Dave Woods said would "justify work on the sequel".<ref name=pczonebg2>{{cite magazine | author=Woods, Dave | title=It's Time for Double-Damage... ''Baldur's Gate II: Shadows of Amn'' | date=January 2000 | issue=85 | magazine=[[PC Zone]] | pages=16, 17}}</ref> The game instead became an unexpected commercial hit.<ref name=mattchat1 /><ref name=pcp /> Ray Muzyka attributed this success in part to the ''Dungeons & Dragons'' license, and to the team's decision to use fan feedback during development, which he felt had increased the game's mass-market appeal.<ref name=pcp />

Following its shipment to retailers on December 21,<ref name="releasedate"/> ''Baldur's Gate'' began to sell at a "phenomenal rate", according to Mark Asher of ''[[CNET Gamecenter]]''. He wrote at the time that its "first run of 50,000 copies sold out immediately and Interplay's elves are working hard to get more games to the stores".<ref name=50k>{{cite web | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20001212134300/http://gamecenter.com/News/Item/0,3,0-2378,00.html | url=http://gamecenter.com/News/Item/0,3,0-2378,00.html | title=Game Spin: Retail Wrestling | author=Asher, Mark | date=December 31, 1998 | work=[[CNET Gamecenter]] | archive-date=December 12, 2000 | url-status = dead}}</ref> The title debuted in the United States at #3 on [[PC Data]]'s computer game sales rankings for the week ending on January 2, 1999.<ref name=week1>{{cite web | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20000229134100/http://headline.gamespot.com/news/99_01/12_pc_pcdata/index.html | url=http://headline.gamespot.com:80/news/99_01/12_pc_pcdata/index.html | title=''Brood War'' Tops PC Data List | author=Mullen, Micheal | date=January 12, 1999 | work=[[GameSpot]] | archive-date=February 29, 2000 | url-status = dead | access-date=June 2, 2019}}</ref> It [[Sell-through|sold-through]] 55,071 copies in the country by the end of 1998, for revenues of $2.56 million.<ref name=pcgsales2>{{cite magazine<!-- | author=Staff--> | date=April 1999 | volume=6 | issue=4 | title=The Numbers Game; Does Award Winner = Best Seller? | magazine=[[PC Gamer US]] | page=50}}</ref> In its second week, ''Baldur's Gate'' rose to #2 in the United States.<ref name=week2>{{cite web | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050406153004/http://www.cdmag.com/articles/016/180/pc_data_010399.html | url=http://www.cdmag.com:80/articles/016/180/pc_data_010399.html | title=''StarCraft: Brood Wars'' Tops Charts, ''Baldur's Gate'' Close Behind | author=Fudge, James | date=January 19, 1999 | work=[[Computer Games Magazine|Computer Games Strategy Plus]] | archive-date=April 6, 2005 | url-status = dead | access-date=July 22, 2018 | df=mdy-all}}</ref> Internationally, it debuted at #1 on {{Interlanguage link|Media Control|de}}'s computer game charts for the German market in the first half of January 1999,<ref name=jancharts>{{cite web | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/19990209014933/http://www.vud.de/charts/chart1.html | url=http://www.vud.de:80/charts/chart1.html | title=CD-ROM Spiele über DM 55,--; Stand 2. Sales of ''Baldur's Gate'' continued in 2000: by March, it had surpassed 500,000 copies sold in the United States, which led Desslock of ''[[GameSpot]]'' to describe the title as an "undisputed commercial blockbuster".<ref name=desslocksales2>{{cite web |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20010203124200/http://desslock.gamespot.com/archives/200005/20000511.html |url=http://desslock.gamespot.com:80/archives/200005/20000511.html |title=Desslock's Ramblings – RPG Sales Figures |author=Desslock |date=May 11, 2000 |work=[[GameSpot]] |archive-date=February 3, 2001 |url-status = dead}}</ref> U.S. sales had risen to 600,000 units by April 2001,<ref name=600k>{{cite web | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20020201192655/http://desslock.gamespot.com/archives/200104/200104.html#20010411-01 | url=http://desslock.gamespot.com:80/archives/200104/200104.html#20010411-01 | title=Desslock's Ramblings -- ''Heart of Winter'' Review and Editorial Follow-ups; Readers of the Week | author=Desslock | date=April 11, 2001 | work=[[GameSpot]] | archive-date=February 1, 2002 | url-status = dead | access-date=June 2, 2019}}</ref> while global sales totaled 1.5 million copies that May.<ref name=bg2postmortem>{{cite web | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120510051328/https://www.gamasutra.com/view/feature/131493/baldurs_gate_ii_the_anatomy_of_a_.php | url=https://www.gamasutra.com/view/feature/131493/baldurs_gate_ii_the_anatomy_of_a_.php | title=''Baldur's Gate II'': The Anatomy of a Sequel | author=Muzyka, Ray | author-link=Ray Muzyka | date=May 2, 2001 | work=[[Gamasutra]] | archive-date=May 10, 2012}}</ref> The game proceeded to sell 83,208 units in the United States from February 2001 through the first week of November alone.<ref name=desslock2001>{{cite web | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20011124191748/http://desslock.gamespot.com/#20011123-01 | url=http://desslock.gamespot.com/#20011123-01 | title=Desslock's Ramblings - ''Wizardry 8'' Arrives, Kinda; RPG Sales Stats Updated | author=Desslock | date=November 23, 2001 | work=[[GameSpot]] | archive-date=November 24, 2001 | url-status = dead}}</ref> Worldwide, ''Baldur's Gate'' ultimately surpassed 2.2 million sales by early 2003.<ref name=aboutbioware>{{cite web |url=http://www.bioware.com:80/bioware_info/about/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20030207041224/http://www.bioware.com/bioware_info/about/ |archive-date=February 7, 2003 |title=About BioWare |website=[[BioWare]] |access-date=July 25, 2009 |url-status=dead}}</ref> The game sold about 2.8 million copies by 2015.<ref>{{cite web|first=Carson|last=Jerema|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/89325400/edmonton-journal/|title=The resurrection of Baldur's Gate|newspaper=[[Edmonton Journal]]|page=33|date=July 11, 2015|accessdate=November 22, 2021|via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref> By 2006, total sales for all releases in the series was almost five million copies.<ref name=plunkett2009/>

}}

''Baldur's Gate'' received positive reviews from virtually every major computer gaming publication that reviewed it. At the time of the game's release, ''[[PC Gamer]] US'' said that ''Baldur's Gate'' "reigns supreme over every RPG currently available, and sets new standards for those to come".<ref name=pcgus/> ''[[Computer Shopper (US magazine)|Computer Shopper]]'' called it "clearly the best ''Advanced Dungeons & Dragons'' (AD&D) game ever to grace a PC screen".<ref name=computer-shopper>{{cite magazine |url= http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1G1-54299108.html |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20150329145358/http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1G1-54299108.html |url-status = usurped|archive-date= March 29, 2015 |author= Ryan, Michael E. |title= Baldur's Gate: Better Gate Than Never |magazine= [[Computer Shopper (US magazine)|Computer Shopper]] |date= May 1, 1999 |via= HighBeam Research |url-access= subscription |access-date= September 26, 2012}}</ref> ''[[Maximum PC]]'' magazine compared the gameplay to ''[[Diablo (video game)|Diablo]]'', but noted its more extensive selection of features and options. The pixel-based characters were panned, but the reviewer stated that "the gloriously rendered backgrounds make up for that shortcoming". The main criticism was of the problems with the [[path finding]] [[algorithm]] for [[non-player character]]s. Despite this, the game was deemed an "instant classic" because of the amount of customization allowed, the "fluid story lines", and the replayability.<ref name=maxpc/> The reviewer from ''[[Pyramid (magazine)|Pyramid]]'' felt that the "basic buzz was positive" surrounding the development of the game. The "actual results are a mixed bag, but there's real promise for the future" thanks to the inclusion of the Infinity Engine.<ref>{{cite web |work= [[Pyramid (magazine)|Pyramid]] |url= http://www.sjgames.com/pyramid/sample.html?id=593 |title= Baldur's Gate}}</ref>

''Baldur's Gate'' was awarded "[[D.I.C.E. Award for Role-Playing Game of the Year|PC Role-Playing Game of the Year]]" by the [[Academy of Interactive Arts & Sciences]] during the [[2nd Annual Interactive Achievement Awards]].<ref name=aias1998>{{cite web |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/19991104003923/http://www.interactive.org/iaa/finalists_pc.html |url=http://www.interactive.org:80/iaa/finalists_pc.html |title=Second Interactive Achievement Awards; Personal Computer |website=Interactive.org |publisher=[[Academy of Interactive Arts & Sciences]] |archive-date=November 4, 1999 |url-status = dead}}</ref> The game also won computer role-playing game awards by the [[Origins Award|Academy of Adventure Gaming Arts & Design]],<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.originsgamefair.com/awards/1998/list-of-winners |title=Origins Award Winners (1998) |website=Origins Game Fair |publisher=Academy of Adventure Gaming, Arts & Designs ==Legacy==
{{quote box|width=32%|align=right|quote="Just how big was Interplay's role-playing game ''Baldur's Gate''? Big enough to almost single-handedly revitalize the traditional RPG genre. Big enough to keep Interplay shareholders at least moderately appeased. And apparently big enough to spur new titles based on both its engine ... and its retail success".|author=—Gordon Goble of [[CNET Gamecenter]] in 1999<ref name=blackice>{{cite web | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20010211215855/http://www.gamecenter.com/News/Item/0,3,0-3267,00.html | url=http://www.gamecenter.com:80/News/Item/0,3,0-3267,00.html | title=Black Isle on Ice | author=Goble, Gordon | date=October 13, 1999 | work=[[CNET Gamecenter]] | archive-date=February 11, 2001 | url-status = dead | access-date=June 2, 2019}}</ref>}}
According to ''IGN'', ''Baldur's Gate'' did much to revive the role-playing video game genre.<ref name="IGN profile">{{cite web |title= Baldur's Gate (PC) |url= http://uk.pc.ign.com/objects/009/009942.html|work= [[IGN]]}}</ref> John Harris of ''Gamasutra'' wrote that it "rescued computer D&D from the wastebasket".<ref name="jharris" /> ''[[GameSpy]]'' said that ''Baldur's Gate'' was a "triumph" that "single-handedly revived" the computer role-playing game and "almost made gamers forgive Interplay for ''[[Descent to Undermountain]]''".<ref name="rauschIV">{{cite web |last=Rausch |first=Allen |date= August 18, 2004 |url= http://pc.gamespy.com/articles/540/540115p3.html |title=A History of ''D&D'' Video Games - Part IV |work= Game Spy |access-date= November 17, 2012}}</ref> IGN ranked ''Baldur's Gate'' number five on their list of "The Top 11 Dungeons & Dragons Games of All Time" in 2014.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.ign.com/articles/2014/02/05/the-top-11-dungeons-dragons-games-of-all-time|title=The Top 11 Dungeons & Dragons Games of All-Time|last=Johnson|first=Leif|date=February 5, 2014|website=IGN|language=en-US|access-date=December 10, 2017}}</ref> ''Baldur's Gate'' set the standard for other games using [[Editions of Dungeons & Dragons#Advanced Dungeons & Dragons|AD&D]] rules, especially those developed by [[BioWare]] and [[Black Isle Studios]]: ''[[Planescape: Torment]]'' (1999), ''[[Icewind Dale]]'' (2000), and ''[[Icewind Dale II]]'' (2002).

Phil Savage of ''[[PC Gamer]]'' praised Bioware's level design for the titular city in ''Baldur's Gate'', stating that "Baldur's Gate feels vast, exciting and dangerous—just like a proper city".<ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://www.pcgamer.com/best-cities-in-pc-games/ |title=Our favourite cities in PC gaming |magazine=PC Gamer |access-date=September 10, 2019}}</ref> Writing for ''Gamesradar'', Lorenzo Veloria cited ''Baldur's Gate'' as an influence on video games like ''[[Pillars of Eternity]]''.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.gamesradar.com/pillars-eternity-returns-classic-rpg-adventuring/|title=Pillars of Eternity brings back old-school, Baldur's Gate-style gameplay|author1=Lorenzo Veloria|date=July 24, 2014|website=gamesradar}}</ref> Scholarly analysis of ''Baldur's Gate'' has examined the game's use of party members as part of its approach to computer role-playing game storytelling. Rather than serving only as combat units, companions provide distinct personalities, viewpoints and conflicts that shape the player's experience through dialogue and party interactions.<ref>{{cite book |title=Computer Games: Text, Narrative and Play |publisher=Polity |year=2006}}</ref>

''Baldur's Gate'' was the first game in the [[Baldur's Gate (series)|''Baldur's Gate'' series]]. It was followed by the expansion pack ''[[Baldur's Gate: Tales of the Sword Coast|Tales of the Sword Coast]]'' (1999), then the sequel ''[[Baldur's Gate II: Shadows of Amn]]'' (2000) and its expansion pack ''[[Baldur's Gate II: Throne of Bhaal|Throne of Bhaal]]'' (2001). In 2023, ''[[Baldur's Gate 3]]'' developed by [[Larian Studios]] left early access and saw a full release on 3 August 2023.

======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Call of Cthulhu (role-playing game)
======================================================================

{{Short description|Tabletop horror role-playing game}}
{{Use mdy dates|date=August 2024}}
{{Italic title}}
{{Infobox game
| title = ''Call of Cthulhu''
| subtitle = Horror Roleplaying in the Worlds of H.P. Lovecraft
| logo = Call of Cthulhu RPG logo.png
| logo_caption = The ''Call of Cthulhu'' Logo
| image = Call of Cthulhu RPG 1st ed 1981.jpg
| caption = 1st edition box cover by [[Gene Day]], 1981
| designer = [[Sandy Petersen]]
| publisher = [[Chaosium]]
| date = {{Start date and age|1981|br=yes}}
| genre = [[Cosmic horror]]<br>[[Mystery fiction]]
| system = [[Basic Role-Playing]] (adaptations into other systems also available)
| web = {{URL|www.chaosium.com/call-of-cthulhu-rpg}}
| isbn = 978-1568824307
}}
[[File:CHA23135_-_Call_of_Cthulhu_7ed_Chaosium_RPG_supplement_2014_cover.jpg|thumb|7th edition cover by [[Sam Lamont]], 2014]]
'''''Call of Cthulhu''''' is a [[horror fiction]] [[role-playing game]] based on [[H. P. Lovecraft]]'s [[The Call of Cthulhu|story of the same name]] and the associated [[Cthulhu Mythos]].<ref name="HG">{{Cite book |last=Cook |first=Monte |title=[[Hobby Games: The 100 Best]] |publisher=[[Green Ronin Publishing]] |year=2007 |isbn=978-1-932442-96-0 |editor-last=Lowder |editor-first=James |editor-link=James Lowder |pages=42–45 |chapter=Call of Cthulhu |author-link=Monte Cook}}</ref> The game, often abbreviated as ''CoC'', is published by [[Chaosium]] and was originally created by [[Sandy Petersen]]; it was first released in 1981 and is in its seventh edition, with licensed foreign language editions available as well. Its game system is based on Chaosium's [[Basic Role-Playing]] (BRP) with additions for the [[horror genre]]. These include special rules for sanity and luck.<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Petersen |first1=Sandy |last2=Willis |first2=Lynn |title=Game Info: Call of Cthulhu |url=http://index.rpg.net/display-entry.phtml?mainid=20 |access-date=March 29, 2015 |website=RPG.net |publisher=Skotos Tech, Inc.}}</ref> It is one of the longest-running tabletop role-playing games still in publication.

In ''Call of Cthulhu'', players control ordinary people: investigators, typically in the game's default historical [[1920s]] setting, seeking to solve and uncover [[paranormal]] mysteries, usually linked to the [[Cthulhu Mythos]], and survive its deadly creatures that are harmful to their lives and the human psyche. At its release in 1981, the game was notable for its emphasis on [[psychological horror]], investigation, and character vulnerability rather than combat and heroic adventures, departing from the conventions of many contemporary role-playing games. Widely regarded as a pioneering horror role-playing game, it influenced numerous later games and helped establish horror as a major tabletop RPG genre.<ref name="mahg" />

''Call of Cthulhu'' has also been adapted for video, card and board games using the setting and the ''Call of Cthulhu'' brand. Some include ''[[Call of Cthulhu: The Card Game]]'', the [[board game]] ''[[Arkham Horror]]'', and [[video games]] ''[[Call of Cthulhu: Dark Corners of the Earth]]'' and [[Call of Cthulhu (video game)|''Call of Cthulhu (2018)'']].

==Gameplay==
===Setting===
''Call of Cthulhu'' is set in a [[Dark fantasy|darker]] version of our world based on H. P. Lovecraft's observation (from his essay, "[[Supernatural Horror in Literature]]") that "The oldest and strongest emotion of mankind is fear, and the oldest and strongest kind of fear is fear of the unknown." The original edition, first published in 1981, uses [[Basic Role-Playing]] as its basis and is set in the 1920s, the setting of many of Lovecraft's stories. Many supplements expanded the game's setting beyond the original 1920s to different historical periods and otherworldly locales. The ''[[Cthulhu by Gaslight]]'' supplement blends the occult and [[Sherlock Holmes|Holmesian]] mystery and is mostly set in England during the 1890s. ''[[Cthulhu Now]]'' and ''[[Delta Green]]'' are set in a modern/1980s era and deal with conspiracies. Recent settings include 1000 AD (''Cthulhu: Dark Ages''), the 23rd century (''Cthulhu Rising'') and Ancient Rome (''Cthulhu Invictus''). The protagonists may also travel to places that are not of this earth, such as the [[Dreamlands]] (which can be accessed through dreams as well as being physically connected to the earth), [[Carcosa]], other planets, or the voids of space. In keeping with the Lovecraftian theme, the [[gamemaster]] is called the Keeper of Arcane Lore ("the keeper"), while [[player character]]s are called Investigators of the Unknown ("investigators").

While predominantly focused on Lovecraftian fiction and horror, playing in the Cthulhu Mythos is not required. The system also includes ideas for non-Lovecraft games, such as using [[folklore|folk horror]] or the settings of other authors and horror movies, or with entirely custom settings and creatures by the gamemaster and/or players.

===Mechanics===
[[File:King-in-Yellow-Earl-Geier.jpg|thumb|"[[The King in Yellow]]", illustration by Earl Geier for the ''Fatal Experiments'' adventure book. The Yellow Sign adorning the back of the throne was designed by Kevin A. Ross for the ''Call of Cthulhu'' scenario ''Tell Me, Have You Seen the Yellow Sign?'']]
''CoC'' uses the [[Basic Role-Playing]] system first developed for ''[[RuneQuest]]'' and used in other Chaosium games. It is skill-based, with player characters getting better with their skills by succeeding at using them for as long as they stay functionally healthy and sane. They do not, however, gain hit points and do not become significantly harder to kill. The game does not use [[Experience point#Level-based progression|level]]s.

''CoC'' uses [[Dice notation#Percentile dice (d%)|percentile dice]] (with results ranging from 1 to 100) to determine success or failure. Every player statistic is intended to be compatible with the notion that there is a probability of success for a particular action given what the player is capable of doing. For example, an artist may have a 75% chance of being able to draw something (represented by having 75 in Art skill), and thus rolling a number under 75 would yield a success. Rolling {{fract|1|5}} or less of the skill level (1–15 in the example) would be a "special success" (or an "impale" for combat skills) and would yield some extra bonus to be determined by the keeper. For example, the artist character might draw especially well or especially fast, or catch some unapparent detail in the drawing.

The players take the roles of ordinary people drawn into the realm of the mysterious: detectives, criminals, scholars, artists, war veterans, etc. Often, happenings begin innocently enough, until more and more of the workings behind the scenes are revealed. As the characters learn more of the true horrors of the world and the irrelevance of humanity, their sanity (represented by "Sanity Points", abbreviated SAN) inevitably withers away. The game includes a mechanism for determining how damaged a character's sanity is at any given point; encountering the horrific beings usually triggers a loss of SAN points. To gain the tools they need to defeat the horrors – mystic knowledge and magic – the characters may end up losing some of their sanity, though other means such as pure firepower or simply outsmarting one's opponents also exist. ''CoC'' has a reputation as a game in which it is quite common for a player character to die in gruesome circumstances or end up in a mental institution. Eventual triumph of the players is not guaranteed.

==History==
The original conception of ''Call of Cthulhu'' was ''Dark Worlds'', a game commissioned by the publisher Chaosium but never published.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Maliszewski |first=James |date=August 16, 2010 |title=The Prehistory of Call of Cthulhu |url=http://grognardia.blogspot.com/2010/08/prehistory-of-call-of-cthulhu.html |access-date=February 22, 2023 |website=GROGNARDIA}}</ref> [[Sandy Petersen]] contacted them regarding writing a supplement for their popular fantasy game ''[[RuneQuest]]'' set in Lovecraft's [[Dreamlands]]. He took over the writing of ''Call of Cthulhu'', and the game was released in 1981.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Turnbull |first=Don |date=August 1982 |title=Open Box: Call of Cthulhu |journal=[[White Dwarf (magazine)|White Dwarf]] |publisher=[[Games Workshop]] |issue=32 |pages=18 |issn=0265-8712}}</ref> Petersen oversaw the first four editions with only minor changes to the system. Once he left, development was continued by [[Lynn Willis]], who was credited as co-author in the fifth and sixth editions. After the death of Willis, Mike Mason became ''Call of Cthulhu'' line editor in 2013, continuing its development with Paul Fricker. Together they made the most significant rules alterations, more so than in any previous edition, culminating in the release of the 7th edition in 2014.<ref name="Inside Call of Cthulhu 7th Edition">{{Cite web |last=Ivey |first=Shane |author-link=Shane Ivey |date=July 24, 2012 |title=Inside Call of Cthulhu 7th Edition |url=http://theunspeakableoath.com/home/?p=1024 |access-date=January 25, 2013 |publisher=The Unspeakable Oath |archive-date=March 28, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130328020340/http://theunspeakableoath.com/home/?p=1024 |url-status=dead }}</ref>
