== Plot ==
The interview tapes feature a woman who introduces herself as Hannah Smith (portrayed by [[Viva Seifert]]), whose husband, Simon, has gone missing and is later found murdered. Hannah admits that she and Simon had argued, but has an [[alibi]] placing her in [[Glasgow]] when Simon disappeared. As more pieces of the interviews are discovered, it is claimed that "Hannah" is actually two women: Hannah and Eve, [[identical twins]] separated at birth by the midwife, Florence. Florence desperately wanted to have kids but did not believe in remarrying after her husband died, so she faked Eve's death to claim the baby for herself. Florence deliberately kept Eve indoors as much as possible and the twins were unaware of each other's existence until years later. When Florence died, Eve secretly moved in with Hannah and they decided to act as a single person, keeping a common diary and a set of rules defining their actions as "Hannah". Hannah's parents were oblivious, assuming Eve was Hannah's imaginary friend.<ref name="Walkthrough">{{cite web|url=http://www.pocketgamer.co.uk/r/iPhone/Her+Story/feature.asp?c=66078 |title=Her Story explained – the complete story walkthrough (Spoilers!) |last=Brown |first=Mark |authorlink=Game Maker's Toolkit |work=[[Pocket Gamer]] |publisher=Steel Media |date=25 June 2015 |access-date=14 January 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160115230848/http://www.pocketgamer.co.uk/r/iPhone/Her+Story/feature.asp?c=66078 |archive-date=15 January 2016 |url-status=live  }}</ref>

Hannah eventually began dating Simon, whom she had met at a [[glazier]] where they both worked. Despite their rules to share equally, Hannah slept with Simon and became pregnant. She gradually became possessive of Simon and forbade Eve from interacting with him. Because of the pregnancy, Hannah and Simon were married and moved in together while Eve moved out to her own apartment and began wearing a wig. Hannah miscarried in her eighth month and believed she was [[infertile]] afterward. Some time later, Simon encountered Eve in a bar she was singing at. Smitten by her resemblance, the two began an affair. Eve became pregnant but never told Simon and hid the identity of the father from Hannah.

On their birthday, after Simon gifted Hannah a handmade mirror, she revealed the existence of Eve and her pregnancy. Hannah realised Simon was the father of Eve's child. After kicking Simon out of the house, she argued with Eve over the affair, causing the latter to leave for Glasgow. Simon returned and, thinking Hannah was Eve, gifted her a similar handmade mirror and professed his desire to be with Eve instead of Hannah. Hannah became furious and revealed her identity. She later claims that, as they fought, she shattered the mirror and inadvertently cut Simon's throat with it while fending him off. When Eve returned, she found Hannah sitting next to Simon's lifeless body. Agreeing that Eve's baby was the priority, they hid Simon's body and agreed to use Eve's trip to Glasgow as an alibi.<ref name="Walkthrough"/>

At the end of the final interview, Eve says that Hannah is "gone ... and she's never coming back" but mockingly asks "can you arrest someone who doesn't exist?".<ref>{{cite video game |title=Her Story |developer=[[Sam Barlow (game designer)|Sam Barlow]] |date=24 June 2015 |platform=[[Windows]] |version=1.0 |scene=D769 |quote=My sister is gone. And she's never coming back. }}</ref><ref>{{cite video game |title=Her Story |developer=[[Sam Barlow (game designer)|Sam Barlow]] |date=6 March 2022 |platform=[[Windows]] |version=1.0 |scene=D770 |quote=Can you arrest someone who doesn't exist? }}</ref> She then requests a lawyer, and says that her comments are just "stories".<ref>{{cite video game |title=Her Story |developer=[[Sam Barlow (game designer)|Sam Barlow]] |date=24 June 2015 |platform=[[Windows]] |version=1.0 |scene=D771 |quote=I'd like to speak to a lawyer now. Please. You have no murder weapon. You have nothing. And all these stories we've been telling each other? Just that ... stories.}}</ref> It is unclear if Eve's story of being an identical twin is true, an intentional fabrication meant to confuse the police, or a case of [[dissociative identity disorder]], with pieces of evidence lending credence to each theory.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.rockpapershotgun.com/2015/06/25/her-story-verdict-analysis/ |title=In Conversation: RPS Discusses Her Story |work=[[Rock, Paper, Shotgun]] |date=25 June 2015 |access-date=29 April 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170924224702/https://www.rockpapershotgun.com/2015/06/25/her-story-verdict-analysis/ |archive-date=24 September 2017 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.thunderboltgames.com/opinion/her-story-the-unreliable-narrator |title=Her Story: The unreliable narrator |last=Kemph |first=Calvin |publisher=Thunderbolt |date=29 September 2015 |access-date=29 April 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170708162104/http://www.thunderboltgames.com/opinion/her-story-the-unreliable-narrator |archive-date=8 July 2017 |url-status=dead }}</ref> As the player uncovers enough of the story, a chat window appears asking if they are finished. Upon answering affirmatively, it is revealed that the player is Sarah, Eve's daughter. The chat asks Sarah if she understands her mother's actions, and asks to meet her outside.<ref>{{cite video game |title=Her Story |developer=[[Sam Barlow (game designer)|Sam Barlow]] |date=24 June 2015 |platform=[[Windows]] |version=1.0 }}</ref>

== Development ==
[[File:Sam Barlow headshot (cropped).png|thumb|upright|[[Sam Barlow (game designer)|Sam Barlow]] left [[Climax Studios]] and became an [[Independent video game development|independent developer]] to work on ''Her Story''.<ref name="Develop"/>|alt=Headshot of a man with short brown hair, smiling at the camera.]]

''Her Story'' was developed by [[Sam Barlow (game designer)|Sam Barlow]], who previously worked on games such as ''[[Silent Hill: Origins]]'' (2007) and ''[[Silent Hill: Shattered Memories]]'' (2009) at [[Climax Studios]]. Barlow had conceived the idea of a police procedural game while working at Climax Studios, but decided to become [[Independent video game development|independent]] to create the game,<ref name="Develop"/> in order to develop a game that is "deep on story".<ref name="Edge"/> He became frustrated by publishers rejecting game pitches for being "too [[kitchen sink realism|kitchen sink [realism]]]" in favor of video game tropes like a "cyborg assassin from the future", and found that becoming independent allowed him to create his own game of the sort.<ref name="Vice"/> He also wished to become independent after playing games like ''[[Year Walk]]'' (2013) and ''[[80 Days (2014 video game)|80 Days]]'' (2014).<ref name="Gamesindustry"/> Barlow avoided development until he had an idea that was possible to execute. "I could probably quite easily have gone and made an exploration horror game ... but I kind of knew that there would be big compromises there because of budget," he said.<ref name="Develop"/> Barlow spent his savings to work on the game, allowing him a year of development time.<ref name="GamesRadar"/> He followed through with the concept of ''Her Story'', as it focused on an "intimate setting, dialogue and character interaction", which he found was often dismissed in larger titles.<ref name="Develop"/> Barlow felt particularly inspired to develop ''Her Story'' after seeing the continuous support of his 1999 game ''[[Aisle (video game)|Aisle]]''.<ref name="Gamesindustry"/> When referring to how ''Her Story'' challenges typical game conventions, Barlow compares it to the [[Dogme 95]] filmmaking movement, and [[Alfred Hitchcock]]'s 1948 film ''[[Rope (film)|Rope]]''.<ref name="Virgin"/>

''Her Story'' was approved through [[Steam Greenlight]], and was [[crowdfunded]] by [[Indie Fund]]. It was released on 24 June 2015 for [[iOS]], [[OS X]], and [[Windows]].<ref name="Polygon Release"/> Barlow wanted to launch the game on all platforms simultaneously, as he was unsure where the audience would be.<ref name="Pocket Gamer"/> "If I'd just gone for just one I'd have lost a lot of the potential audience," he commented.<ref name="App Unwrapper"/> Barlow found that playing ''Her Story'' on mobile devices is a "'sofa' experience".<ref name="MCV"/> He also noted that it felt "natural" for it to be released on mobile devices, as they are regularly used to watch videos and search the internet; similar tasks are used as gameplay mechanics in ''Her Story''.<ref name="MCV"/> The [[iPhone]]'s smaller pixel size of 640×480 as opposed to 800×600 led to Barlow's doubts of a release on the platform, but he was influenced to release it upon receiving positive feedback through [[Game testing|testing]].<ref name="App Unwrapper"/> As development neared completion, the game underwent testing, which allowed Barlow to "balance some aspects" and "polish items together".<ref name="Taylor Holmes"/> An [[Android (operating system)|Android]] version was released on 29 June 2016.<ref name="Eurogamer Android"/> ''Her Story'' runs on the [[Unity (game engine)|Unity]] [[game engine]].<ref name="Gamasutra IGF"/>

=== Gameplay design ===
[[File:Her Story screenshot 04.jpg|thumb|left|Barlow decided to implement live action footage into the game after becoming frustrated with the technical challenge of translating an actor's performance into a [[game engine]].<ref name="PC Gamer 1"/>|alt=Old computer footage of a 37-year-old woman with long brown hair in a red jacket, sitting at a police interview desk. She is holding her hands together in front of her, and is looking to the right of the camera.]]

Barlow described the game as a "desktop thriller".<ref name="Eurogamer"/> His immediate idea was to create a game involving police interviews, but he "didn't know exactly what that meant".<ref name="Pocket Gamer"/> He then conceived the idea to involve real video footage, and the ability to access the footage through a database interface; he described the interface as being "part [[Apple II]], part [[Windows 3.1]] and part [[Windows 98]]".<ref name="Pocket Gamer"/> The interface design was inspired by Barlow's appreciation of the police procedural genre, commenting that "the conceit of making the computer itself a prop in the game was so neat".<ref name="Guardian"/> He also compared the searching mechanic to the [[Google Search|Google]] search engine, and wanted to "run with the idea" that the player is "essentially Googling".<ref name="Guardian"/> The game's concept was inspired by the TV series ''[[Homicide: Life on the Street]]'' (1993–1999), which Barlow found depicted police interviews being a "gladiatorial arena for detectives".<ref name="Develop"/> Barlow intentionally made the game's opening screen to be "slightly too long", to immediately notify the player of the slow pacing that would follow.<ref name="Fantastic Arcade"/>

Inspiration to work on ''Her Story'' stemmed from Barlow's disappointment of other detectives games: he felt that ''[[L.A. Noire]]'' (2011) never allowed him to feel like "the awesome detective who was having to read things and follow up threads of investigation", and he called the [[Ace Attorney|''Ace Attorney'' series]] (2001–present) "rigid".<ref name="Eurogamer"/> When Barlow began development on ''Her Story'', he added more typical game aspects, but the game mechanics became more minimalist as development progressed.<ref name="RPS"/> The initial plan for the game was for the player to work towards a definitive resolution, ultimately solving the crime. However, when Barlow tested the concept on pre-existing interview transcripts of convicted murderer [[Christopher Porco]], he began to discover themes surfacing within the interviews,<ref name="PC Gamer 2"/> particularly relating to the concept of money, which was ultimately a large factor in Porco's trial.<ref name="Kotaku"/> He took this concept of recurring themes and threads, and decided to "move beyond the clearly scripted stuff" when developing ''Her Story''.<ref name="PC Gamer 2"/> Barlow felt that the story's appeal was the ambiguity of the investigation, comparing ''Her Story'' to the podcast ''[[Serial (podcast)|Serial]]'' (2014–present), which he listened to late in development. He found that the attraction of ''Serial'' was the lack of a definitive solution, noting that "people lean towards certain interpretations ... what makes it interesting is the extent to which it lives on in your imagination".<ref name="PC Gamer 2"/>

=== Story and characters ===
[[File:Her Story (video game) - VHS footage development.JPG|thumb|right|After the filming was complete, Barlow ran the footage through two [[VHS player]]s, to make it resemble video from the time period of 1994.<ref name="Pocket Gamer"/>|alt=A laptop with the game footage sits atop two VHS players. Wires connect them to another laptop nearby, with a VHS cartridge to the right.]]

Barlow decided to feature live action footage in the game after becoming frustrated with his previous projects, particularly with the technical challenge of translating an actor's performance into a game engine.<ref name="PC Gamer 1"/> Barlow set out to work with an actor on ''Her Story'', having enjoyed the process while working at Climax Studios, albeit with a larger budget.<ref name="Develop"/> He contacted [[Viva Seifert]], whom he had intermittently worked with on ''[[Legacy of Kain: Dead Sun]]'' for a year, before its cancellation.<ref name="PC Gamer 1"/> He felt that Seifert is "very good at picking up a line and intuitively pulling a lot of the subtext into her performance", which led him to believe that she was "perfect" for the role in ''Her Story''.<ref name="Game Mob"/> When Barlow asked Seifert to audition, he sent her a 300-page script, which he managed to reduce to 80 pages, by altering font size, as well as some dialogue; she accepted the role.<ref name="PC Gamer 1"/>

Seifert began to feel pressure midway through filming, when she realised that "the whole game is hinging" on her performance.<ref name="PC Gamer 1"/> She described the shoot as "intense" and "rather exhausting", and felt as if she was "subtly being scrutinised" by Barlow, which helped her performance.<ref name="App Unwrapper 2"/> Barlow also felt that the intensity helped Seifert's performance, taking cues from director Alfred Hitchcock, who would upset his actors in order to achieve the greatest performance.<ref name="Kotaku"/> Seifert felt that there were small nuances in her performance that may have "added some twists and turns" for the player that Barlow had not anticipated.<ref name="App Unwrapper 2"/> The game's seven police interviews were filmed roughly in chronological order<ref name="PC Gamer 2"/> over five days,<ref name="App Unwrapper 2"/> in a process that Barlow called "natural".<ref name="App Unwrapper"/> Like Seifert though, Barlow thought the shoot was intense, remarking "at the end of the shoot, it was just a huge relief it was all over and we hadn't forgotten to record or anything."<ref name="E283" /> Barlow travelled to Seifert's home county of [[Cornwall]] to film.<ref name="App Unwrapper 2"/> He felt that finding the locations for the interrogation rooms was the simplest part of production, because "everywhere has crappy looking rooms", with footage being recorded in a council building in [[Truro]].<ref name="GamesRadar"/><ref name="PC Gamer 2"/> When filming was complete, Barlow wanted to give the impression that the videos had been recorded in 1994, but found [[digital filter]]s were unable to capture this time frame appropriately. Instead, he recorded the footage through two [[VHS player]]s to create imperfections in the video before digitising the video into the game.<ref name="Pocket Gamer"/><ref name="Gamasutra IGF"/>

Barlow played the part of the detectives during filming, asking scripted questions to Seifert's character,<ref name="Polygon"/> but is never featured in ''Her Story''.<ref name="PC Gamer 2"/> When watching police interviews for research, Barlow found himself empathising with the interviewee, which inspired him to exclude the detective from the game. He stated that the interviews typically feature "double betrayal", in which the detectives are "pretending to be the best friend".<ref name="PC Gamer 3"/> Barlow felt that removing the detective from the game empowers Seifert's character, allowing the player to empathise.<ref name="PC Gamer 3"/> When conducting research for ''Her Story'', Barlow looked at the case regarding the [[murder of Travis Alexander]], which made him consider the manner that female murder suspects are treated in interrogations, stating that they "tend to be fetishised, more readily turned into archetypes".<ref name="Pocket Gamer"/> This was further proved to Barlow when studying the interviews of [[Casey Anthony]] and [[Amanda Knox]]; he found that media commentary often ignored the evidence of the investigation, instead focusing on the expressions of the suspects during the interviews.<ref name="LA Times"/> Barlow conducted further research by studying texts about [[psychology]], and the use of language.<ref name="Gamesindustry"/>

After conceiving the game's main mechanics, Barlow began developing the story, conducting research and "letting [the story] take on a life of its own".<ref name="Pocket Gamer"/> To develop the story, Barlow placed the script into a [[spreadsheet]], which became so large it often [[Crash (computing)|crashed]] his laptop upon opening it.<ref name="GamesRadar"/> He mapped out every character involved in the investigation, including their backstories and agendas.<ref name="Kotaku"/> He spent about half of development creating detailed documents charting the story's characters and events.<ref name="Gamesindustry"/> He also determined the dates on which the police interviews would take place, and what the suspect was doing in the interim.<ref name="Kotaku"/> Once he had determined the game's concept more precisely, Barlow ensured the script contained "layers of intrigue", in order to interest the player to finish the game.<ref name="Develop"/> Barlow often replaced words of the script with synonyms, to ensure that some clips were not associated with irrelevant words.<ref name="Develop"/> When writing the script, Barlow generally avoided [[supernatural]] themes, but realised that it would involve a "slight dreamlike surreal edge".<ref name="IB Times"/> Working on the script, he often found that he was "very much in the moment, writing from inside the characters' heads".<ref name="Vice"/> He found it difficult to create a new idea for the story, as detective fiction has been explored many times before.<ref name="Game Mob"/>

{{Listen |pos=right |filename=The 49th Street Galleria - Chris Zabriskie.ogg |title="The 49th Street Galleria" |description=[[Chris Zabriskie]]'s "The 49th Street Galleria" was used as the game's opening theme. |alt1=The track is a slow piano piece, with some organ being played in the middle. |filename2=That Kid in Fourth Grade Who Really Liked the Denver Broncos - Chris Zabriskie.ogg|title2="That Kid in Fourth Grade Who Really Liked the Denver Broncos" |description2="That Kid in Fourth Grade Who Really Liked the Denver Broncos", composed by Zabriskie, was used in the game's closing credits. |alt2=The track is a slow piano piece. }}

=== Audio ===
When searching for music to use in ''Her Story'', Barlow looked for songs that sounded "slightly out-of-time".<ref name="App Unwrapper"/> He ultimately used eight tracks from musician [[Chris Zabriskie]],<ref name="Sound"/> and found that his music invoked nostalgia, and had a "modern edge".<ref name="App Unwrapper"/> He felt that the music "highlights the gap between the 'fake computer world'" and the game.<ref name="Pocket Gamer"/> The "emotional intensity" of the clips also influences the music changes in ''Her Story''.<ref name="Vice"/> Barlow also intended to feature a song for Seifert to sing in some of the clips that fit within the game. He settled on the murder ballad "[[The Twa Sisters]]", which he felt would trigger the mythical elements of the game.<ref name="App Unwrapper"/> Seifert and Barlow both altered the ballad, to fit the game.<ref name="App Unwrapper 2"/> Barlow intended for the sound design to be "all about authenticity".<ref name="Pocket Gamer"/> He used an old keyboard to provide sound effects for the computer, using [[stereo panning]] for the keys to have the correct 3D position in playback.<ref name="Pocket Gamer"/>

===Sequel===
{{main|Telling Lies (video game) {{!}} ''Telling Lies'' (video game)}}
''Telling Lies'' was Barlow's [[spiritual sequel]] to ''Her Story'';<ref name="PC Gamer TL"/> rather than focusing on one central character, it features live-action footage from the video conversations of four characters (played by [[Logan Marshall-Green]], [[Alexandra Shipp]], [[Kerry Bishé]], and [[Angela Sarafyan]]), and requires the player to piece together events by searching the video clips to determine why these characters were under surveillance. The game was published by [[Annapurna Interactive]] on Windows and macOS systems on 23 August 2019.<ref name="Polygon TL"/>

{{Clear}}

== Reception ==
=== Critical reception ===
{{Video game reviews
| MC        = (iOS) 91/100<ref name="MC"/><br />(PC) 86/100<ref name="MC"/>
| AdvGamers = 4/5<ref name="Adventure Gamers Review"/>
| Destruct  = 10/10<ref name="Destructoid Review"/>
| Edge      = 9/10<ref name="E283"/>
| GI        = 8.5/10<ref name="Game Informer Review"/>
| GSpot     = 8/10<ref name="GameSpot Review"/>
| GB        = 4/5<ref name="Giant Bomb Review"/>
| IGN       = 8.5/10<ref name="IGN Review"/>
| PCGUS     = 90/100<ref name="PC Gamer Review"/>
| Poly      = 8.5/10<ref name="Polygon Review"/>
| VG        = 8/10<ref name="VideoGamer Review"/>
}}
''Her Story'' received "universal acclaim" for the iOS and "generally favorable" reviews for Windows, according to [[review aggregator]] website [[Metacritic]].<ref name="MC"/> Praise was directed at the narrative,<ref name="Game Informer Review"/><ref name="Polygon Review"/><ref name="Telegraph Review"/> gameplay mechanics,<ref name="Destructoid Review"/><ref name="Game Informer Review"/><ref name="VideoGamer Review"/> and Seifert's performance.<ref name="Adventure Gamers Review"/><ref name="GameSpot Review"/><ref name="PC Gamer Review"/> ''[[IGN]]''{{'}}s Brian Albert called ''Her Story'' "the most unique game I've played in years",<ref name="IGN Review"/> and Steven Burns of ''VideoGamer.com'' named it "one of the year's best and most interesting games".<ref name="VideoGamer Review"/> Adam Smith of ''[[Rock, Paper, Shotgun]]'' remarked that it "might be the best [[Full motion video|FMV]] game ever made";<ref name="RPS Review"/> Michael Thomsen of ''[[The Washington Post]]'' declared it "a beautiful amalgam of the cinema and video game formats".<ref name="Washington Post Review"/>

Critics lauded the game's narrative. ''[[Edge (magazine)|Edge]]'' considered it "a superlatively told work of crime fiction."<ref name="E283">{{cite magazine | author=<!--Staff writer(s); no by-line--> | title=Her Story| magazine=[[Edge (magazine)|Edge]] | publisher=[[Future plc|Future]] | issue=283 | date= September 2015 | pages=110–112 | issn=1350-1593}}</ref> Kimberley Wallace of ''[[Game Informer]]'' wrote that the "fragmented" delivery of the story "works to its benefit".<ref name="Game Informer Review"/> She appreciated the subtlety of the narrative, and the ambiguity surrounding the ending.<ref name="Game Informer Review"/> ''[[Polygon (website)|Polygon]]''{{'}}s Megan Farokhmanesh noted that ''Her Story'' "nails the dark, voyeuristic nature of true crime".<ref name="Polygon Review"/> Chris Schilling of ''[[The Daily Telegraph]]'' was impressed by the coherence of the narrative, "even when presented out of order".<ref name="Telegraph Review"/> ''[[Eurogamer]]''{{'}}s Simon Parkin found the effects of the narrative to be similar to well-received [[HBO]] thrillers, particularly in terms of audience attention.<ref name="Eurogamer Review"/> [[Stephanie Bendixsen]] of ''[[Good Game (TV program)|Good Game]]'' was disappointed that large plot points were revealed early in the game, but attributed this to the uniqueness of each player's experience.<ref name="Good Game Review"/>

[[File:Viva Seifert, Rough Trade East 2009.png|thumb|left|upright|Musician [[Viva Seifert]]'s performance as the lead character was praised by critics.<ref name="Adventure Gamers Review" /><ref name="GameSpot Review" /><ref name="PC Gamer Review" />|alt=A 32-year-old woman with long brown hair, and a yellow and brown outfit. She is playing drums, and is surrounded by music equipment.]]

Seifert's performance in the game received praise. ''[[GameSpot]]''{{'}}s Justin Clark felt that the performance "anchored" the game.<ref name="GameSpot Review"/> Chris Kohler of ''[[Wired (magazine)|Wired]]'' similarly described Seifert's performance as "so captivating that I couldn't imagine this game working any other way".<ref name="Wired Review"/> Katie Smith of ''[[Adventure Gamers]]'' wrote that Seifert is convincing in the role, particularly with small details such as body language, but was startled by the lack of emotion.<ref name="Adventure Gamers Review"/> ''Game Informer''{{'}}s Wallace echoed similar remarks, noting that Seifert "nailed the role".<ref name="Game Informer Review"/> ''Rock, Paper, Shotgun''{{'}}s Smith wrote that "the whole thing might collapse" without Seifert's "convincing" performance.<ref name="RPS Review"/> ''IGN''{{'}}s Albert named the acting "believable", stating that Seifert's performance is "appropriately both grounded and absurd".<ref name="IGN Review"/> Joe Donnelly of ''[[Digital Spy]]'' wrote that Seifert's performance has the potential to inspire similar games,<ref name="Digital Spy Review"/> and Andy Kelly of ''[[PC Gamer]]'' called the performance "understated, realistic, and complex".<ref name="PC Gamer Review"/> Burns of ''VideoGamer.com'' felt generally impressed by Seifert's performance, but noted some "occasional bad acting".<ref name="VideoGamer Review"/> Rich Stanton of ''[[The Guardian]]'' wrote that "Seifert's delivery is usually matter-of-fact and emotionally convincing".<ref name="Guardian Review"/> ''Polygon'' named Hannah among the best video game characters of the 2010s, dubbing Seifert's performance as "superbly".<ref name="Polygon Characters"/>

The unconventional gameplay mechanics also received positive remarks from critics. ''[[Destructoid]]''{{'}}s [[Laura Kate Dale]] felt that the game's pacing and structure assisted the narrative,<ref name="Destructoid Review" /> and Wallace of ''Game Informer'' found that making a connection between key points in the narrative was entertaining.<ref name="Game Informer Review" /> Burns of ''VideoGamer.com'' praised the game's ability to make the player realise their own biases, and challenge their "sense of self".<ref name="VideoGamer Review" /> Albert of ''IGN'' felt that the searching tool was "gratifying", and positively contributes to the pacing of the game,<ref name="IGN Review" /> while ''The Washington Post''{{'}}s Thomsen wrote that the database mechanic created "contemplative gaps between scenes", allowing for "poignance and power" within the narrative.<ref name="Washington Post Review" /> ''Edge'' thought that by having game mechanics which require the player to deduce the story through investigation and intuition, ''Her Story'' was one of few games "that truly deliver on the foundational fantasy of detective work."<ref name="E283" /> Bendixsen of ''Good Game'' described the desktop as "appropriately [[retro]]", noting that she was "drawn in immediately".<ref name="Good Game Review" />

The game sold over 100,000 copies by 10 August 2015;<ref name="100K" /> about 60,000 copies were sold on Windows, with the remaining 40,000 sold on iOS.<ref name="Pocket Gamer" /> Barlow stated that the game's instant popularity surprised him, as he had instead expected the game to slowly spread by word of mouth "and maybe over six months it would pay for itself."<ref name="E283" />

=== Accolades ===
''Her Story'' has received multiple nominations and awards from [[gaming publications]]. It won [[List of Game of the Year awards|Game of the Year]] from ''Polygon'',<ref name="Polygon GOTY"/> as well as Game of the Month from ''Rock, Paper, Shotgun''<ref name="RPS GOTM"/> and GameSpot.<ref name="GSpot GOTM"/> It received the Breakthrough Award at the 33rd [[Golden Joystick Award]]s,<ref name="Golden Joystick"/> [[British Academy Video Games Award for Debut Game|Debut Game]] and Game Innovation at the [[12th British Academy Games Awards]],<ref name="BAFTA"/> the award for Most Original game from ''[[PC Gamer]]'',<ref name="PC Gamer Awards"/> and the [[Seumas McNally Grand Prize]] at the [[Independent Games Festival]] Awards.<ref name="IGFwinners"/> At [[The Game Awards 2015]], ''Her Story'' won Best Narrative, and Seifert won Best Performance for her role in the game;<ref name="The Game Awards"/> she also won the Great White Way Award for Best Acting in a Game at the 5th Annual [[New York Game Awards]].<ref name="NYGA"/> ''Her Story'' won Best Emotional Mobile & Handheld at the Emotional Games Awards 2016,<ref name="EGA"/> Mobile Game of the Year at the [[SXSW Gaming Awards]],<ref name="SXSW"/> Mobile & Handheld at the British Academy Games Awards,<ref name="BAFTA"/> and awards for excellence in story and innovation at the International Mobile Gaming Awards,<ref name="IMGA"/> while ''The Guardian'' named it the best iOS game of 2015,<ref name="Guardian 2015"/> In 2015, ''[[Edge (magazine)|Edge]]'' ranked ''Her Story'' as 94th in their list of the greatest videogames of all time.<ref>{{cite magazine |title=The 100 Greatest Videogames |date=2015 |magazine=[[Edge (magazine)|Edge]] |publisher=[[Future plc|Future]] |isbn=978178389244-0 |location=Bath, UK |page=20 }}</ref>

WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: It Takes Two (video game)
======================================================================

{{Short description|2021 video game}}
{{good article}}

| released = '''PS4, PS5, Windows, Xbox One, Xbox Series X/S'''{{Video game release|WW|March 26, 2021}}'''Nintendo Switch'''{{Video game release|WW|November 4, 2022}}'''Nintendo Switch 2'''{{vgrelease|WW|October 15, 2026}}

'''''It Takes Two''''' is a 2021 cooperative [[action-adventure game]] developed by [[Hazelight Studios]] and published by [[Electronic Arts]]. It was released for [[PlayStation 4]], [[PlayStation 5]], [[Windows]], [[Xbox One]], and [[Xbox Series X/S]] in March 2021, for [[Nintendo Switch]] in November 2022, and for [[Nintendo Switch 2]] in October 2026. The game follows Cody and May, a husband and wife on the brink of divorce whose daughter unknowingly transports their consciousnesses into handmade dolls, forcing to work together as they try to repair their relationship and return to their human bodies.

The game is designed around two-player cooperative multiplayer, playable either online or locally in [[Split screen (computer graphics)|split-screen]]. Gameplay combines [[Platform game|platforming]], [[Puzzle video game|puzzle-solving]], and action elements, with both players receiving different abilities that must be used together to progress. Each level introduces new mechanics tied to the story and setting, while optional [[minigame]]s provide competitive diversions between the two players. [[Josef Fares]] directed the game, which Hazelight developed around collaboration as its central design theme.

''It Takes Two'' received critical acclaim, with reviewers praising its cooperative design, mechanical variety, creativity, and connection between gameplay and story. It won multiple year-end awards, including Game of the Year awards at [[The Game Awards 2021]] and the [[25th Annual D.I.C.E. Awards]]. By April 2026, the game had sold over 30 million units, making it one of the [[List of best-selling video games|best-selling video games]]. Film and television adaptations were announced in 2022, with the film planned as an [[Amazon Prime Video]] release.

==Gameplay==
[[File:It Takes Two gamepaly scerenshot.jpg|thumb|upright=1.2|''It Takes Two'' is specifically designed for [[Split screen (video games)|split-screen]] multiplayer. To progress in the game, the two players must fulfill different roles and achieve their objectives cooperatively.]]

''It Takes Two'' is a cooperative [[action-adventure game]] with elements from [[platform game]]s. It is designed exclusively for two players, either through local [[Split screen (computer graphics)|split-screen]] or online [[Cooperative video game|cooperative multiplayer]], with each player controlling one of the two [[player character]]s, Cody or May. There is no [[Single-player video game|single-player]] option, and both players are required to work together to progress through the story.<ref name="EAFeatures">{{cite web |url=https://www.ea.com/games/it-takes-two/it-takes-two/features |title=About It Takes Two |website=[[Electronic Arts]] |access-date=May 1, 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.polygon.com/2020/12/10/22167732/it-takes-two-game-friend-pass-release-date-trailer-details-gameplay|title=The new co-op game from the A Way Out team lets multiplayer pals play free|first=Ryan|last=Gilliam|work=[[Polygon (website)|Polygon]]|date=December 10, 2020|access-date=January 20, 2021|archive-date=December 11, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201211014826/https://www.polygon.com/2020/12/10/22167732/it-takes-two-game-friend-pass-release-date-trailer-details-gameplay|url-status=live}}</ref> The game uses a split-screen presentation for both local and online play, allowing each player to see their own character and their partner's actions at the same time.<ref name="EAFeatures"/>

Gameplay is built around cooperation, platforming, [[Puzzle video game|puzzle-solving]], and action sequences. Players travel through a series of fantastical environments based on Cody and May's home and relationship, with each area introducing new objectives, tools, and mechanics. Progress often requires the two players to perform complementary tasks, such as activating mechanisms, creating paths, solving environmental puzzles, or coordinating during combat and [[Boss (video games)|boss]] encounters.<ref name="PlayStation">{{cite web |url=https://www.playstation.com/en-us/games/it-takes-two/ |title=It Takes Two – PS4 & PS5 Games |website=[[PlayStation]] |access-date=May 1, 2026}}</ref> If a character dies, they respawn quickly, and during more difficult sections such as boss fights the defeated player can speed up their return by repeatedly pressing a button.<ref name="GSpotFares">{{cite web|url=https://www.gamespot.com/articles/josef-fares-it-takes-two-is-co-op-because-i-like-to-f-k-with-the-players-minds/1100-6488262/|title=Josef Fares: It Takes Two Is Co-Op Because "I Like To F—k With The Players' Minds"|first=Phil|last=Hornshaw|work=[[GameSpot]]|date=March 2, 2021|access-date=May 1, 2026}}</ref>

The game frequently gives Cody and May different abilities that are tied to the theme of the current level. For instance, in one level, Cody gains the ability to rewind time, whereas May can replicate herself. In other sections, the characters receive different tools or powers that must be combined to move forward. Hazelight designed the game so that major mechanics change regularly rather than repeating from level to level, with the gameplay ideas connected to the story and setting of each chapter.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.videogamer.com/news/it-takes-two-offers-a-look-at-its-co-operative-gameplay-in-latest-trailer |title=It Takes Two offers a look at its co-operative gameplay in latest trailer |last=Borthwick |first=Ben |website=VideoGamer.com |date=February 23, 2021 |access-date=March 17, 2021 |archive-date=February 23, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210223103609/https://www.videogamer.com/news/it-takes-two-offers-a-look-at-its-co-operative-gameplay-in-latest-trailer |url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="GSpotFares"/>

In addition to the main cooperative challenges, ''It Takes Two'' includes combat encounters, traversal sequences, boss fights, and optional competitive [[minigame]]s. These minigames are found on short side paths throughout the levels and allow the two players to compete against each other outside the main cooperative objectives, with the game tracking wins and losses between them.<ref name="GSpotFares"/> The game also draws on several genres, with sections involving platforming, shooting, racing, flight, and arcade-style challenges.<ref name="PlayStation"/><ref name="GSpot"/>

==Plot==
Cody ([[Joseph Balderrama]]) and May ([[Annabelle Dowler]]), a married couple, are planning to divorce. After they tell their daughter Rose ([[Clare Corbett]]) the news, she takes her hand-made dolls modeled after her parents into the family shed and tries to repair their relationship by play-acting. Rose's tears fall onto the dolls, causing Cody and May's consciousnesses to become trapped inside them. They are then confronted by Dr. Hakim (also Balderrama), an anthropomorphic relationship therapy book, who says he has been tasked with fixing their relationship as they try to reach Rose.

At first, Cody and May focus on reaching Rose, hoping she knows how to return them to their human bodies. Hakim repeatedly interferes with their progress, placing obstacles and tests in their way to force them to collaborate. They also encounter anthropomorphic versions of their old possessions, who criticize Cody and May for neglecting both their belongings and Rose. As they travel around their property, Cody and May are reminded of positive memories from their relationship and begin to work together more effectively. They come close to communicating with Rose several times but learn she cannot see or hear their doll forms, though she can see objects appear to move by themselves as her parents move them.

In a final series of obstacles, Hakim encourages Cody and May to rediscover their passions and support each other. This first takes them through Cody's overgrown, abandoned garden and greenhouse, which May helps him restore. They then work together to help May rediscover her passion for music and singing.

Meanwhile, Rose continues trying to mend her parents' relationship, but Cody and May's real bodies have fallen unconscious and do not respond to her. Believing her parents are ignoring her and that she is the reason their marriage is failing, Rose decides to run away in the hope that it will make them stay together.

After a long journey, Cody and May complete Hakim's final test by gathering an orchestra and audience for May to perform in front of. As May sings, their relationship is repaired, and they kiss, reversing the spell. They awaken in their real bodies and realize that Rose has run away. They find her at a nearby bus stop and assure her that she is not responsible for their arguments and that they will always love her. The family then returns home with a new perspective on their relationship.

==Development and release==
[[File:Josef Fares, Gamelab 2018 - 08 (cropped 2).jpg|thumb|[[Josef Fares]] ''(pictured in 2018)'' served as the creative director.]]

[[Josef Fares]], the director of Hazelight's previous game ''[[A Way Out (video game)|A Way Out]]'' (2018) and [[Starbreeze Studios|Starbreeze]]'s ''[[Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons]]'' (2013), returned to direct ''It Takes Two'' with a development staff of 60 people. After releasing ''A Way Out'', Hazelight decided to create another co-op-only video game, as the studio felt it had become more experienced and could further expand the design concepts introduced in that game.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.ign.com/articles/not-even-ea-thought-a-way-out-would-sell-josef-fares-on-why-hes-making-games-in-a-genre-he-had-to-invent|title='Not Even EA Thought A Way Out Would Sell' – Josef Fares on Why He's Making Games in a Genre He Had to Invent|first=Joe|last=Skrebels|work=[[IGN]]|date=January 15, 2020|access-date=January 20, 2021|archive-date=January 15, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210115122103/https://www.ign.com/articles/not-even-ea-thought-a-way-out-would-sell-josef-fares-on-why-hes-making-games-in-a-genre-he-had-to-invent|url-status=live}}</ref> Fares said Hazelight designs its cooperative games from the beginning around two players rather than adding co-op to a single-player structure, and that communication between players was intended to be essential to progression.<ref name="VergeInterview">{{cite web|url=https://www.theverge.com/22352157/it-takes-two-interview-developer-josef-fares-hazelight-studio-co-op|title=It Takes Two is Josef Fares' latest attempt to show the power of co-op gaming|first=Chaim|last=Gartenberg|work=[[The Verge]]|date=March 26, 2021|access-date=May 2, 2026}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.theringer.com/2021/04/22/video-games/josef-fares-it-takes-two-interview-co-op-gaming|title=Josef Fares Is Keeping Couch Co-Op Gaming Alive|first=Ben|last=Lindbergh|work=[[The Ringer (website)|The Ringer]]|date=April 22, 2021|access-date=May 2, 2026}}</ref>

The central design theme of ''It Takes Two'' was collaboration. Fares said that Hazelight used a guiding word for each of its games: ''Brothers'' was about "loss", ''A Way Out'' was about "trust", and ''It Takes Two'' was about "collaboration".<ref name="NWRInterview">{{cite web|url=https://www.nintendoworldreport.com/interview/62009/it-takes-two-interview-with-hazelight-and-turn-me-up|title=It Takes Two Interview with Hazelight and Turn Me Up|first=Gregory|last=Soyk|work=Nintendo World Report|date=November 2, 2022|access-date=May 2, 2026}}</ref> Hazelight worked to connect gameplay with the narrative, with mechanics changing as the story progresses and with Cody and May receiving abilities that reflected their personalities and the themes of each level.<ref name="VergeInterview"/> Fares pushed the developers to include many different mechanics and set pieces because he believed repeated gameplay mechanics would become "less special".<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.ign.com/articles/it-takes-two-could-take-15-hours-to-complete-and-should-win-a-world-record-for-mechanics-says-josef-fares|title=It Takes Two Could Take 15 Hours to Complete and Should Win a World Record for Mechanics, Says Josef Fares|first=Joe|last=Skrebels|work=[[IGN]]|date=December 15, 2020|access-date=January 20, 2021|archive-date=December 11, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201211020254/https://www.ign.com/articles/it-takes-two-could-take-15-hours-to-complete-and-should-win-a-world-record-for-mechanics-says-josef-fares|url-status=live}}</ref> He also said the game was designed to make players continually encounter new situations rather than repeat the same ideas.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.inverse.com/gaming/josef-fares-it-takes-two-interview |title=Josef Fares reveals why 'It Takes Two' is a "f*cked up" game |first1=Just |last1=Lunning |first2=Giovanni |last2=Colantonio |website=[[Inverse (website)|Inverse]] |date=March 31, 2021 |access-date=May 2, 2026}}</ref>

Fares described the game as a romantic comedy, saying that the genre was unusual for video games and suited the cooperative premise.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.thesixthaxis.com/2021/03/02/interview-josef-fares-on-it-takes-two-relationship-advice-co-operation-favourite-swear-words/ |title=Interview – Josef Fares on It Takes Two, relationship advice, co-operation & favourite swear words |author=Stefan L |website=TheSixthAxis |date=March 2, 2021 |access-date=May 2, 2026}}</ref><ref name="GamesBeatInterview">{{cite web|url=https://gamesbeat.com/josef-fares-interview-why-youre-going-to-love-it-takes-two/|title=Josef Fares interview: Why you're going to love It Takes Two|first=Dean|last=Takahashi|work=GamesBeat|date=March 2, 2021|access-date=May 2, 2026}}</ref> The developers drew inspiration from [[Pixar]] films, particularly in the game's visual tone and character presentation.<ref name="GamesBeatInterview"/> Fares provided [[motion capture]] for Dr. Hakim.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.gamespot.com/articles/it-takes-two-and-the-relentless-positivity-of-josef-fares/1100-6485340/|title=It Takes Two and the relentless positivity of Josef Fares|first=Steve|last=Watts|work=[[GameSpot]]|date=December 10, 2020|access-date=January 20, 2021|archive-date=December 11, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201211015233/https://www.gamespot.com/articles/it-takes-two-and-the-relentless-positivity-of-josef-fares/1100-6485340/|url-status=live}}</ref> Fares said that the team storyboarded the game's scenes before building much of the gameplay, but that the story and gameplay were adjusted together during production.<ref name="NWRInterview"/> The actors for Cody and May performed motion capture at Hazelight, and Fares said the actors were allowed to improvise so that the characters could be brought closer to the performers.<ref name="NWRInterview"/> The game was written mostly in [[AngelScript]], using Hazelight's UnrealEngine-Angelscript integration.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://angelscript.hazelight.se/ |title=Unreal Engine Angelscript |website=Unreal Engine Angelscript |publisher=[[Hazelight Studios]] |access-date=May 5, 2026}}</ref>

''It Takes Two'' was published under the [[EA Originals]] label, allowing Hazelight to retain full creative control while receiving most of the game's profit after development costs were recouped.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://gamesbeat.com/a-way-out-creator-if-you-dont-like-it-you-can-break-my-legs/ |title=A Way Out creator Josef Fares: 'If you don't like it, you can break my legs' |last=Takahashi |first=Dean |website=GamesBeat |date=June 11, 2017 |access-date=May 5, 2026}}</ref> EA signed a publishing deal with Hazelight in June 2019.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.gamesindustry.biz/articles/2019-06-08-ea-sign-fresh-indie-publishing-deals-with-zoink-glowmade-and-hazelight|title=EA signs fresh indie publishing deals with Zoink, Glowmade and Hazelight|first=Christopher|last=Dring|work=GamesIndustry.biz|date=June 8, 2019|access-date=January 20, 2021|archive-date=June 8, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190608220140/https://www.gamesindustry.biz/articles/2019-06-08-ea-sign-fresh-indie-publishing-deals-with-zoink-glowmade-and-hazelight|url-status=live}}</ref> The game was officially revealed during EA Play in June 2020.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.polygon.com/2020/6/18/21296330/ea-play-2020-josef-fares-it-takes-two|title=New co-op game from A Way Out creator, It Takes Two, launches in 2021|first=Julia|last=Lee|work=[[Polygon (website)|Polygon]]|date=June 18, 2020|access-date=January 20, 2021|archive-date=June 19, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200619120803/https://www.polygon.com/2020/6/18/21296330/ea-play-2020-josef-fares-it-takes-two|url-status=live}}</ref> Before the game's release, [[Take-Two Interactive]] filed a trademark claim against ''It Takes Two''. Hazelight Studios later abandoned its trademark application for the game's name, while saying it could not comment on ongoing disputes but was "hopeful it will be resolved".<ref>{{cite web|last=Phillips|first=Tom|url=https://www.eurogamer.net/josef-fares-it-takes-two-hit-by-take-two-trademark-claim|title=Josef Fares' It Takes Two hit by Take-Two claim|work=[[Eurogamer]]|date=December 3, 2021|access-date=December 3, 2021|archive-date=December 3, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211203124520/https://www.eurogamer.net/articles/2021-12-03-josef-fares-it-takes-two-hit-by-take-two-trademark-claim|url-status=live}}</ref> EA and Hazelight introduced Friend's Pass, which allows the player who purchased the game to invite a friend to play for free.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.eurogamer.net/articles/2020-12-11-heres-our-first-look-at-it-takes-two-gameplay|title=Here's our first look at It Takes Two gameplay|first=Wesley|last=Yin-Poole|work=[[Eurogamer]]|date=December 11, 2020|access-date=January 20, 2021|archive-date=December 11, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201211015141/https://www.eurogamer.net/articles/2020-12-11-heres-our-first-look-at-it-takes-two-gameplay|url-status=live}}</ref> The game was released for [[PlayStation 4]], [[PlayStation 5]], [[Windows]], [[Xbox One]] and [[Xbox Series X and Series S|Xbox Series X/S]] on March 26, 2021.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.destructoid.com/it-takes-two-is-an-out-of-control-co-op-adventure-from-the-makers-of-a-way-out/ |title=It Takes Two is an out-of-control co-op adventure from the makers of A Way Out |last=Devore |first=Jordan |website=[[Destructoid]] |date=December 10, 2020 |access-date=January 20, 2021 |archive-date=December 11, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201211020553/https://www.destructoid.com/stories/it-takes-two-is-an-out-of-control-co-op-adventure-from-the-makers-of-a-way-out-613034.phtml |url-status=live}}</ref>

A [[Nintendo Switch]] port was developed by Turn Me Up Games and released on November 4, 2022. Turn Me Up producer Louis Polak said that local wireless play required a custom solution because the original game had not been built around the Switch's local wireless system.<ref name="NWRInterview"/> Executive producer Scott Cromie said the port targeted 720p resolution in handheld mode, 1080p in docked mode, and 30 frames per second.<ref name="NWRInterview"/> Fares said Hazelight did not focus on Switch during the original production because the studio prioritized the main version of the game, but he praised Turn Me Up's port and said the game reflected his admiration for Nintendo's approach to accessible design.<ref name="NWRInterview"/><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UJ9Iz7HhU-I|title=Nintendo Direct 9.13.2022|publisher=[[Nintendo]]|date=September 13, 2022|access-date=September 13, 2022|archive-date=September 16, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220916144107/https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UJ9Iz7HhU-I|url-status=live|via=[[YouTube]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://nintendoeverything.com/it-takes-two-confirmed-for-switch/ |title=It Takes Two Switch version confirmed |author=Brian |website=Nintendo Everything |date=September 13, 2022 |access-date=September 13, 2022 |archive-date=September 13, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220913140519/https://nintendoeverything.com/it-takes-two-confirmed-for-switch/ |url-status=live}}</ref>

==Reception==
''It Takes Two'' sold over 1 million units within one month of release.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.ign.com/articles/it-takes-two-selling-1-million-copies-shows-that-players-want-co-op-only-games-josef-fares-says|title=It Takes Two Selling 1 Million Copies Shows That Players Want Co-op Only Games, Josef Fares Says|first=Adam|last=Bankhurst|work=[[IGN]]|date=April 24, 2021|access-date=April 25, 2021|archive-date=October 8, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211008040425/https://www.ign.com/articles/it-takes-two-selling-1-million-copies-shows-that-players-want-co-op-only-games-josef-fares-says|url-status=live}}</ref> Sales reached 7 million by mid-2022,<ref>{{cite web|last=Benfell|first=Grace|title=It Takes Two Celebrates 7 Million Copies Sold|url=https://www.gamespot.com/articles/it-takes-two-celebrates-7-million-copies-sold/1100-6505263/|date=July 8, 2022|access-date=July 10, 2022|website=[[GameSpot]]|archive-date=July 10, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220710032359/https://www.gamespot.com/articles/it-takes-two-celebrates-7-million-copies-sold/1100-6505263/|url-status=live}}</ref> and surpassed 20 million by late 2024.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.gematsu.com/2024/10/it-takes-two-sales-top-20-million |title=It Takes Two sales top 20 million |last=Romano |first=Sal |website=Gematsu |date=October 16, 2024 |access-date=October 16, 2024}}</ref> By April 2026, it had sold over 30 million copies worldwide.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.gamespot.com/articles/split-fiction-which-had-double-the-budget-of-it-takes-two-has-sold-1-3-the-copies-so-far/1100-6539268/ |title=Split Fiction Studio Has Sold 50 Million Games So Far |last=Makuch |first=Eddie |website=[[GameSpot]] |date=April 8, 2026 |access-date=April 8, 2026}}</ref><ref>{{Cite ''It Takes Two'' received "generally favorable" reviews from critics, according to review aggregator [[Metacritic]].<ref name="Metacritic"/> Reviewers praised the game's cooperative design, variety of mechanics, and connection between gameplay and story. ''[[GameSpot]]'' praised its creativity and pacing, saying that the frequent introduction of new ideas kept the experience from feeling stagnant,<ref name="GSpot"/> while ''[[IGN]]'' described it as an inventive cooperative game whose mechanics evolved throughout the adventure.<ref name="IGN"/> ''[[GamesRadar+]]'' similarly praised its commitment to split-screen play and shared problem-solving, calling it one of the most inventive cooperative platform games in recent years.<ref name="GRadar"/>

Several reviewers highlighted how the game gave Cody and May distinct abilities that required cooperation. ''[[Game Informer]]'' praised the way the game connected its emotional story to cooperative challenges,<ref name="GI"/> while ''[[Shacknews]]'' commended the variety of gameplay ideas and the way the game encouraged players to work together.<ref name="SN"/> ''[[Jeuxvideo.com]]'' and Gamer.no also praised the game's cooperative structure and variety, with both reviews giving the game high scores.<ref name="JXV"/><ref name="GamerNo"/>

Other critics also emphasized the game's variety and cooperative structure. ''[[The Guardian]]'' described it as an engrossing puzzle adventure that used teamwork effectively,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/games/2021/mar/31/it-takes-two-review-it-electronic-arts-ps45-xbox-pc|title=It Takes Two review – joyful family adventure for socially distanced duos|first=Keith|last=Stuart|work=[[The Guardian]]|date=March 31, 2021|access-date=May 1, 2026}}</ref> while ''[[Video Games Chronicle]]'' called it an inventive two-player experience with a steady stream of ideas.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.videogameschronicle.com/review/it-takes-two-game/|title=It Takes Two review: Hazelight's co-op adventure is a rom-com rollercoaster|first=Chris|last=Scullion|work=[[Video Games Chronicle]]|date=March 24, 2021|access-date=May 1, 2026}}</ref> ''[[NME]]'' described the game as a Pixar-like cooperative platformer and praised its charm,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nme.com/reviews/it-takes-two-review-a-pixar-esque-cutesy-co-op-delight-2917178|title='It Takes Two' review: a Pixar-esque, cutesy co-op delight|first=Tom|last=Regan|work=[[NME]]|date=April 9, 2021|access-date=May 1, 2026}}</ref> and ''[[Nintendo Life]]'' wrote that the later Switch version retained the game's cooperative appeal despite technical compromises.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nintendolife.com/reviews/nintendo-switch/it-takes-two|title=It Takes Two Review (Switch)|first=Ollie|last=Reynolds|work=[[Nintendo Life]]|date=November 2, 2022|access-date=May 1, 2026}}</ref>

The game's story and tone received a more mixed response. Reviewers praised the emotional focus on Cody and May's strained marriage, but some criticism was directed at uneven writing and the character of Dr. Hakim. ''[[PC Gamer]]'' criticized parts of the script and found Dr. Hakim irritating, while still praising the game's imagination and cooperative design.<ref name="PCGUS"/>

===Accolades===
''It Takes Two'' received several major industry awards and nominations following its release. It won [[The Game Award for Game of the Year|Game of the Year]] at [[The Game Awards 2021]],<ref name="TGA2021Winners"/> [[D.I.C.E. Award for Game of the Year|Game of the Year]] at the [[25th Annual D.I.C.E. Awards]],<ref name="DICE2022"/> and Best Multiplayer Game at the [[Golden Joystick Awards]].<ref name="GJ2021win"/> It also won Better With Friends at [[The Steam Awards]]<ref name="SteamAwards2021"/> and Excellence in Multiplayer at the [[SXSW Gaming Awards]],<ref name="SXSW2022"/> and received multiple nominations and two wins at the [[18th British Academy Games Awards|British Academy Games Awards]].<ref name="BAFTA2022Winners"/>

==Adaptations==
A [[feature film]] and television adaptation were announced in January 2022, with both projects in development from [[Dmitri M. Johnson]]'s dj2 Entertainment.<ref name="Adaptations_Variety">{{cite web |url=https://variety.com/2022/tv/news/it-takes-two-series-film-dj2-entertainment-1235167573/ |title='It Takes Two' Developer Hazelight Studios Teams With dj2 Entertainment to Adapt Game for Film, TV (EXCLUSIVE) |last=Otterson |first=Joe |website=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]] |date=January 31, 2022 |access-date=April 21, 2022 |archive-date=February 1, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220201025756/https://variety.com/2022/tv/news/it-takes-two-series-film-dj2-entertainment-1235167573/ |url-status=live}}</ref> In April 2022, [[Amazon MGM Studios|Amazon]] acquired distribution rights for the film as part of a [[first-look deal]] involving Story Kitchen and screenwriters [[Patrick Casey (writer)|Pat Casey]] and [[Josh Miller (filmmaker)|Josh Miller]]. The film was planned to follow the premise of the game, with May and Cody transported into dolls of themselves after contemplating divorce. [[Dwayne Johnson]], [[Dany Garcia]], and Hiram Garcia joined the production in producing roles, alongside Dmitri M. Johnson, [[Michael Lawrence Goldberg]], and Timothy I. Stevenson. The project is planned as a joint-venture production between Hazelight Studios, Story Kitchen, [[Seven Bucks Productions]], and Amazon, with an intended release as a [[Amazon Prime Video|Prime Video]] original film; Johnson was also being courted to star in the film.<ref name="Film_Deadline">{{cite web |url=https://deadline.com/2022/04/it-takes-two-video-game-film-lands-at-amazon-seven-bucks-productions-boards-1235006592/ |title=Dwayne Johnson's Seven Bucks Productions Boards 'It Takes Two' As Video WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Keep Driving (video game)
======================================================================

{{Short description|2025 video game}}

'''''Keep Driving''''' is a 2025 [[adventure video game]] developed and published by YCJY Games. The game blends the genres of [[role-playing video game|RPG]], [[Adventure game|adventure]], and [[construction and management simulation|resource management sim]], requiring players to take a road trip while picking up hitchhikers, working in odd jobs, surviving bad roads and other bad drivers, and more. The game was released for [[Windows]] in February 2025, and for the [[Nintendo Switch]], [[PlayStation 5]], and [[Xbox Series X/S]] in September 2026. ''Keep Driving'' received generally favorable reviews upon release and is one of the highest rated games of 2025.

== Plot ==
The unnamed protagonist driver has one of several background stories selected by the player, such as part-time mechanic or student. The driver has received a letter from a friend inviting him to a concert across the country. The driver needs to pick up a ticket to the concert festival and, if they want, a tent to use while there. The driver drives their car—selecting from vehicles like an early 1980s sedan or a pickup truck—away from home and onto the first stop on the map.<ref name="RPSReview" />

[[File:KeepDrivingDrivingScreenshot.png|thumb|left|Players in ''Keep Driving'' travel from location to location over a variety of road times and biomes with randomized events to navigate.]]
Between stops, the driver must navigate a challenging road trip, including items in the roadway like an abandoned car, road kill, or birds; having an angry bee in the car; slow cars; and aggressive police officers. These challenges can delay the driver from getting to the concert on time by breaking the car or taking away from precious resources. The driver may also encounter [[hitchhiking|hitchhikers]] who hope that the driver will help them out in some way. For example, a lost child is looking for her parents, and the driver must now consider taking her home. If the driver chooses to help the hitchhiker, the hitchhiker could be useful in dealing with the road trip's challenges.<ref name="RPSReview" />

Along the way, the driver's goals may change. For example, instead of going to the concert, the driver may choose to inherit some property from a recently deceased relative or participate in a drag race. There are at least 9 different endings to ''Keep Driving'' depending on the driver's choices.<ref name="RPSReview" />

== Gameplay ==
The road trip primarily takes place with a side-view of the car moving between destinations and a dashboard with actions the driver can take. When a challenge during the road trip arises, a series of colored icons appear on the dashboard. The driver must eliminate all of the icons in order to advance past the challenge. The driver does so by matching the icons with icons from skills and items with the icons given by the challenge.

[[File:KeepDrivingBattleScreenshot.png|thumb|When players are faced with an event in ''Keep Driving'', they must use skills and items to eliminate the threat.]]

The driver can have up to five skills, which are unlocked through choices made during the trip, and four items, which are placed in the glovebox. Hitchhikers can add additional skills. Most skills and items have limited uses that can be replenished by resting or by purchasing more items at towns. Additional items can be placed in the trunk, to be retrieved outside of battle.<ref name="HardcoreGamerReview" />

If the driver is unsuccessful in removing all of the icons in a turn, the driver will face consequences such as fatigue or damage to the car. If the driver becomes fully fatigued or the car completely damaged, the driver may have to stop and rest on the side of the road or have the car towed to a nearby garage for fixing. These outcomes stress the driver's finances and ability to get to objectives on time.

In towns or other points on the map, the driver may choose from a variety of tasks depending on the location. Many locations have gas stations to fill up the tank and stores from which to buy additional items for use in road challenges and to upgrade the vehicle. The towns can have employment offices which allow the driver to earn money in exchange for time, and they can have garages which allow for upgrading the vehicle. Some towns have places to sleep that provide more benefits than sleeping in the car.<ref name="HardcoreGamerReview" />

== Development ==
The [[Gothenburg]]-based video game developer YCJY Games—consisting of Christopher Andreasson and Josef Martinovsky—began developing ''Keep Driving'' in 2016,<ref name="Edge Preview"/> shortly after the release of ''[[The Aquatic Adventure of the Last Human]]''.<ref name="Dread Interview"/> They considered it a [[spiritual sequel]] to their first game, ''Keep Walking EP'', and felt it was their "big thing" with which they had more personal attachment.<ref name="Goomba Stomp Interview"/> Development was halted after a year due to a lack of funds and experience, opting instead to work on smaller games like ''Sea Salt'' (2019).<ref name="YCJY Press"/> Full-time development resumed in 2020 after the release of ''Post Void''.<ref name="IndieCade Roundtable"/>{{rp|loc=10:28}} They felt their experience developing other games left them more prepared; like with ''Post Void'', they planned the full game in advance to avoid repeating mistakes.<ref name="Dread Interview"/> The game was funded by [[Creative Europe Media]] and [[Kowloon Nights]],<ref name="TBL Preview"/><ref name="Kowloon"/> and uses the [[game engine]] [[GameMaker]].<ref name="YCJY Engine"/>

The game was originally structured with several gameplay systems and minigames like ''[[The Oregon Trail (series)|The Oregon Trail]]'', but the developers found it complicated and felt its direction lacked focus, prompting several redesigns.<ref name="Edge Preview"/> They created it as a [[tabletop game]] in two weeks to understand the mechanics before approaching it from the [[Role-playing video game|role-playing]] perspective,<ref name="Dread Interview"/> settling on a genre more akin to a [[roguelike]].<ref name="Edge Preview"/> Mechanically, the game is inspired by ''[[Diablo (series)|Diablo]]''.<ref name="Dread Interview"/> Earlier iterations featured more sophisticated car controls but the developers found a simplified approach more rewarding, especially after gameplay interruptions. They had concerns about the game's lengthy quiet periods but found they "just had to be confident about it, and keep it in".<ref name="Edge Preview"/> The early-2000s time period was chosen due to the lack of [[smartphone]]s and consequently the complexities of navigation. Martinovsky found the concept reminiscent of his childhood spent playing games with friends.<ref name="Edge Preview"/>

The developers took inspiration from games like ''[[FTL: Faster Than Light]]'' (2012), ''[[Jalopy (video game)|Jalopy]]'' (2018), and ''[[Oregon Trail II]]'' (1995), board games like ''[[The 7th Continent]]'' and ''[[Gloomhaven]]'' (both 2017), and [[road movie]]s like ''[[Paris, Texas (film)|Paris, Texas]]'' (1984) and ''[[Two-Lane Blacktop]]'' (1971).<ref name="Edge Preview"/><ref name="RPS Reveal"/> ''Keep Driving''{{'}}s art style was modelled on Gothenburg and its surroundings, with some later areas inspired by Martinovsky's experience living in Los Angeles.<ref name="Edge Preview"/> He found the art style more realistic and grounded than his previous work. The backgrounds have around eight or nine [[parallax]] layers.<ref name="Dread Interview"/>

=== Soundtrack ===
The game features more than 50 songs. The developers wanted to ensure it featured "smaller bands" like those from Gothenburg's [[indie rock]] scene, with which they had several connections.<ref name="Edge Preview"/> Martinovsky described the music as "a very [[skate-punk]] early-2000s feeling".<ref name="Edge Preview"/>

While driving, the player can queue up to 6 songs from the game's soundtrack using songs that the driver starts with or purchases along the way. The songs chosen for ''Keep Driving'' were coordinated by Karl Robb Kaardal, a Swedish pizza restauranteur. The local Swedish rock bands that contributed to the soundtrack for the game include [[Westkust]], Mundane, [[The Honeydrips]], Crystal Boys, Dorena, Aasma, Zimmer Grandioso, [[Makthaverskan]], Holy Now, and [[El Huervo]]. Music was also contributed by the Y/CJ/Y team under Martinovsky's own name and by [[My darling YOU!]], the latter of which is Johansson's music project. Several of the musicians featured in ''Keep Driving'' were also featured in the Swedish game ''[[Hotline Miami]]'', including [[Fucking Werewolf Asso]], which is ''Hotline Miami'' artist Dennis Wedin's band.{{citation needed|date=February 2025}}

== Release ==
YCJY Games announced ''Keep Driving''{{'}}s existence on [[Twitter]] in July 2016.<ref name="YCJY 2016"/> The game was showcased at [[Gamescom]] in August 2024.<ref name="YCJY Gamescom"/> It was formally announced on October 2, 2024, with its first trailer,<ref name="Bleeding Cool Announce"/><ref name="Hardcore Gamer Announce"/> featuring music by Swedish rock band [[Westkust]].<ref name="4Gamer Launch"/> The game was showcased with a [[Game demo|demo]] as part of [[Steam Next Fest]] in October.<ref name="VG247 Preview"/> The demo remained on [[Steam (service)|Steam]] after the event;<ref name="Vice Preview"/> it received over 70,000 downloads and led to over 170,000 users adding the game to their wishlist.<ref name="GamesRadar Launch"/> In January 2025, YCJY Games announced the February 6 release date for [[Windows]],<ref name="VG247 Date"/> alongside a new trailer featuring music by the Swedish band Holy Now.<ref name="4Gamer Launch"/><ref name="Destructoid Date"/> The game was released for the [[Nintendo Switch]], [[PlayStation&nbsp;5]], and [[Xbox Series&nbsp;X/S]] on September 28, 2026.<ref name="RPGamer Consoles"/>

== Reception ==
{{Video game reviews
| title = Reception
| MC = 84/100<ref name="Metacritic" />
| OC = 90% recommend<ref name="OpenCritic" />
| HCG = 4.5/5<ref name="HardcoreGamerReview" />
| PCGUS = 90/100<ref name="PCGamerReview" />
| RPG = 3.5/5<ref name="RPGamerReview" />
| TGMIt = 8.5/10<ref name="TGMItalyReview" />
| rev1 = ''[[Digital Spy]]''
| rev1Score = 4/5<ref name="DigitalSpyReview" />
| rev2 = ''[[Game Rant]]''
| rev2Score = 10/10<ref name="GameRantReview" />
| rev3 = ''[[Gamereactor]]''
| rev3Score = 7/10<ref name="GamereactorReview" />
| rev4 = ''[[Rock Paper Shotgun]]''
| rev4Score = Bestest Best<ref name="RPSReview" />
| rev5 = ''[[Vandal (website)|Vandal]]''
| rev5Score = 8.5/10<ref name="VandalReview" />
}}

''Keep Driving'' received "generally favorable" reviews from critics, according to [[review aggregator]] website [[Metacritic]],<ref name="Metacritic" /> and 90% of critics recommended the game according to [[OpenCritic]].<ref name="OpenCritic" />

''[[Hardcore Gamer]]'' praised the story of ''Keep Driving'', saying that it "captures the vibes of a good old-fashioned road trip, but also serves as a beautiful portrait of the human spirit, following our main character as they grapple with coming of age, entering the real world and finding their purpose" and compared the game favorably to other games with artistic storytelling like ''[[Disco Elysium]]'' and ''[[Road 96]]''.<ref name="HardcoreGamerReview" /> ''[[PC Gamer]]'' specifically praised the way the hitchhiking characters were developed, writing that "with minimal text, their stories and personalities come through, and by the end of the trip, it's clear we're all crammed into this car for the same reason: because we're all a little damaged, a little aimless, a little adrift."<ref name="PCGamerReview" /> ''[[Polygon (website)|Polygon's]]'' take on the hitchhikers was that ''Keep Driving'' "delivered a master class in economical characterization and storytelling through game design."<ref name="PolygonReview" />

Particular praise was garnered for the soundtrack. ''PC Gamer'' said that despite never having heard of any of the Swedish bands in the soundtrack, "their tracks will be part of my next real roadtrip."<ref name="PCGamerReview" /> ''RPGamer'' called the soundtrack "a treat for the ears" and noted that "all good road trips start with an amazing soundtrack, and Y/CJ/Y Games and Westkust nailed this part of the assignment."<ref name="RPGamerReview" />

The gameplay was less well received. Of the turn-based combat system, ''Polygon'' noted "there's a big conceptual gap between it and the action being described by the game."<ref name="PolygonReview" /> ''RPGamer'' called the battle system "simple" and "servicable".<ref name="RPGamerReview" /> Several reviewers found the aesthetic of the game to be great, but the gameplay loop itself as repetitive, monotonous, and boring.<ref name="DigitalSpyReview" /><ref name="GamereactorReview" />

''Keep Driving'' won the Grand Jury Award at [[IndieCade]] in 2024<ref name="IndieCade 2024"/> and was nominated for Best Self Published Indie Game at the [[Golden Joystick Awards]]<ref name="Golden Joystick"/> and Chumley's Speakeasy Award for Best Hidden Gem at the [[New York Game Awards]] in 2025.<ref name="NYGA"/>
