'''''Resident Evil'''''{{efn|Known in Japan as '''''Biohazard''''', stylized as {{nihongo|'''''biohazard'''''|バイオハザード|baiohazādo|lead=yes}}. The Japanese version of the remake has the title spelled entirely in lowercase letters, as opposed to the uppercase style used in the original game.}} is a 2002 [[survival horror]] game developed and published by [[Capcom]] for the [[GameCube]]. It is a [[Video game remake|remake]] of the 1996 [[PlayStation (console)|PlayStation]] game ''[[Resident Evil (1996 video game)|Resident Evil]]'', the first installment in the ''[[Resident Evil]]'' video game series. The story takes place in 1998 near the fictional [[Midwestern United States|Midwestern]] town of Raccoon City where a series of bizarre murders have taken place.  The player takes on the role of either [[Chris Redfield]] or [[Jill Valentine]], [[Special Tactics And Rescue Service|S.T.A.R.S.]] officers sent in by the city and the [[Raccoon City Police Department|R.P.D.]] to investigate the murders.

''Resident Evil'' was developed over the course of fourteen months as part of an exclusivity deal between Capcom and [[Nintendo]] for the series in their [[Capcom Five]] partnership. It was directed by [[Shinji Mikami]], who also designed and directed the original ''Resident Evil''. Mikami decided to produce a remake because he felt that the original had not aged well enough and that the GameCube's capabilities could bring it closer to his original vision. The game retains the same graphical presentation, with [[3D modeling|3D models]] superimposed over [[Pre-rendering|pre-rendered]] backgrounds. However, the quality of the graphics was vastly improved. The remake also features new gameplay mechanics, revised [[Puzzle video game|puzzles]], additional explorable areas, a revised script, and new story details including an entire subplot cut from the original game.

Upon release, ''Resident Evil'' received acclaim from video game journalists, who praised its graphics and improved gameplay over the original game. It is often described as one of the best, scariest, and most visually impressive entries in the ''Resident Evil'' series. However, the game sold worse than expected, leading Capcom to change the direction of the series to a more [[Action game|action-oriented]] approach. In 2008, the game was [[porting|ported]] to the [[Wii]], featuring a new control system. In 2015, a [[High-definition video|high-definition]] [[Video game remaster|remaster]] was released to critical and commercial success for [[PlayStation 3]], [[PlayStation 4]], [[Windows]], [[Xbox 360]], and [[Xbox One]], then later for [[Nintendo Switch]] in 2019. Retrospectively, critics and fans regard ''Resident Evil'' as one of the greatest game remakes ever made.

==Gameplay==
[[File:Resident Evil GCN remake.png|thumb|left|The player, controlling [[Chris Redfield]], can use defensive weapons such as daggers when grabbed by zombies. The game features [[3D modeling|3D models]] over [[Pre-rendering|pre-rendered]] backgrounds.]]

''Resident Evil'' is a [[survival horror]] game where the player controls the on-screen character from a [[Virtual camera system|third-person]] perspective to interact with the environment. To advance, the player must explore a mansion and its surrounding areas while avoiding, outsmarting and defeating monsters including [[Zombies in Resident Evil|zombie]]s and giant spiders.<ref name="Official Strategy Guide Monsters"/> The player can open doors, push certain objects, climb obstacles, and pick up items. When an item is collected, it is stored in an inventory that the player can access at any time. Items in the inventory can be used, examined, and combined to solve [[Puzzle video game|puzzles]] and gain access to areas that were previously inaccessible.<ref name="Official Strategy Guide Basics"/> The inventory is limited to a certain number of slots, and the player must often move items from the inventory to storage boxes located in certain areas to manage space.<ref name="Official Strategy Guide Basics"/>

Although the player can use firearms to kill monsters, ''Resident Evil'' emphasizes evasion over fast-paced combat by providing the player with limited ammunition. The player has a limited amount of [[Health (gaming)|health]], which decreases when attacked by monsters. Players can regain health by collecting and using herbs, which can be mixed with other herbs to increase their healing effect.<ref name="Official Strategy Guide Basics"/> Some monsters can also infect the player with a poisoning effect, which gradually depletes the player's health over time until the poison is cured with serum or special herbs.<ref name="Official Strategy Guide Basics"/> Zombies that are defeated but not beheaded or burned eventually revive and mutate into faster and deadlier forms.<ref name="GSpot review"/><ref name=BeforeYouDie/>{{rp|176}}

The player can control either [[Chris Redfield]] or [[Jill Valentine]], each with advantages and disadvantages.<ref name="IGN review"/> For example, Chris can take and deal more damage than Jill, but Jill can carry more items and unlock certain doors with a [[Lock picking|lock pick]]. Both characters can equip defensive weapons that can save them from taking damage when seized by an enemy. These defensive weapons include a dagger and a unique special weapon: Jill can use a [[taser]], while Chris can shove [[stun grenade]]s into zombies' mouths and detonate them with a pistol shot.<ref name="Official Strategy Guide Weapons"/> Defensive weapons are limited and can only be used when the player is grabbed by a monster.<ref name="Official Strategy Guide Weapons"/>

The game features an [[automap]] to help players navigate the different areas of the game. Additionally, the player can pick up maps of certain sections to reveal unexplored areas.<ref name="Official Strategy Guide Basics"/> To [[Saved game|save]] their progress, players need to find ink ribbons and use them with a typewriter; the game features a limited supply of ink ribbons, so players cannot save their progress as many times as they want.<ref name="Official Strategy Guide Basics"/> The story is slightly altered by the character the player chooses to play as,<ref name="IGN review"/> and certain choices the player makes in the game can impact the direction of the game and its ending.<ref name="Official Strategy Guide Path"/> Upon completing the game under a certain difficulty setting and time limit, the player may unlock secret costumes for the main characters, bonus weapons, and special difficulty modes.<ref name="Official Strategy Guide Secrets"/>

==Plot==
On July 24, 1998, a series of bizarre murders occur on the outskirts of the [[Midwestern United States|Midwestern]] town of Raccoon City. The Raccoon City Police Department's [[Special Tactics And Rescue Service]] (S.T.A.R.S.) are assigned to investigate. After contact with Bravo Team is lost, Alpha Team is sent to locate their whereabouts. Finding Bravo Team's crashed helicopter in a forest, they descend to investigate, but are attacked by a pack of monstrous dogs, killing one of them. After Alpha Team's helicopter pilot, [[Brad Vickers]], panics and flies off alone, remaining members Chris Redfield, Jill Valentine, [[Albert Wesker]], and [[Barry Burton]] retreat inside a nearby abandoned mansion, where they decide to split up.

While exploring the mansion, the player-controlled character (either Chris or Jill) finds several members of Bravo Team, including Kenneth J. Sullivan, who is devoured alive by a zombie; [[Richard Aiken]], who is either killed by a giant snake or eaten by a large shark; Forest Speyer, who is found dead and reanimates as a zombie; and Bravo Team leader Enrico Marini, who reveals there is a traitor among Alpha Team before being killed by an unseen shooter. [[Rebecca Chambers]], a survivor from Bravo Team, joins Chris. The player character then learns about a series of illegal experiments conducted by a clandestine research team under the authority of biomedical company [[Umbrella Corporation]]. The mansion teems with monstrous creatures resulting from these experiments, which have exposed both personnel and wildlife to a highly infectious and mutagenic biological agent known as the T-virus.

The player character discovers a secret underground laboratory housing Umbrella's experiments. Inside, they find Jill or Chris (depending on the player's character choice) in a cell and witness Wesker programming a Tyrant, a humanoid bioweapon. Wesker reveals that he is a [[double agent]] working for Umbrella, and plans to use the Tyrant to kill the S.T.A.R.S. members. In the ensuing confrontation, Wesker is seemingly killed and the player character defeats the Tyrant. After activating the lab's self-destruct mechanism, the player character reaches the heliport and contacts Brad for extraction. The game's ending varies depending on the player's actions at key points: in the best ending, Chris, Jill, Barry, and Rebecca all escape via helicopter after defeating the Tyrant once more; in the worst ending, the mansion remains intact and the player character emerges as the sole survivor.

==Development==
[[File:JuliaVoth09TIFF.jpg|thumb|upright|Canadian model [[Julia Voth]] served as the basis for Jill Valentine's facial and physical appearance.<ref name="Julia Voth"/>]]

''Resident Evil'' was developed by [[Capcom Production Studio 4]]<ref name="Studio 4"/> and directed by [[Shinji Mikami]], who designed and directed the original ''[[Resident Evil (1996 video game)|Resident Evil]]'' for the [[PlayStation (console)|PlayStation]] console.<ref name="Official Navigation Book"/> The game was part of an [[Console exclusivity|exclusivity]] agreement between Capcom and [[Nintendo]] to bring previous and new ''[[Resident Evil]]'' games to the [[GameCube]].<ref name="IGN RE to Cube"/><ref name="Hyper Capcom Special"/> Unlike ''[[Resident Evil 2]]'', ''[[Resident Evil 3: Nemesis]]'', and ''[[Resident Evil – Code: Veronica]]'', which were simply [[porting|ported]] to the GameCube, Mikami decided to produce a [[video game remake|remake]] of the original game because he felt its graphics had not aged well, making it hard for new players to appreciate it.<ref name="Official Navigation Book"/> Programmer Yasuhiro Anpo also cited the original game's poor [[Video game localization|localization]] as another reason for the remake.<ref name="GSpot article"/> Mikami<ref name="NGC Mag preview"/> and producer [[Hiroyuki Kobayashi (producer)|Hiroyuki Kobayashi]]<ref name=BeforeYouDie/>{{rp|175}} agreed the GameCube would allow them to bring the game closer to the original vision the team had for the series. As Capcom's marketing director Todd Thorson said, the main goal was to "achieve motion picture-quality visuals and create even more suspense and fear than the original".<ref name="IGN RE ships"/>

Production started at the beginning of 2001 with a team of only four programmers.<ref name="Staff Interview 7"/> Because ''Resident Evil'' was one of the first Capcom games developed for the GameCube, the development team had to study the system's performance during the first stages of development.<ref name="Staff Interview 7"/> In the process of development, the team wanted to make sure that those who had already played the 1996 version would find things to enjoy in the remake.<ref name=BeforeYouDie/>{{rp|176}} Initially, the team considered creating the environments with computer graphic animation but then realized that this approach would require too much hardware capacity and processing to achieve realistic graphics.<ref name="Staff Interview 3"/> As a result, the graphical style of the remake features [[3D modeling|3D models]] on top of [[Pre-rendering|pre-rendered]] backgrounds like early ''Resident Evil'' games.<ref name="NGC Mag preview"/> Despite this, the [[Virtual camera system|camera]] is more dynamic and can track the player at varying angles.<ref name="GSpot preview"/> The backgrounds also make use of [[particle effects]] and [[full motion video]] layers to simulate effects such as rushing water or swaying tree branches.<ref name="RE History"/> Creating fear in players was a priority, and many of the game's backgrounds were designed to have a high contrast between dark and light so that enemies could appear unexpectedly.<ref name="Staff Interview 1"/>

Originally, the developers planned to only upgrade the graphics and tweak the gameplay. However, as the game approached completion, Capcom started making more substantial changes.<ref name="Official Navigation Book"/> For example, the inventory was expanded so that players could carry a standard item like Jill's lockpick, while defense items, which were initially included in the main inventory, were introduced to make the game easier than the original.<ref name="Official Navigation Book"/> Several new weapons were also added in order to expand the range of approaches to combat. Enemies in the game were rebalanced to accommodate for this.<ref name=BeforeYouDie/>{{rp|176}} The developers originally planned to make all enemies invisible but the idea was discarded because it would have made the remake very different from the original game. However, they designed the zombies so that they could eventually come back to life after being killed, in the form of more dangerous Crimson Heads.<ref name=BeforeYouDie/>{{rp|176}} The developers added new areas for the player to explore, changed most of the puzzle designs, and included an additional control scheme whereby players move their characters by pressing the R button of the [[GameCube controller]] and steer them with the [[analog stick]].<ref name="IGN review"/><ref name="IGN Exploring RE"/> Another addition is a subplot involving the character Lisa Trevor.<ref name="Lisa Trevor addition"/> Instead of using adjectives to describe [[difficulty levels]], Mikami decided to have unique questions so that the player would pick the hard one.<ref name="Hyper Capcom Special"/> In a later interview Kobayashi stated that many of these additions and substantial changes were a deliberate effort to attract veteran players.<ref name=BeforeYouDie/>{{rp|176}}

Capcom [[audition]]ed actors to be used as references by the character designers.<ref name="GSpot preview"/> The faces of the protagonists were based on real people and [[motion capture]] was used to animate their models.<ref name="Official Navigation Book"/> About 60 percent of the character motions were animated based on the captured data, while the rest was created from scratch.<ref name="GSpot preview"/> The developers initially struggled to develop a system for computer graphic animation. However, Nintendo provided Capcom with assistance and the problems were eventually solved.<ref name="Hyper Capcom Special"/> Capcom also hired new [[Voice acting|voice actors]] and rewrote the game's script to make the plot more convincing.<ref name="RE History"/><ref name=BeforeYouDie/>{{rp|176}} The game was developed over the course of one year and two months.<ref name="Official Strategy Guide Interview"/> Final development was very intense, as programmers had to work for two straight months with no days off to meet the deadline.<ref name="Staff Interview 7"/> ''Resident Evil'' was released in 2002 on March 22 in Japan,<ref>{{Cite web |date=February 6, 2002 |title=''Resident Evil'' Retail Info |url=https://www.ign.com/articles/2002/02/06/resident-evil-retail-info |access-date=May 23, 2024 |website=[[IGN]] |language=en}}</ref> April 30 in North America,<ref name="IGN RE ships" /> and September 13 in Europe,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Bramwell |first=Tom |date=September 2, 2002 |title=Resident Spring |url=https://www.eurogamer.net/article-46600 |access-date=May 23, 2024 |website=[[Eurogamer]]}}</ref> and September 20 in Australia.<ref>{{Cite web |date=August 12, 2002 |title=''Resident Evil''...Coming September 20th to the Nintendo GameCube |url=http://www.nintendo.com.au/nintendo/news/index.php |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20020816212601/http://www.nintendo.com.au/nintendo/news/index.php |archive-date=August 16, 2002 |access-date=May 23, 2024 |website=[[Nintendo|Nintendo Australia]]}}</ref><ref name="NGC Mag preview"/>

| GameRev = A−<ref name="GameRev review"/>
| GSpot   = 8.9/10<ref name="GSpot review"/>
| GSpy    = 4.5/5<ref name="GSpy review"/>
| IGN     = 9.0/10<ref name="IGN review"/>
| NGC     = 89/100<ref name="NGC Mag review"/>
}}

Upon its release on the GameCube, ''Resident Evil'' received critical acclaim.<ref name="Metacritic"/> ''[[IGN]]'' reviewer Matt Casamassina felt that the game is "a triumph as a stand-alone adventure and a major accomplishment as a remake", calling it "the prettiest, most atmospheric and all-around scariest game we've ever played."<ref name="IGN review"/> Similarly, ''[[GameSpot]]'' reviewer Shane Satterfield described the remake as "one amazing game that clearly stands as the best the series has to offer",<ref name="GSpot review"/> while ''[[Edge (magazine)|Edge]]'' magazine remarked that the game's unforgiving gameplay and technical artistry improve the tension and anxiety that the original offered.<ref name="Edge review"/>

The game was widely praised for its graphics.<ref name="GSpot review"/><ref name="GamePro review"/><ref name="GameRev review"/><ref name="NGC Mag review"/> ''GameSpot'' credited the attention to detail, realistic gore, volumetric fog, and integration of real-time lighting and shadows with pre-rendered backgrounds, commenting that Capcom had "finally perfected the art of mixing prerendered scenery with ambient animations and [[Polygon (computer graphics)|polygonal]] objects, and the result is the most visually impressive video game ever released."<ref name="GSpot review"/> ''IGN'' highlighted the complex geometry of the character models, stating that "close shots of Chris or Jill look almost [[Photorealism|photo-realistic]]."<ref name="IGN review"/> Writing for ''[[NGC Magazine]]'', Jes Bickham remarked that, unlike in the original ''Resident Evil'', the contrast between character models and backgrounds is seamless.<ref name="NGC Mag review"/> He also noted that the game is "so visually rich that simply seeing the next area is an experience to be treasured."<ref name="NGC Mag review"/>

The game's suspenseful and cinematic atmosphere received praise, with ''[[GameRevolution]]'' going so far as to say that the game makes the original ''Resident Evil'' look like ''[[Pong]]''.<ref name="GameRev review"/> ''Resident Evil'' was also praised for its realistic sound. ''[[AllGame]]'' reviewer Scott Alan Marriott felt that the game "[creates] a constant sense of dread without relying too much on obvious shock values",<ref name="Allgame review"/> while ''GameSpot'' highlighted the quality and variety of sound effects, noting that "there seem to be dozens of sound effects for footsteps alone."<ref name="GSpot review"/> However, some publications considered the voice acting to be weak due to its exaggerated delivery.<ref name="GSpot review"/><ref name="IGN review"/>

Although the game's limiting controls and inventory management were criticized,<ref name="NGC Mag review"/> changes to many aspects of the gameplay were positively viewed. Mike Weigand of ''[[GamePro]]'' wrote, "It's like playing ''Resident Evil'' for the first time."<ref name="GamePro review"/> ''GameSpot'' remarked that the defensive weapons add a new layer of strategy to the game.<ref name="GSpot review"/> However, the controls were criticized for their lack of analog precision, a feature that was previously available in the [[Nintendo 64]] version of ''Resident Evil 2''.<ref name="NGC Mag review"/> Hector Guzman of ''[[GameSpy]]'' criticized the fact that the original game's "laborious" [[Tank controls (video games)|tank controls]], whereby the analog stick moves the player character in the direction they are facing, was not changed, stating that it can cause unnecessary difficulties when players try to evade monsters.<ref name="GSpy review"/> ''IGN''{{'}}s criticism was similar but considered the game's alternative control schemes a welcome addition.<ref name="IGN review"/>

''GameSpot'' editors named ''Resident Evil'' the best video game of April 2002.<ref name="GSpot gotm"/> At the ''GameSpot''{{'}}s Best and Worst of 2002 awards, ''Resident Evil'' was nominated for Best Story on GameCube,<ref name="GSpot awards story"/> Best Graphics (Technical) on GameCube,<ref name="GSpot awards graphics"/> and Best Action Adventure Game on GameCube.<ref name="GSpot awards adventure nom"/><ref name="GSpot awards adventure"/> As of November 2003, 445,176 copies of the game had been sold in the United States.<ref name="GC US sales"/> In May 2008, Capcom revealed that a total of 1.35 million copies of the game were sold.<ref name="GC total sales"/>

===Legacy===
''Resident Evil'' is often regarded as one of the greatest and most visually impressive games in the series.<ref name="RE History"/><ref name="GI ranking"/><ref name="Digital Spy ranking"/> According to ''IGN'', the game's graphics "became the new standard by which all future installments in the series would be compared."<ref name="IGN retro"/> In 2009, ''[[Official Nintendo Magazine]]'' ranked the game 43rd in a list of greatest Nintendo games.<ref>{{cite web | author=East, Tom | date=February 23, 2009 | title=100 Best Nintendo Games: Part 3 | url=http://www.officialnintendomagazine.co.uk/article.php?id=7258 | work=[[Official Nintendo Magazine]] | publisher=[[Future plc]] | access-date=September 9, 2022| archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090831020618/http://www.officialnintendomagazine.co.uk/article.php?id=7258 | archive-date=August 31, 2009 | url-status=dead }}</ref> ''[[Digital Spy]]'' writer Liam Martin remarked that the game is "the definitive version of a true classic" and that it still looked "fantastic" nearly 13 years after it was first released.<ref name="Digital Spy ranking"/> In Capcom's 2003 Annual Report the company stated that the game had "made good sales" and viewed the game's commercial performance favorably.<ref>{{cite web |title=Annual Report 2003 |url=https://www.capcom.co.jp/ir/english/data/pdf/Annual2003.pdf |website=capcom.co.jp |publisher=CAPCOM CO., LTD |access-date=17 June 2026}}</ref>  Despite this, Mikami was disappointed with sales numbers which drove the decision that subsequent games in the ''Resident Evil'' series would shift away from the survival horror genre and incorporate more [[Action game|action-based]] elements, starting with ''[[Resident Evil 4]]'' in 2005.<ref name="Why action"/> Before that happened, Capcom developed ''[[Resident Evil Zero]]'', a direct prequel using the same graphics [[game engine|engine]] and released in late 2002.<ref name="Zero engine"/>

==Re-release and remaster==
===Wii version===
On December 25, 2008, ''Resident Evil'' was ported to the GameCube's successor, the [[Wii]], along with ''Resident Evil Zero''.<ref name="Wii controls" /> The port, ''Resident Evil Archives: Resident Evil'', features a control system that supports both the [[Wii Remote]] and the GameCube controller.<ref name="Wii controls" /> Although Capcom originally had no plans to release the Wii version outside of Japan, arguing that the game would not sell very well, the game was eventually released in North America on June 23,<ref>{{Cite web |last=IGN Nintendo Team |first= |date=June 19, 2009 |title=Wii Games of Summer 2009 |url=https://www.ign.com/articles/2009/06/19/wii-games-of-summer-2009 |access-date=May 23, 2024 |website=[[IGN]] |language=en}}</ref> Australia on June 25,<ref>{{Cite web |title=''Resident Evil Archives'' (Nintendo Wii) |url=http://palgn.com.au/video-game/6879/nintendo-wii/resident-evil-archives/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090519234714/http://palgn.com.au/video-game/6879/nintendo-wii/resident-evil-archives/ |archive-date=May 19, 2009 |access-date=May 23, 2024 |website=PALGN}}</ref> and in Europe on June 26, 2009,<ref>{{Cite Q|Q131175916|title=''Resident Evil'' (Nintendo Wii)|publication-date=2009|access-date=November 14, 2024}}</ref> due to the commercial success of ''[[Resident Evil 5]]''.<ref name="Softpedia"/> The Wii version received generally favorable reviews from critics,<ref name="Metacritic Wii"/> but some publications criticized it for its outdated controls, lack of new features, and lack of [[widescreen]] support.<ref name="IGN Wii review"/><ref name="EuroG Wii review"/>

===HD remaster===
{{Video game reviews
| OC = 79% recommend<ref>{{Cite web |title=''Resident Evil HD Remaster'' |url=https://opencritic.com/game/127/resident-evil-hd-remaster}}</ref>
| MC      = PC: 82/100<ref name="Metacritic HD PC"/><br />PS4: 83/100<ref name="Metacritic HD PS4"/><br />XONE: 82/100<ref name="Metacritic HD XONE"/><br />NS: 80/100<ref name="Metacritic HD NS"/>
| EuroG   = 7/10<ref name="EuroG HD review"/>
| GI      = 9.5/10<ref name="GI HD review"/>
| GameRev = 4/5<ref name="GameRev HD review"/>
| GSpot   = 7/10<ref name="GSpot HD review"/>
| IGN     = 8.0/10<ref name="IGN HD review"/>
}}

A [[High-definition video|high-definition]] (HD) version, ''Resident Evil HD Remaster'', was released for [[PlayStation 3]], [[PlayStation 4]], [[Windows]], [[Xbox 360]], and [[Xbox One]] in January 2015.<ref name="GSpot HD release"/> The HD version supports [[5.1 surround sound]] as well as a resolution of [[1080p]] and a widescreen [[Aspect ratio (image)|aspect ratio]] of [[16:9]].<ref name="GSpot HD release"/> Although the original pre-rendered backgrounds have a [[4:3]] format, the developers decided against re-rendering them in 16:9 because it would allow players to see more of the environment than intended, reducing the sense of immersion and danger.<ref name="GI interview"/> As a result, the developers added vertical scrolling to the backgrounds, which respond to the movement of the character, to fit the remaster's widescreen aspect ratio.<ref name="GI interview"/> A new control scheme was also included, allowing players to move their character in the direction of the analog stick.<ref name="GSpot HD release"/>

The remaster was a commercial success, breaking sales records.<ref name="HD records"/> It became the [[PlayStation Network]]'s biggest launch game and Capcom's fastest-selling digital game across North America and Europe.<ref name="GI PSN sales"/><ref name="EuroG HD sales"/> Capcom announced that the remaster exceeded sales of one million copies by April 2015.<ref name="IGN HD WW sales"/> Its commercial success resulted in Capcom's announcement of a similar edition of ''Resident Evil Zero'' in 2015.<ref name="Forbes"/> Critical reception towards the remaster was generally favorable.<ref name="Metacritic HD PS4"/> Several critics noted that some features like the inventory system and the insistence on having to revisit previously explored areas have not aged very well, but generally agreed that the remaster was a solid revival of a classic.<ref name="EuroG HD review"/><ref name="GSpot HD review"/><ref name="IGN HD review"/><ref name="GameRev HD review"/> The new control scheme was also considered more intuitive and satisfying, especially for new players.<ref name="GI HD review"/> As of September 2022, the remaster had sold 3.7 million copies worldwide across all platforms.<ref name="Capcom Platinum Titles" />

====''Resident Evil: Origins Collection''====
''Resident Evil Zero'' and ''Resident Evil'' became a compilation called ''Resident Evil: Origins Collection'',<ref name="Origins collection"/> which was released on multiple consoles in 2015 and 2016, and on the [[Nintendo Switch]] in 2019.<ref name="Switch release"/>

======================================================================
WIKIPEDIA ARTICLE: Sandbox game
======================================================================

{{Use American English|date=October 2024}}
{{short description|Type of freeform video game encouraging creativity}}
[[File:Minetest high-res texture pack 2.png|thumb|upright=1.3|Screenshot of a player constructing minecart rails in a sandbox game in the [[Free software|free]] engine ''[[Luanti]]'']]
{{Video games}}
A '''sandbox game''' is a [[video game]] that gives players broad freedom to experiment with interacting systems and pursue self-chosen goals. Sandbox design may minimize predetermined objectives or narrative progression and often supports [[emergent gameplay]], in which complex situations arise from the interaction of comparatively simple mechanics.<ref name="Breslin-2009" />

Sandbox design is often combined with an [[open world]], but the terms describe different features. An open world concerns freedom of movement through the game space, whereas a sandbox concerns freedom to experiment with the game's systems. A game can therefore be open-world without offering substantial sandbox-style interaction.<ref name="Breslin-2009" /><ref>{{cite web |last=Harris |first=John |date=26 September 2007 |title=Game Design Essentials: 20 Open World Games |url=https://www.gamedeveloper.com/design/game-design-essentials-20-open-world-games |work=Game Developer |access-date=15 October 2026}}</ref>

Early sandbox games took the form of [[Space flight simulation game|space trading and combat games]] like ''[[Elite (video game)|Elite]]'' (1984) and [[City-building game|city-building simulations]] and [[Business simulation game|tycoon games]] like ''[[SimCity (1989 video game)|SimCity]]'' (1989). The release of ''[[The Sims (video game)|The Sims]]'' and ''[[Grand Theft Auto III]]'', in 2000 and 2001 respectively, demonstrated that games with highly detailed interacting systems that encouraged player experimentation could also be seen as sandbox games. Some sandbox games involve the ability to interact socially and share [[user-generated content]] across the [[Internet]], as in ''[[Second Life]]'' (2003). Sandbox games ''[[Garry's Mod]]'' (2006) and ''[[Dreams (video game)|Dreams]]'' (2020) allow players to use the game's systems to create new environments and modes. ''[[Minecraft]]'' (2009) is the most successful example of a sandbox game, with players able to enjoy both creative modes and more progression-driven [[Survival game|survival]] modes. ''[[Roblox]]'' (2006) allows users to create their own games using the [[Roblox#Roblox Studio and game design|Luau]] programming language.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Brumbaugh |first1=Zander |title=Coding Roblox Games Made Easy |date=2021 |publisher=Packt Publishing, Limited |isbn=9781800561991 |edition=1st}}</ref> ''[[Fortnite]]'' (2017) has game modes which allow players to interact competitively, or socialise.

==Terminology==
From a video game development standpoint, a sandbox game incorporates elements of sandbox design, a range of game systems that encourage free play and creativity.<ref name="Breslin-2009">{{cite web|last=Breslin|first=Steve|date=July 16, 2009|title=The History and Theory of Sandbox Gameplay|url=https://www.gamedeveloper.com/design/the-history-and-theory-of-sandbox-gameplay|access-date=May 2, 2020|work=GameDeveloper}}</ref> Sandbox design can either describe a game or a [[Game mechanics#Game modes|game mode]], with an emphasis on free-form [[gameplay]], relaxed rules, and minimal goals. Sandbox design can also describe a type of game development where a designer slowly adds features to a minimal game experience, experimenting with each element one at a time.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Carreker|first=Dan|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=y-BvCgAAQBAJ&q=%22sandbox+design%22+game&pg=PA372|title=The Game Developer's Dictionary: A Multidisciplinary Lexicon for Professionals and Students|date=2012|publisher=Course Technology|isbn=978-1-4354-6082-9|language=en}}</ref> There are "a lot of varieties" of sandbox design, based on "a wide range of dynamic interactive elements".<ref name="Breslin-2009" /> Thus, the term is used often, without a strict definition.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Graft|first=Kris|title=EVE Online and the meaning of 'sandbox'|url=https://www.gamedeveloper.com/design/-i-eve-online-i-and-the-meaning-of-sandbox-|access-date=2020-05-14|website=www.gamedeveloper.com|date=29 October 2012 |language=en}}</ref> Game designers sometimes define a sandbox as what it is not, where a game can "subtract the missions, the main campaign, the narrative or whatever formatively binds the game's progression, and you have a sandbox."<ref name="Breslin-2009" />

In game design, a sandbox is a [[metaphor]] for playing in a literal [[Sandpit|sandbox]].<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Oosterhuis|first1=Kas|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=tXBdOoZ-faYC&q=%22sandbox+metaphor%22+game&pg=PA20-IA17|title=The Architecture Co-laboratory: GameSetandMatch II : on Computer Games, Advanced Geometries, and Digital Technologies|last2=Feireiss|first2=Lukas|date=2006|publisher=episode publishers|isbn=978-90-5973-036-6|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|last1=Watkins|first1=S. Craig|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=JWN0DwAAQBAJ&q=%22sandbox+metaphor%22+game&pg=PA143|title=The Digital Edge: How Black and Latino Youth Navigate Digital Inequality|last2=Cho|first2=Alexander|date=2018-12-11|publisher=NYU Press|isbn=978-1-4798-4985-7|language=en}}</ref> Game historian Steve Breslin describes "the metaphor [as] a child playing in a sandbox ... produc[ing] a world from sand", compared to games with more fully formed content.<ref name="Breslin-2009" /> This metaphor between the virtual and literal sandbox is noted by [[Architecture|architectural]] scholar [[Alexandra Lange]], with a sandbox describing any bounded environment that offers freedom to explore and construct.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Lange|first=Alexandra|date=2018-06-15|title=The Sandbox: an Intellectual History|url=https://slate.com/human-interest/2018/06/history-of-the-sandbox-the-origins-of-a-playground-for-kids-and-ideas.html|access-date=2020-05-14|website=Slate Magazine|language=en}}</ref> This can distinguish it from conventional ideas of a game, where the metaphorical sandbox is a "play space in which people can try on different roles and imaginary quests ... rather than a 'game' to play."<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Information Behavior and the Formation and Maintenance of Peer Cultures in Massive Multiplayer Online Role-Playing Games|url=http://www.digra.org/wp-content/uploads/digital-library/06278.15067.pdf|journal=Authors & Digital Games Research Association|archive-date=2017-08-12|access-date=2020-05-14|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170812120054/http://www.digra.org/wp-content/uploads/digital-library/06278.15067.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref>

[[File:GeoFS - EC135 Helicopter over North Western america.jpg|thumb|Open world flight simulator ''GeoFS'']]
In describing video games, sandbox design is often associated with the [[open world]] gameplay mechanic and vice versa, but these are two disparate concepts. Open worlds are those where the player's movement in the virtual world is typically not limited by the game allowing the player to roam freely through it.<ref>{{cite web|last=Harris|first=John|date=September 26, 2007|title=Game Design Essentials: 20 Open World Games|url=https://www.gamedeveloper.com/design/game-design-essentials-20-open-world-games|access-date=May 2, 2020|work=[[Gamasutra]]}}</ref> ''[[Adventure (Atari 2600)|Adventure]]'' on the Atari 2600 is considered an open world game as the player can explore the entire game world save for through locked gates from the start, but it is not considered to have sandbox design as the player's actions are generally restricted.<ref name="Breslin-2009" /> Similarly, games like ''[[Microsoft Flight Simulator]]'' are also open world since the player can take their plane anywhere in the game's virtual world, but as there is no creative aspects to the game, would not be considered a sandbox.<ref name="Breslin-2009" />

== Characteristics ==
Sandbox design can incorporate several different [[game mechanics]] and structures, including [[open world]]s, [[Nonlinear narrative|nonlinear storytelling]], [[Emergent gameplay|emergent behaviors]], and [[Artificial intelligence in video games|automation]] of [[Intelligent agent|believable agents]].<ref name="Breslin-2009" /><ref>{{Cite web|title=Good Game Stories - Backwards Compatible - History of Sandbox Games|url=https://www.abc.net.au/tv/goodgame/stories/s2389739.htm|access-date=2020-05-14|website=www.abc.net.au}}</ref> It represents a shift [[Nonlinear gameplay|away from linear gameplay]].<ref>{{Cite news|last=Stuart|first=Keith|date=2008-09-10|title=Users are now the game developers|language=en-GB|work=The Guardian|url=https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2008/sep/11/1|access-date=2020-05-14|issn=0261-3077}}</ref><ref name="gamedeveloper.com-2010a">{{Cite web|title=The Contradiction Of Linearity|url=https://www.gamedeveloper.com/design/the-contradiction-of-linearity|access-date=2021-09-17|website=www.gamedeveloper.com|date=7 October 2010 |language=en}}</ref> This freedom is always a question of degree, as a sandbox design "engenders a sense of player control, without actually handing over the reins entirely".<ref name="Breslin-2009" />

Player creativity is often included in sandbox design. When a player is allowed to use a game as a sandbox, they gain the freedom to be creative with their gameplay.<ref>{{Cite web|title=The Designer's Notebook: A Few Remarks on Creative Play|url=https://www.gamedeveloper.com/design/the-designer-s-notebook-a-few-remarks-on-creative-play|access-date=2021-09-17|website=www.gamedeveloper.com|date=29 April 2005 |language=en}}</ref> A sandbox will have a combination of game mechanics and player freedom that can lead to emergent gameplay, where a player discovers solutions to challenges that may not be intended by the developers.<ref name="Breslin-2009" /> A sandbox sometimes gives the player "transformative" power over the game world, where "the free movement of play alters the more rigid structure in which it takes shape."<ref>{{Cite book|last=Warmelink|first=Harald|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=LELIAgAAQBAJ&q=%22play+that+occurs+when+the+free+movement+of+play+alters+the+more+rigid+structure+in+which+it+takes+shape%22+sandbox&pg=PA81|title=Online Gaming and Playful Organization|date=2014-02-03|publisher=Routledge|isbn=978-1-135-04024-6|language=en}}</ref> Will Wright describes this generative aspect of sandbox designs, leading to a measurable increase in player possibilities.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Remo|first=James Huck, Chris|title=Exclusive: Will Wright - Video Games Close To 'Cambrian Explosion' Of Possibilities|url=https://www.gamedeveloper.com/pc/exclusive-will-wright---video-games-close-to-cambrian-explosion-of-possibilities|access-date=2021-09-17|website=www.gamedeveloper.com|date=9 June 2008 |language=en}}</ref> [[John Smedley (video games)|John Smedley]] describes this type of emergent gameplay more succinctly, having seen in [[EverQuest]] "how hungry people are for sandboxes -- for building stuff".<ref>{{Cite web|last=Miller|first=Patrick|title=Emergent gameplay, F2P key for MMO user retention problems|url=https://www.gamedeveloper.com/business/emergent-gameplay-f2p-key-for-mmo-user-retention-problems|access-date=2021-09-17|website=www.gamedeveloper.com|date=10 October 2012 |language=en}}</ref> ''GameDeveloper.com'' notes the growth of player-generated content as a "particular brand of sandbox design: that game design is so fun in itself that, if properly packaged, it can well be reinterpreted as gameplay itself".<ref name="Breslin-2009" />

Some games offer a separate sandbox mode, where the player can use a game's creative systems with fewer constraints.<ref name="Adams-2010">{{Cite book|last=Adams|first=Ernest|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-BCrex2U1XMC&q=%22sandbox%22|title=Fundamentals of Game Design: Fundamentals of Game Design_2|date=2010-04-07|publisher=New Riders|isbn=978-0-13-210475-3|language=en}}</ref> "This mode has few restrictions on what he may do and offers no guidance on what he should do."<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Adams|first1=Ernest|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=jHghAQAAIAAJ&q=%22sandbox+mode%22|title=Fundamentals of Game Design|last2=Rollings|first2=Andrew|date=2007|publisher=Pearson Prentice Hall|isbn=978-0-13-168747-9|language=en}}</ref> For example, a sandbox mode might unlock unlimited resources, or disable enemy threats.<ref>{{cite book|author1=Jorge A. Blanco-Herrera|title=Video Games and Creativity|author2=Christopher L. Groves|author3=Ann M. Lewis|author4=Douglas A. Gentile|date=2015|publisher=[[Elsevier]]|isbn=978-0128017050|editor1=James C. Kaufman|pages=139–158|chapter=Chapter 7 - Teaching Creativity: Theoretical Models and Applications|editor2=Garo Green}}</ref> A sandbox mode is separate from the campaign mode, without a main narrative progression.<ref name="Breslin-2009" /> In one sense, an approach to this design is to "enable the player to continue after the main storyline has been 'won'."<ref>{{Cite book|last=Domsch|first=Sebastian|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=OJfoBQAAQBAJ&q=stild+andbox&pg=PA67|title=Storyplaying: Agency and Narrative in Video Games|date=2013-08-28|publisher=Walter de Gruyter|isbn=978-3-11-027245-1|language=en}}</ref>

Many games' [[Tutorial (video games)|tutorials]] utilize this type of design, since "sandboxes are game play much like the real game, but where things cannot go too wrong too quickly or, perhaps, even at all. Good games offer players, either as tutorials or as their first level or two, sandboxes."<ref>{{Cite web|title=Learning by Design: Games as Learning Machines|url=https://www.gamedeveloper.com/design/learning-by-design-games-as-learning-machines|access-date=2021-09-17|website=www.gamedeveloper.com|date=24 March 2004 |language=en}}</ref> The game designers allow players to experiment in a safe environment, as "the point about open-ended/sandbox design and when they work best in teaching the player is through learning by doing".<ref name="Bycer-2015">{{Cite web|date=2015-02-17|title=The Problems With Aimless Game Design|url=https://game-wisdom.com/critical/problems-aimless-game-design|access-date=2020-06-07|website=Game Wisdom|language=en-US|last=Bycer|first=Josh}}</ref>

Cohesive narratives in sandbox design can be difficult since the player can progress through the game in a non-linear manner.<ref>{{cite book|last=Domsch|first=Sebastian|title=Storyplaying: Agency and Narrative in Video Games|publisher=[[Walter de Gruyter]]|year=2013|isbn=978-3110272451|pages=61–68|chapter=3.2 Non-Unilinear Existents}}</ref> Some sandbox designs empower players to create their own stories, which is described as sandbox storytelling.<ref name="gamedeveloper.com-2010">{{Cite web|title=The Designer's Notebook: Sandbox Storytelling|url=https://www.gamedeveloper.com/design/the-designer-s-notebook-sandbox-storytelling|access-date=2020-05-14|website=www.gamedeveloper.com|date=25 August 2010 |language=en}}</ref> Sandbox stories can either replace or enhance a main plot.<ref name="gamedeveloper.com-2018">{{Cite web|title=The Four Basics of Open World Storytelling|url=https://www.gamedeveloper.com/design/the-four-basics-of-open-world-storytelling|access-date=2021-09-17|website=www.gamedeveloper.com|date=April 2018 |language=en}}</ref> Some games give players "pure agency by giving them tools and a sandbox",<ref>{{Cite book|last=Sainsbury|first=Matt|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=8_abCgAAQBAJ&q=sandbox|title=Game Art: Art from 40 Video Games and Interviews with Their Creators|date=2015|publisher=No Starch Press|isbn=978-1-59327-665-2|language=en}}</ref> sacrificing the story in favor of player creativity.<ref name="Dawson-2012">{{cite web|last=Dawson|first=Christopher|date=May 25, 2012|title=How 'Minecraft' became an Xbox blockbuster|url=https://www.cnn.com/2012/05/25/tech/gaming-gadgets/minecraft-xbox/index.html|access-date=May 2, 2020|work=[[CNN]]}}</ref> Where the game systems are reactive enough, this "does not remove the narrative, but rather transforms predetermined narrative into dynamic, responsive narrative".<ref name="Breslin-2009" /> According to [[Ernest Adams (game designer)|Ernest Adams]], "in sandbox storytelling, the idea is to give the player a big open world populated with opportunities for interesting interactions ... in any order".<ref name="gamedeveloper.com-2010" /> Sandbox stories can also be told through shorter quests, conversations, collectables, and encounters, all of which reward players for engaging with the world.<ref name="gamedeveloper.com-2018" /> This side-content becomes an "extremely common and an excellent format for sandbox gameplay: one central campaign (itself perhaps multi-threaded), plus a large number of side-missions".<ref name="Breslin-2009" /> In general, sandbox storytelling occurs when the player can move through the story independently of their movement through the game space.<ref name="gamedeveloper.com-2010" />

Designers also refer to sandbox worlds and sandbox game spaces, which create the feeling of a large [[open world]].<ref name="Totten-2018">{{Cite book|last=Totten|first=Christopher W.|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=WH06DwAAQBAJ&q=%22sandbox%22&pg=PA143|title=An Architectural Approach to Level Design|date=2018-09-03|publisher=CRC Press|isbn=978-1-351-98292-4|language=en}}</ref> The concept of an open world is much older than the term sandbox.<ref name="Breslin-2009" /> Overall, "a sandbox design usually means that the game space is not divided into discrete units", which emphasizes continuity and exploration.<ref name="Domsch-2013">{{Cite book|last=Domsch|first=Sebastian|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=OJfoBQAAQBAJ&q=sandbox&pg=PA67|title=Storyplaying: Agency and Narrative in Video Games|date=2013-08-28|publisher=Walter de Gruyter|isbn=978-3-11-027245-1|language=en}}</ref> This can sometimes overwhelm the player, which is why successful game designers draw on "urban design principles that can be used to build successful sandbox spaces".<ref name="Totten-2018" /> As a best practice "when creating these sandbox worlds, [designers] should divide them up into distinct areas to aid the player's navigation and orientation."<ref>{{Cite book|last=Rogers|first=Scott|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=UT5jAwAAQBAJ&q=%22sandbox%22&pg=PA233|title=Level Up! The Guide to Great Video Game Design|date=2014-04-16|publisher=John Wiley & Sons|isbn=978-1-118-87719-7|language=en}}</ref> Overall, a sandbox world should "provide the player with a large open set of spaces in which to play, and give him or her things to do".<ref name="Totten-2018" /> "The more a game's design tends towards a sandbox style, the less a player will feel obliged to follow the main quest."<ref name="Domsch-2013" />

Game designers often need to create more dynamic game systems to support sandbox-style gameplay. Physics systems are part of the sandbox experience of several games.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Moss|first=Richard|title=7 examples of great game physics that every developer should study|url=https://www.gamedeveloper.com/design/7-examples-of-great-game-physics-that-every-developer-should-study|access-date=2021-09-17|website=www.gamedeveloper.com|date=21 April 2016 |language=en}}</ref> The popularity of [[voxel]]s has also shown another system that can create "colourful sandboxes to dismantle and reconstruct."<ref>{{Cite web|last=Yarwood|first=Jack|title=How a new wave of developers are using voxels to create jaw-dropping worlds|url=https://www.gamedeveloper.com/design/how-a-new-wave-of-developers-are-using-voxels-to-create-jaw-dropping-worlds|access-date=2021-09-17|website=www.gamedeveloper.com|date=21 February 2020 |language=en}}</ref>

There is also the value of more robust artificial intelligence. ''GameDeveloper.com'' notes how "a sandbox means that the whole game becomes more of a simulation where AI plays an important role."<ref name="Staff-2008">{{Cite web|last=Staff|first=Alex J. Champandard|title=Special: Top 5 Game AI Trends For 2008|url=https://www.gamedeveloper.com/pc/special-top-5-game-ai-trends-for-2008|access-date=2020-06-12|website=www.gamedeveloper.com|date=February 2008 |language=en}}</ref> This means that "believable and self-motivated characters have become key to sandbox play, because they produce a rich space for interactivity and greatly help establish the open-world aesthetic."<ref name="Breslin-2009" /> Game designer John Krajewski observes for "a game that features sandbox-style play, the AI needs to provide enough different and interesting characters to interact within the world, and the size of the world doesn't have to get very big before it becomes unfeasible to hard code them all."<ref>{{Cite web|title=Creating All Humans: A Data-Driven AI Framework for Open Game Worlds|url=https://www.gamedeveloper.com/programming/creating-all-humans-a-data-driven-ai-framework-for-open-game-worlds|access-date=2021-09-17|website=www.gamedeveloper.com|date=4 February 2009 |language=en}}</ref>

An open-ended sandbox experience is sometimes contrasted with goal-oriented gameplay.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Postmortem: Poptop Software's Tropico|url=https://www.gamedeveloper.com/disciplines/postmortem-poptop-software-s-i-tropico-i-|access-date=2021-09-17|website=www.gamedeveloper.com|date=10 October 2001 |language=en}}</ref> Sandbox design usually minimizes the importance of goals. Rather than 'winning' a game, a sandbox design allows players to 'complete' a game by exploring and actualizing all of its options.<ref name="Domsch-2013" /> This lack of victory condition may define sandbox as [[Non-game|not a game]] at all. "For many, a game needs rules and a goal to be a game, which excludes sandbox/simulators."<ref name="Mitchell-2012">{{Cite book|last=Mitchell|first=Briar Lee|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=UZglGi-MDZIC&q=%22sandbox%22&pg=PT17|title=Game Design Essentials|date=2012-03-05|publisher=John Wiley & Sons|isbn=978-1-118-23933-9|language=en}}</ref> In sandbox mode, "the game resembles a tool more than a conventional video game".<ref name="Adams-2010" />

==History==

[[File:Actsmudgnome.png|thumb|upright=1.35|A screenshot of a MUD]]
[[Multi-user dungeon]]s (MUDs) are early examples of the principles of sandbox games originating in 1980;<ref>{{Cite web |last=Kelly |first=Kevin |last2=Rheingold |first2=Howard |year=1993 |title=Wired 1.03: The Dragon Ate My Homework |url=http://www.wired.com/wired/archive/1.03/muds.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121025101648/http://www.wired.com/wired/archive/1.03/muds.html |archive-date=October 25, 2012 |access-date=April 12, 2026 |website=[[Wired (magazine)|WIRED]]}}</ref> users of MUDs would generally be able to gain the ability to create their content within the MUD's framework, creating opportunities to collaborate with other users. However, MUDs never gained commercial release; while they inspired the first [[massively multiplayer online]] (MMO) games like [[Eve Online|EVE Online]], the creation aspects of MUDs did not carry into commercial games.<ref>{{cite conference | last1 = Acharya | first1 = Devi | first2= Noah | last2= Wardrip-Fruin | title = Building worlds together: understanding collaborative co-creation of game worlds | work = Proceedings of the 14th International Conference on the Foundations of Digital Games | pages = 1–5 | date = 2019 }}</ref>

Before 2000, the bulk of what were considered sandbox games in commercial software came from two genres:

* [[Space flight simulation game|Space trading and combat games]]: ''[[Elite (video game)|Elite]]'' (1984) is considered one of the first sandbox games: the player as a space pilot traveled across a randomly-generated galaxy, engaging in combat with enemies (one of the first games to use simulated 3D combat through wireframe graphics) and trading resources at various planets to improve their ship towards the best class possible, but otherwise the player has freedom towards completing this goal. ''Elite'' led to several similar trading and combat games, including ''[[The Seven Cities of Gold (video game)|The Seven Cities of Gold]]'' (1984), ''[[Sid Meier's Pirates!]]'' (1987), ''[[Star Control]]'' (1990), and ''[[Freelancer (video game)|Freelancer]]'' (2003).<ref name="Breslin-2009" />
* [[City-building game|City-building]] and [[Business simulation game|tycoon games]]: Early city-building games like ''[[Utopia (1981 video game)|Utopia]]'' (1982) were more focused on arranging city features for achieving high scores, but with ''[[SimCity (1989 video game)|SimCity]]'' (1989), [[Will Wright (game designer)|Will Wright]] wanted to give players more freedom to create a city and see how it operates while challenging the player to manage the growth of the city against its finances. ''SimCity''{{'s}} success led to many similar city-building and other tycoon games including ''[[Railroad Tycoon]]'' (1990), ''[[SimIsle: Missions in the Rainforest|SimIsle]]'' (1995), and ''[[Capitalism (video game)|Capitalism]]'' (1995).<ref name="Breslin-2009" />

Two games at the turn of the 21st century redefined the notion of what a sandbox game is.
* ''[[The Sims (video game)|The Sims]]'' (2000) is a [[life simulation game]] where the player interactions with simulated humans in a house as they go about their daily lives. Life simulation games were not a new genre, but prior games such as ''[[Little Computer People]]'' (1985) had very limited [[Artificial intelligence in video games|artificial intelligence]] beyond the simulated humans, limiting the number of interactions that a player had with the simulation and making such games more curiosities. With ''The Sims'', the simulated humans were given more detailed and believable behavior based on studies in [[artificial life]], which led to players experimenting more with the simulated humans and exploring the simulations.<ref name="Breslin-2009" /><ref name=" changing the game sims2">{{cite book|last1=Edery|first1=David1|title=Changing the Game: How Video Games Are Transforming the Future of Business|last2=Mollick|first2=Ethan|publisher=[[FT Press]]|year=2008|isbn=978-0137151752|pages=11–13}}</ref> In terms of defining the sandbox, ''The Sims'' was considered a freeform game, but added sets of minimal goals through the game to guide the player and encourage progression.<ref>{{cite magazine|author1=Alex Fitzpatrick|author2=John Patrick Pullen|author3=Josh Raab|author4=Lev Grossman|author5=Lisa Eadicicco|author6=Matt Peckham|author7=Matt Vella|date=August 23, 2016|title=The 50 Best Video Games of All Time|url=https://time.com/4458554/best-video-games-all-time/|access-date=May 2, 2020|magazine=[[Time (magazine)|Time]]}}</ref> ''The Sims'' became a best-selling title in the United States in 2000 and a long-running franchise for [[Electronic Arts]]. Further life simulation games would follow, such as ''[[Spore (2008 video game)|Spore]]'' (2008).<ref name="Breslin-2009" />
* ''[[Grand Theft Auto III]]'' (2001) is an [[action-adventure game]] in which the player takes the role of a small-time crook in a large city, completing various missions for bosses for the game. This was the first game in the [[open world]] ''[[Grand Theft Auto]]'' series to be set in a three-dimensional world, prior games having been played from a top-down perspective, and the first game to include a detailed [[physics engine]] for the various interaction of objects in the world. The combination of the game's open world and physics system allowed players to explore how they could cause havoc within the game, making the game a virtual sandbox with players to toy with.<ref name=" changing the game gta32">{{cite book|last1=Edery|first1=David1|title=Changing the Game: How Video Games Are Transforming the Future of Business|last2=Mollick|first2=Ethan|publisher=[[FT Press]]|year=2008|isbn=978-0137151752|pages=9–11}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last=Taylor|first=Laurie N.|title=The Meaning and Culture of Grand Theft Auto: Critical Essays|publisher=[[McFarland & Company]]|year=2006|isbn=0786428228|editor-last=Garrelts|editor-first=Nate|pages=115–125|chapter=From Stompin' Mushrooms to Bustin' Heads: Grand Theft Auto III as Paradigm Shift}}</ref> In this manner, ''Grand Theft Auto III'' added the idea of emergent gameplay as a feature of sandbox games.<ref>{{cite book|last=Taylor|first=Laurie N.|title=The Architecture Co-laboratory: GameSetandMatch II : on Computer Games, Advanced Geometries, and Digital Technologies|publisher=Episode Publishers|year=2006|isbn=9059730364|editor-last1=Oosterhuis|editor-first1=Kas|pages=98–106|chapter=Labyrinths, Mazes, Gardens, and Sandboxes: Game Space Metaphors|editor-last2=Feireiss|editor-first2=Lukas}}</ref>   ''Grand Theft Auto III'' succeeded ''The Sims'' as the best-selling game in the United States in 2001; In addition to its highly-successful sequels, ''Grand Theft Auto III'' led to a genre of derivative [[Grand Theft Auto clone|'' Grand Theft Auto'' clones]] focused on criminal activities such as the ''[[Saints Row]]'' series, as well as a broad range of open world, action-adventure games such as the ''[[Assassin's Creed]]'' and ''[[Far Cry]]'' series.<ref name="Breslin-2009" /> This action game broadened expectations of a sandbox, a concept that was previously reserved for experiences like ''SimCity''.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Sheffield|first=Brandon|title=Opinion: Clone Vs. Genre - When Art Imitates Art|url=https://www.gamedeveloper.com/pc/opinion-clone-vs-genre---when-art-imitates-art|access-date=2021-09-17|website=www.gamedeveloper.com|date=21 September 2009 |language=en}}</ref>

These two games would become a major influence on many different games and genres to come. In 2007, game designer [[Warren Spector]] noted the influence of Will Wright on numerous designers, but was surprised that there weren't more who "mimic Wright's games or his sandbox-style, saying titles in the ''Grand Theft Auto'' look-alike genre are about the closest most developers have come to doing so."<ref>{{Cite web|last=Duffy|first=Jill|title=GDC: Deus Ex Star Spector Questions Storytelling|url=https://www.gamedeveloper.com/pc/gdc-i-deus-ex-i-star-spector-questions-storytelling|access-date=2020-06-13|website=www.gamedeveloper.com|date=8 March 2007 |language=en}}</ref> This influence led to a trend, and by 2010 critics were noting that "almost every blockbuster game now contains a considerable 'sandbox' element."<ref name="gamedeveloper.com-2010a"/> This trend was linked to the rise of dynamic storytelling in sandbox worlds,<ref>{{Cite web|title=Gamasutra's Top 20 Trends of 2008|url=https://www.gamedeveloper.com/business/gamasutra-s-top-20-trends-of-2008|access-date=2021-09-17|website=www.gamedeveloper.com|date=17 December 2008 |language=en}}</ref> as well as AI that is dynamic enough to supplement scripted content.<ref name="Staff-2008" />

[[File:Minecraft Bedrock Inventory in Creative Mode.png|thumb|The creative mode inventory in ''[[Minecraft]]''. In creative mode, the player has little to no restrictions and unlimited resources.]]

Another major shift in sandbox games came with the release of ''[[Minecraft]]'', which was first introduced in 2009 in beta form and its first full release in 2011. At its core, ''Minecraft'' is a [[voxel]]-based [[survival game]], where players collect resources to build tools that help them to collect better resources, and to construct shelters to protect them from hostile creatures. However, there are no limits on how players can build these structures, and using the vast array of resources available in the game, players can build nearly anything they could imagine; the game has been compared to digital [[Lego]] bricks.<ref name="Dawson-2012" /> Players' use of ''Minecraft'' in this way led to the developers to add a dedicated "Creative Mode" that stripped the survival elements from the game so that players could build without any hazards or other artificial limits.<ref>{{cite web|last=Matulef|first=Jeffrey|date=October 16, 2012|title=Minecraft adds Creative Mode to the Xbox 360 version|url=https://www.eurogamer.net/articles/2012-10-16-minecraft-adds-creative-mode-to-the-xbox-360-version|access-date=May 2, 2020|work=[[Eurogamer]]}}</ref> ''Minecraft'' became a massive success, having sold more than 180 million copies by May 2019 and being the best selling [[personal computer]] game of all time.<ref name="China-300m2">{{cite news|last=Bailey|first=Dustin|title=Minecraft player count reaches 480 million|work=PCGamesN|url=https://www.pcgamesn.com/minecraft/minecraft-player-count|url-status=live|access-date=19 November 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191119042458/https://www.pcgamesn.com/minecraft/minecraft-player-count|archive-date=19 November 2019}}</ref> ''Minecraft'' has inspired a number of similar games, such as ''Allumeria'' and ''[[Lucid Blocks]]''.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Microsoft Withdraws Copyright Claim Against Indie Dev Over Minecraft Allegations |url=https://www.gamespot.com/articles/microsoft-withdraws-copyright-claim-against-indie-dev-over-minecraft-allegations/1100-6538103/ |access-date=2026-03-20 |website=GameSpot |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Tury |first=Jord |date=2026-03-15 |title=Lucid Blocks Review (PC) |url=https://www.gaming.net/reviews/lucid-blocks-review-pc/ |access-date=2026-03-20 |website=Gaming.net |language=en-US}}</ref>

One pure sandbox game, aimed to offer no goals but allow players to create works to be shared with others, is ''[[Second Life]]'' (2003), a large [[massively multiplayer online game]] set in a [[virtual world]] where users could create various sections of the world as their own. The game was purposely developed as a community-driven world, so while the developers established some of the fundamentals of the in-game economies, much of how the workings and economics of the rest of ''Second Life''{{'}}s world was set by the players, which created several issues around pricing, gambling, and taxes, among other aspects. The game ultimately drew use by businesses as well, seeking to create space within it.<ref>{{cite web|last=Hansen|first=Lauren|date=November 20, 2009|title=What happened to Second Life?|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/8367957.stm|access-date=May 5, 2020|work=[[BBC]]}}</ref>

More recent sandbox games have been aimed at providing interactive works that can be shared with others. ''[[Garry's Mod]]'' allows players to tinker with the [[Source (game engine)|Source engine]] from [[Valve Corporation|Valve]] to make animations and games<ref>{{cite web|last=Donnelly|first=Joe|date=August 27, 2015|title=The making of: Garry's Mod|url=https://www.pcgamesn.com/garrys-mod/the-making-of-garrys-mod|access-date=May 5, 2020|work=[[PCGamesN]]}}</ref> while games like ''[[LittleBigPlanet]]'' and ''[[Dreams (video game)|Dreams]]'' (2019) from [[Media Molecule]] give users assets and primitive programming elements to craft games that can be shared with others.<ref>{{cite web|last=Wen|first=Alan|date=July 17, 2019|title=From LittleBigPlanet to Dreams: Media Molecule and the future of DIY gaming|url=https://www.techradar.com/news/how-littlebigplanets-creators-pioneered-build-your-own-games|access-date=May 5, 2020|work=[[TechRadar]]}}</ref>

==Influence on other genres==
In time, sandbox design have become a mainstay in [[Survival horror|survival games]],<ref name="Bycer-2015" /> as well as a popular subset of [[First-person shooter|shooters]],<ref name="Mitchell-2012" /> and [[Action role-playing game|RPGs]].<ref>{{Cite book|last=Newman|first=Rich|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xu4Dw9GzRZwC&q=%22sandbox%22&pg=PA8|title=Cinematic Game Secrets for Creative Directors and Producers: Inspired Techniques From Industry Legends|date=2013-07-18|publisher=Taylor & Francis|isbn=978-1-136-13853-9|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Focusing Creativity: RPG Genres|url=https://www.gamedeveloper.com/design/focusing-creativity-rpg-genres|access-date=2021-09-17|website=www.gamedeveloper.com|date=24 January 2013 |language=en}}</ref> Long-time series such as ''[[Metal Gear]]'' had made the "shift to an open-world sandbox design," where the game dynamically "adds more missions as the story progresses and players complete the available side-ops".<ref>{{Cite web|date=2015-09-11|title=Metal Gear Solid V: The Phantom Pain Has the Best Open World|url=https://www.gamerevolution.com/features/11745-metal-gear-solid-v-the-phantom-pain-has-the-best-open-world|access-date=2020-06-13|website=GameRevolution}}</ref> Other long-running series such as ''[[Hitman (franchise)|Hitman]]'' were celebrated for their sandbox design.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Reviews round-up: Here's what critics think of Hitman 2|url=https://www.criticalhit.net/gaming/reviews-round-heres-critics-think-hitman-2/|access-date=2020-06-13|website=Critical Hit|date=8 November 2018 |language=en-GB}}</ref> The series became influential, creating a new template of games "that echo the same emphasis on sandbox design, open-ended mission structure, and sneaking".<ref>{{Cite web|date=2020-01-13|title=6 Games Like Hitman If You're Looking for Something Similar|url=https://twinfinite.net/2020/01/games-like-hitman/|access-date=2020-06-13|website=Twinfinite|language=en-US}}</ref> In 2020, [[PC Gamer]] noted ''[[Mount & Blade II: Bannerlord|Mount & Blade]]'' as "a triumph of sandbox design". They observe that "because of its sandbox nature, ''Mount & Blade''{{'}}s quests are procedurally generated around many set templates," which leads to a game where "the simulation is the story".<ref>{{Cite web|last=Savage|first=Phil|date=2017-04-06|title=Mount and Blade 2 is on a mission to be 2017's best RPG|url=https://www.pcgamer.com/mount-and-blade-2-is-on-a-mission-to-be-2017s-best-rpg/|access-date=2020-06-13|website=PC Gamer|language=en-US}}</ref>

Starting in the late 2000s, [[Superhero fiction|superhero games]] have also begun to incorporate sandbox elements. Unlike common sandbox games during that time, where players control a semi-grounded normal human, superhero sandbox games have premises that involved controlling [[Superhero|superpowered beings]] in a large open-world environment.<ref name="Ranty">{{cite news|url=https://gamerant.com/best-open-world-superhero-games/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240210120637/https://gamerant.com/best-open-world-superhero-games/|archive-date=February 10, 2024|title=10 Best Open-World Superhero Games, Ranked|newspaper=GameRant|author=Rodriguez, Jonathan}} February 8, 2024</ref> The first titles to utilize such premise were licensed superhero games such as [[Spider-Man 2 (2004 video game)|''Spider-Man 2'']] and [[The Incredible Hulk: Ultimate Destruction|''Hulk: Ultimate Destruction'']].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Kane |first=Alex |date=2018-07-09 |title=The Oral History of Treyarch's Spider-Man 2: One of the Best Superhero Games Ever |url=https://www.usgamer.net/articles/treyarch-spider-man-2-oral-history-superhero-game-07-09-2018 |access-date=February 9, 2019 |website=USGamer.net |archive-date=February 10, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190210154120/https://www.usgamer.net/articles/treyarch-spider-man-2-oral-history-superhero-game-07-09-2018 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name="AV">{{cite news|url=https://www.gamesradar.com/how-hulk-inspired-prototype-and-9-spiritual-successors-came-be/|title=Prototype was inspired by Hulk: Ultimate Destruction|newspaper=Games Radar|author=Gilbert, Henry}} August 27, 2013</ref> The release of the 2007 game [[Crackdown (video game)|''Crackdown'']], redefined these gameplay elements by adding the ability to level up and earn new weapons and powers. The game went on to influence similar original sandbox games like the 2009 titles [[Infamous (video game)|''Infamous'']] and ''[[Prototype (video game)|Prototype]]''.<ref name="Tel">{{cite web|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/technology/video-games/7880285/Crackdown-2-video-game-review.html|title=Crackdown 2 video game review|publisher=[[The Telegraph (magazine)|The Telegraph]]|author= Cowen, Nick|date=12 July 2010 }} July 12, 2010</ref><ref name="joystiq fleming interview">{{cite web | url = http://www.joystiq.com/2009/03/25/gdc09-an-infamous-interview-with-sucker-punchs-brian-fleming/ | title = GDC09: An inFamous interview with Sucker Punch's Brian Fleming | first = Kevin | last = Kelly | date = 2009-03-25 | access-date = 2009-06-26 | publisher = Joystiq | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20150128000041/http://www.joystiq.com/2009/03/25/gdc09-an-infamous-interview-with-sucker-punchs-brian-fleming/ | archive-date = 2015-01-28 }}</ref> ''Infamous'', in particular, added a morality system where the player can choose to be a superhero or a supervillain.<ref name="joystiq fleming interview"/> Other established sandbox games such as ''[[Saints Row]]'' and [[Just Cause (video game series)|''Just Cause'']], also began to incorporate these gameplay in their recent titles.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.gamesindustry.biz/articles/2013-08-14-critical-consensus-saints-row-4|title=Critical Consensus: Saints Row 4|publisher=gameindustry.biz|author=Martin, Matt|date=14 August 2013 }} August 14, 2013</ref>

==Criticism==
Sandbox design has been criticized for providing a lack of satisfying goals for players. According to [[Ernest Adams (game designer)|Ernest Adams]], "plunking the player down in a sandbox and saying, 'have fun' isn't good enough. Especially at the beginning of a game, the player should have a clear sense of what to do next and, in particular, why."<ref>{{Cite web|last=Adams|first=Ernest|title=The Designer's Notebook: The Bill of Players Rights|url=https://www.gamedeveloper.com/design/the-designer-s-notebook-the-bill-of-players-rights|access-date=2021-09-17|website=www.gamedeveloper.com|date=26 August 2005 |language=en}}</ref> Christopher Totten observes that "sandbox elements can be mistakenly taken as fair replacements of narrative content; indeed, many games have missed their potential because they imagined that free-play would compensate for a lack of narrative. But even for our idealized child, playing around in a physical sandbox gets old pretty quick."<ref name="Totten-2018" /> Critics point to repetitive in-game tasks, arguing that an "overabundance of mundane events can get in the way of enjoying the sandbox."<ref>{{Cite web|last=Doyle|first=Nick|date=2015-01-13|title=Why More Open World Games is a Bad Thing|url=http://gamemoir.com/more-open-world-games-bad-thing/|access-date=2020-06-08|website=Gamemoir|language=en-US|url-status=usurped<!-- Google Malware Detect 26 April 2023 -->|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170115154708/http://gamemoir.com/more-open-world-games-bad-thing/|archive-date=2017-01-15}}</ref> ''GameDeveloper.com'' notes that the quality of sandbox gameplay varies because "the great risk of the sandbox is that it can be boring." This is because "sand by itself is not much fun. Automated, complex, and perhaps most of all, ''directed'' responsiveness is essential to sandbox play, and the more complex and responsive the world, the more interesting the sandbox."<ref name="Breslin-2009" /> In addition, sandbox games tend to be more expensive than other games to produce, in both money and time.<ref name="Breslin-2009" />

==Use in education==
{{Expand section|date=January 2022}}

Some sandbox games have gained traction in educational settings, particularly to develop students' creativity and critical thinking skills.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Chang|first=Dixie|date=December 2012|title=Passion play: Will Wright and games for science learning|journal=Cultural Studies of Science Education|volume=7|issue=4|pages=767–782|doi=10.1007/s11422-012-9456-5|bibcode=2012CSSE....7..767C |s2cid=143547050}}</ref>

Part of [[Microsoft]]'s rationale for acquiring [[Mojang]], developer of ''[[Minecraft]]'', for {{USD|2.5 billion}} in 2014 was for its potential application in [[science, technology, engineering, and mathematics]] (STEM) education, according to CEO [[Satya Nadella]], as the game already helps to pique children's curiosity.<ref>{{cite web|last=Soper|first=Taylor|date=September 15, 2014|title=Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella on Minecraft: 'It's the one game parents want their kids to play'|url=https://www.geekwire.com/2014/microsoft-ceo-satya-nadella-minecraft-one-game-parents-want-kids-play/|access-date=May 12, 2020|work=[[GeekWire]]}}</ref> Microsoft subsequently enhanced the ''MinecraftEDU'' version of the game into ''Minecraft: Education Edition'' (later known as ''[[Minecraft#Minecraft Education|Minecraft Education]]'') that gives teachers and students numerous pre-made resources to work from. It features the ability for teachers to monitor and assist students in their work, but otherwise allows students to create and learn following several lesson plans developed by Microsoft, including within the aforementioned STEM subjects.<ref>{{cite web|last=Kellon|first=Leo|date=January 19, 2016|title=Minecraft to launch education edition|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/technology-35341528|access-date=May 12, 2020|work=[[BBC]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last=Kamenetz|first=Anya|date=August 9, 2017|title='Schoolifying' Minecraft Without Ruining It|url=https://www.npr.org/sections/ed/2017/08/09/539518179/schoolifying-minecraft-without-ruining-it|access-date=May 12, 2020|work=[[NPR]]}}</ref>

Research conducted during the 2018/2019 academic year suggested the educational potential of the ''[[Roblox]]'' platform. The study involved 53 students tasked to create a virtual environment using [[3D modeling|3D models]] of the sculptural heritage of [[Santa Cruz de Tenerife]]. Students reported improvements in their understanding, not only of creating interactive worlds through ''Roblox'', but also understanding of the sculptural heritage of the city.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Meier |first=Cecile |last2=Saorin |first2=Jose |last3=de León |first3=Alejandro Bonnet |last4=Cobos |first4=Alberto Guerrero |year=2020 |title=Using the roblox video game engine for creating virtual tours and learning about the sculptural heritage |url=https://www.learntechlib.org/p/218337/ |journal=[[International Journal of Educational Technology]] |volume=15 |issue=20 |pages=268-280}}</ref>

Educators and schools leverage ''Roblox'' for their computer and programming lessons. Students learning with ''Roblox'' can use their game creation engine ''Roblox Studio''; the creation of these games can inspire students to work creatively with various concepts.{{citation needed|date=January 2026}}

{{Short description|2001 video game}}
{{good article}}
