'''''Artifact''''' is a 2018 [[digital collectible card game]] by [[Valve Corporation|Valve]] for [[Windows]], [[macOS]], and [[Linux]]. It focuses on online [[player-versus-player]] battles and is based on the universe of ''[[Dota 2]]'', a [[multiplayer online battle arena]] game by Valve. ''Artifact'' was designed by ''[[Magic: The Gathering]]'' creator [[Richard Garfield]].

While ''Artifact''{{'s}} gameplay and drafting mechanics received praise, it was criticized for its high [[learning curve]] and [[monetization model]], which some saw as [[pay-to-win]]. It saw a 95% decline in players within two months of its release, with only around a hundred concurrent players by mid-2019. Valve was surprised by the response, describing it as the largest discrepancy between their expectations for a game and the outcome.

Valve reworked the game as ''Artifact 2.0'', altering several features, including removing the need to buy or trade cards with money. It was tested through a [[closed beta]] starting in March 2020. A year later, Valve announced that it had ceased development of the game, citing a lack of player interest, and made both versions of the game [[freeware]]. The original ''Artifact'' was renamed '''''Artifact Classic''''' and ''Artifact 2.0'' was renamed '''''Artifact Foundry'''''.

== Gameplay ==
[[File:Artifact screenshot.jpg|thumb|right|''Artifact'' has players competing in three separate boards in sequential order, mimicking the three lanes of ''Dota 2''{{'s}} map.]]
''Artifact'' is a [[digital collectible card game]] in which players build a deck of collectable cards purchased on the [[Steam Marketplace]] to defeat an opponent in one-on-one battles.<ref name="Gameplay">{{cite web|last1=Marks|first1=Tom|title=Artifact: Everything We Know About Valve's Next Game|url=http://www.ign.com/articles/2018/03/09/everything-we-know-so-far-about-valves-next-game|website=IGN|date=March 9, 2018|access-date=March 9, 2018|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180309125326/http://www.ign.com/articles/2018/03/09/everything-we-know-so-far-about-valves-next-game|archive-date=March 9, 2018}}</ref> It features many elements from the [[multiplayer online battle arena]] game ''[[Dota 2]]'', also developed by Valve.<ref name="announcement">{{cite web |url=https://www.polygon.com/2017/8/8/16116786/valve-artifact-dota-2-card-game |title=Valve announces Artifact, a Dota 2 card game |website=[[Polygon (website)|Polygon]] |first=Arthur |last=Gies |date=August 8, 2017 |access-date=August 9, 2017 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170809073740/https://www.polygon.com/2017/8/8/16116786/valve-artifact-dota-2-card-game |archive-date=August 9, 2017}}</ref> Unlike most collectible card games, it features three "lanes" guarded by a tower at the end, with each lane existing as an independent board. The victor is the first player to either destroy a structure called the Ancient, which appears after a tower has been destroyed, or the first to destroy two towers in total.<ref name="lanes">{{cite web|last1=Bailey|first1=Dustin|title=Artifact has 280 cards and three lanes of play|url=https://pcgamesn.com/artifact/artifact-lanes-card-count|website=PCGamesN|date=March 9, 2018 |access-date=March 9, 2018|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180309073220/https://www.pcgamesn.com/artifact/artifact-lanes-card-count|archive-date=March 9, 2018}}</ref><ref name="Gameplay notes">{{cite web|last1=Clark|first1=Tim|title=Everything you need to know about Valve's Artifact: "The whole point is to steer away from pay-to-win"|url=https://www.pcgamer.com/artifact-guide/|website=PC Gamer|access-date=March 13, 2018|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180314043459/https://www.pcgamer.com/artifact-guide/|archive-date=March 14, 2018}}</ref> As with ''Dota 2'', ''Artifact'' focuses on online [[player versus player]] matchmaking; it has no [[single-player]] mode beyond a tutorial mode against an AI opponent.<ref name="IGN details">{{cite web|last1=Stewart|first1=Sam|title=Valve Releases First Details About Artifact|url=http://www.ign.com/articles/2018/03/09/valve-releases-first-details-about-artifact|website=IGN|access-date=March 8, 2018|date=March 8, 2018|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180309043242/http://www.ign.com/articles/2018/03/09/valve-releases-first-details-about-artifact|archive-date=March 9, 2018}}</ref>

Each deck contains at least 40 cards, with a total of nearly 300 cards available at the game's launch.<ref name="Gameplay notes"/> Cards are grouped into three rarity tiers, common, uncommon, and rare, and are further grouped into four color themes, red, green, black, and blue, that each have their own unique effects on the board.<ref name="Gameplay notes"/><ref name="IGN Marketplace">{{cite web |last1=Marks |first1=Tom |title=How Valve Won't Let Artifact's Marketplace Get Crazy Expensive |url=http://www.ign.com/articles/2018/08/31/how-valve-wont-let-artifacts-marketplace-get-crazy-expensive |website=IGN |date=August 31, 2018 |access-date=August 31, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180831214617/http://www.ign.com/articles/2018/08/31/how-valve-wont-let-artifacts-marketplace-get-crazy-expensive |archive-date=August 31, 2018 |url-status=live  }}</ref> Each lane also has its own independent [[Magic (gaming)|mana pool]], which is used for casting hero abilities and grows by one point after each round while also fully replenishing. In addition to hero abilities, [[Item (gaming)|item]] cards can also be freely placed and used in any lane. Each time a card is played, the initiative passes to the opposing player. After all cards have been played in a lane, heroes and "creeps", which are weak but numerous [[Mob (gaming)|mobs]] that can not be directly controlled and respawn every round, begin attacking whatever is opposite them, including the opposing tower if there are no units left.<ref name="Gameplay notes"/> This repeats until all three lanes have been played, after which it goes to the "Shopping Phase", where gold accumulated during battles is spent on buying items and upgrading hero equipment in three different slots for weapons, armor, and accessories.<ref name="Gameplay notes"/>

== Development ==
Development of ''Artifact'' began in late 2014, with lead designer [[Richard Garfield]] brought in to help make a digital card game due to his experience with creating the popular ''[[Magic: The Gathering]]'' franchise.<ref name="Gameplay notes"/><ref>{{cite web|publisher=Valve News Network|title=Exclusive Artifact Interview, Unused Content & Card Reveal|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VTS4rF6-DiY|website=YouTube|date=September 23, 2018 |access-date=September 24, 2018|type=Video|archive-date=December 2, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181202224357/https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VTS4rF6-DiY|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="EurogamerGarfield">{{cite web|publisher=Eurogamer|title=We interview Artifact's lead designer, Richard Garfield (AKA the creator of Magic: The Gathering)|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_If41SYSg3c|website=YouTube|date=May 2, 2018 |access-date=May 2, 2018|type=Video|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180502215651/https://www.youtube.com/watch?feature=youtu.be&v=_If41SYSg3c&app=desktop|archive-date=May 2, 2018}}</ref> The game was then announced via a [[teaser trailer]] played at [[The International 2017]], a large ''Dota 2''-specific [[esports]] tournament organized by [[Valve Corporation|Valve]], although no specific details were revealed.<ref name="announcement"/> More details regarding its concept and gameplay were revealed by Valve president [[Gabe Newell]] during a meeting with gaming press at Valve's headquarters in March 2018.<ref name="IGN details"/> There, Newell stated that it was not originally intended to be based on ''Dota 2'', but it was decided to do so later in development as it was "useful".<ref>{{cite web|last1=Scott-Jones|first1=Richard|title=Artifact will add to Dota 2's lore and hero roster|url=https://www.pcgamesn.com/artifact/artifact-dota-2-heroes-lore|website=PCGamesN|date=March 9, 2018 |access-date=March 9, 2018|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180309063425/https://www.pcgamesn.com/artifact/artifact-dota-2-heroes-lore|archive-date=March 9, 2018}}</ref> Newell also stated that it would not be [[free-to-play]] like ''Dota 2'' and other similar card game competitors, and that the team wished for it to avoid becoming "[[pay-to-win]]". He hoped ''Artifact'' would be for card games what ''[[Half-Life 2]]'' had been for single-player action games.<ref name="Gameplay notes"/><ref name="f2p">{{cite web|last1=Bailey|first1=Dustin|title=Artifact won't be free-to-play or pay-to-win|url=https://www.pcgamesn.com/artifact/artifact-free-to-play|website=PCGamesN|date=March 9, 2018 |access-date=March 9, 2018|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180309073132/https://www.pcgamesn.com/artifact/artifact-free-to-play|archive-date=March 9, 2018}}</ref>

''Artifact'' was created using Valve's [[Source 2]] game engine, and features direct integration with the [[Steam Marketplace]] for buying and selling cards.<ref name="IGN Marketplace"/><ref name="Source 2">{{cite web|last1=Bailey|first1=Dustin|title=Artifact will use Source 2, bringing the engine to iOS and Android|url=https://www.pcgamesn.com/artifact/artifact-source-2-ios-android|website=PCGamesN|date=March 9, 2018 |access-date=March 9, 2018|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180309192121/https://www.pcgamesn.com/artifact/artifact-source-2-ios-android|archive-date=March 9, 2018}}</ref> While acknowledging that card games and Steam Marketplace transactions can both get expensive, such as with gun cosmetics in Valve's own ''[[Counter-Strike: Global Offensive]]'', Garfield notes that printing restrictions do not exist with digital cards, and that Valve would directly control the production of them to limit extreme rarity.<ref name="IGN Marketplace"/> In addition, purchased card packs always include a rare card in them, which Valve hoped would prevent single cards being sold for high prices as it would be more valuable to purchase packs.<ref name="IGN Marketplace"/> ''Artifact'' also allows players to assemble decks outside of the game by using third-party tools, which can then be imported back into the game.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Horti |first1=Samuel |title=Artifact will let you build decks online and then import them into the game |url=https://www.pcgamer.com/artifact-will-let-you-build-decks-online-and-then-import-them-into-the-game/ |website=PC Gamer |date=November 10, 2018 |access-date=November 10, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181111043849/https://www.pcgamer.com/artifact-will-let-you-build-decks-online-and-then-import-them-into-the-game/ |archive-date=November 11, 2018 |url-status=live  }}</ref> Wanting to build upon what they had learned from ''Dota 2'', ''Global Offensive'', and ''[[Team Fortress 2]]'', Valve planned for the game to have a professional esports scene, with revenue made from card pack purchasing feeding into tournament prize pools, similar to ''Dota 2''{{'s}} "Compendium" [[crowdfunding]] system.<ref name="f2p"/><ref name="eSports">{{cite web|last1=Scott-Jones|first1=Richard|title=Artifact on track for 2018 release, will have a $1m tournament early next year|url=https://www.pcgamesn.com/artifact/artifact-esports|website=PCGamesN|date=March 9, 2018 |access-date=March 9, 2018|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180310010104/https://www.pcgamesn.com/artifact/artifact-esports|archive-date=March 10, 2018}}</ref> Valve planned for a million-dollar tournament to take place in 2019, but due to the game's commercial failure, no tournament was ever held.<ref name="eSports"/>

''Artifact'' was planned to be developed alongside ''Dota 2'', where both games would share new heroes and other content. Writer Steve Jaros wrote character lore for ''Dota 2'' and continued that role with ''Artifact'' by having each individual card provide more of it, all fully voiced, which he hopes would keep both games narratively connected.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Marks |first1=Tom |title=9 Things Artifact Doesn't Tell You |url=https://www.ign.com/articles/2018/11/28/9-things-artifact-doesnt-tell-you |website=IGN |date=November 28, 2018 |access-date=November 28, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181129013356/https://www.ign.com/articles/2018/11/28/9-things-artifact-doesnt-tell-you |archive-date=November 29, 2018 |url-status=live  }}</ref> Programmer Jeep Barnett said they planned to have card set expansions progress over time, so that heroes in one set may have an aged version in a future set, or may die in one, and events of previous expansions can influence future ones.<ref name="EurogamerGarfield"/><ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.pcgamesn.com/artifact/artifact-expansions | title = Artifact heroes can age and die between card expansions | first = Ali | last = Jones | date = May 4, 2018 | access-date = May 4, 2018 | website = [[PCGamesN]] | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20180504155958/https://www.pcgamesn.com/artifact/artifact-expansions | archive-date = May 4, 2018 | url-status = live | df = mdy-all }}</ref> The soundtrack was written by [[Tim Larkin (composer)|Tim Larkin]], who also composed for ''Dota 2''.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Larson |first1=Randall |title=ARTIFACT – Music for Digital Card Gaming |url=https://musiquefantastique.com/further-examinations/artifact-music-for-digital-card-gaming/ |website=musiquefantastique.com |date=November 30, 2018 |access-date=December 6, 2018 |archive-date=December 7, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181207045827/https://musiquefantastique.com/further-examinations/artifact-music-for-digital-card-gaming/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

=== Release ===
''Artifact'' entered [[closed beta]] in early 2018, with numerous gaming industry members and professional card game players invited to test it.<ref name="IGN details"/> It was publicly playable for the first time at [[PAX West]] 2018, with a tournament hosted and all attendees receiving signed artwork prints and [[product key]]s for two free copies of the game.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Fogel |first1=Stefanie |title=Valve's 'Artifact' Will Be Playable at PAX West |url=https://variety.com/2018/gaming/news/valve-artifact-pax-west-1202892399/ |website=Variety |date=August 2018 |access-date=August 2, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180801195309/https://variety.com/2018/gaming/news/valve-artifact-pax-west-1202892399/ |archive-date=August 1, 2018 |url-status=live  }}</ref> A [[beta]] for the PC version was released a week before the official launch, with attendees of [[The International 2018]] ''Dota 2'' tournament and its showing at PAX West given access to it.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Bailey |first1=Dustin |title=Artifact beta launches in October |url=https://www.pcgamesn.com/artifact/artifact-beta |website=PCGamesN |access-date=August 20, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180820235232/https://www.pcgamesn.com/artifact/artifact-beta |archive-date=August 20, 2018 |url-status=live  }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Horti |first1=Samuel |title=Artifact's open beta appears to have been delayed until November 19 |url=https://www.pcgamer.com/artifacts-open-beta-appears-to-have-been-delayed-until-november-19-just-nine-days-before-full-release/ |website=PC Gamer |date=October 20, 2018 |access-date=October 20, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181020170130/https://www.pcgamer.com/artifacts-open-beta-appears-to-have-been-delayed-until-november-19-just-nine-days-before-full-release/ |archive-date=October 20, 2018 |url-status=live  }}</ref>

''Artifact'' was released for [[Windows]], [[macOS]] and [[Linux]] on November 28, 2018, and was planned for [[Android (operating system)|Android]] and [[iOS]] devices in 2019.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Cryer|first1=Hirun|title=Artifact, Valve's Card Game – Release Date, Gameplay, Dota 2 Cards – Everything we Know|url=https://www.usgamer.net/articles/09-03-2018-artifact-valves-card-game-release-date-gameplay-dota-2-cards|website=USGamer|access-date=March 9, 2018|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180310200808/https://www.usgamer.net/articles/09-03-2018-artifact-valves-card-game-release-date-gameplay-dota-2-cards|archive-date=March 10, 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Chalk |first1=Andy |title=Artifact, Valve's fantasy card game, will be out in November |url=https://www.pcgamer.com/artifact-valves-fantasy-card-game-will-be-out-in-november/ |website=PC Gamer |date=August 2018 |access-date=August 1, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180801195743/https://www.pcgamer.com/artifact-valves-fantasy-card-game-will-be-out-in-november/ |archive-date=August 1, 2018 |url-status=live  }}</ref> To help promote the game, a 128-player tournament featuring a {{USD}}10,000 prize pool was held on November 10–11, 2018.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Wilde |first1=Tyler |title=Valve is running an Artifact 'preview tournament' to show off its built-in tournament system |url=https://www.pcgamer.com/valve-is-running-an-artifact-preview-tournament-to-show-off-its-built-in-tournament-system/ |website=PC Gamer |date=November 3, 2018 |access-date=November 3, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181103021531/https://www.pcgamer.com/valve-is-running-an-artifact-preview-tournament-to-show-off-its-built-in-tournament-system/ |archive-date=November 3, 2018 |url-status=live  }}</ref> In addition, two [[webcomic]]s by Valve were released to coincide with the game's launch.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Chalk |first1=Andy |title=Artifact's debut comic teases events that will 'transform the world of Dota forever' |url=https://www.pcgamer.com/artifacts-debut-comic-teases-events-that-will-transform-the-world-of-dota-forever/ |website=PC Gamer |date=November 27, 2018 |access-date=November 27, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181127081434/https://www.pcgamer.com/artifacts-debut-comic-teases-events-that-will-transform-the-world-of-dota-forever/ |archive-date=November 27, 2018 |url-status=live  }}</ref> All owners of the game were given a redeemable token worth a free month of "Dota Plus", ''Dota 2''{{'s}} [[battle pass]] feature.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Daro |first1=Catherine |title=Purchase Artifact & Receive A Free Month of Dota Plus |url=https://www.gamespace.com/all-articles/news/artifact-free-month-dota-plus/ |website=Game Space |date=November 29, 2018 |access-date=December 2, 2018 |archive-date=December 2, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181202224357/https://www.gamespace.com/all-articles/news/artifact-free-month-dota-plus/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

=== ''Artifact 2.0'' ===
In 2020, following a lack of player interest, Newell told ''[[Edge (magazine)|Edge]]'' that Valve had begun reworking ''Artifact'' as a new game, ''Artifact 2.0.''<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|last=Avard|first=Alex |title=Valve's digital card game Artifact "reboot" is so large, it's internally being called Artifact 2, says Gabe Newell|url=https://www.gamesradar.com/artifact-2-edge-magazine/|url-status=live|access-date=2021-03-04|website=[[GamesRadar]]|date=March 20, 2020|language=en|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200320163120/https://www.gamesradar.com/artifact-2-edge-magazine/ |archive-date=March 20, 2020 }}</ref> The primary change was to eliminate card purchases and make all three lanes visible at the same time.<ref name="a2.0 closed beta">{{cite web|last1=Gilliam|first1=Ryan|title=Valve details major changes for Artifact's new beta|url=https://www.polygon.com/2020/3/30/21200184/valve-artifact-beta-2-0-return-rework-card-game|access-date=March 30, 2020|website=Polygon|date=March 30, 2020|archive-date=March 31, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200331151420/https://www.polygon.com/2020/3/30/21200184/valve-artifact-beta-2-0-return-rework-card-game|url-status=live}}</ref> The game would also include a [[single-player]] campaign.<ref>{{cite web|last=Cox|first=Matt|date=April 21, 2020|title=Artifact 2.0 will have a singleplayer campaign|url=https://www.rockpapershotgun.com/2020/04/21/artifact-2-0-will-have-a-singleplayer-campaign/|access-date=April 21, 2020|work=[[Rock Paper Shotgun]]|archive-date=April 29, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200429000041/https://www.rockpapershotgun.com/2020/04/21/artifact-2-0-will-have-a-singleplayer-campaign/|url-status=live}}</ref> A [[Software release life cycle|closed beta]] started in March 2020.<ref name="a2.0 closed beta" /> That month, Garfield and another ''Magic: The Gathering'' designer, [[Skaff Elias]], among other contractors and employees, were laid off from Valve.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Valve layoff includes Artifact designer Richard Garfield|url=https://www.shacknews.com/article/110417/valve-layoff-includes-artifact-designer-richard-garfield|access-date=2021-03-04|website=Shacknews|date=March 11, 2019|language=en|archive-date=November 7, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201107231301/https://www.shacknews.com/article/110417/valve-layoff-includes-artifact-designer-richard-garfield|url-status=live}}</ref>

In March 2021, Valve announced that it had halted development of ''Artifact 2.0.,'' saying they had not attracted enough players to justify further work. They made both ''Artifact'' games, renamed ''Artifact Classic'' and ''Artifact Foundry'', completely free.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Marshall|first=Cass|date=2021-03-04|title=Valve cancels Artifact 2.0, makes existing versions free|url=https://www.polygon.com/2021/3/4/22314068/artifact-next-canceled-free-to-play-valve-dota|access-date=2021-03-04|website=Polygon|language=en|archive-date=March 4, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210304214249/https://www.polygon.com/2021/3/4/22314068/artifact-next-canceled-free-to-play-valve-dota|url-status=live}}</ref>

}}

''Artifact''<nowiki/>'s gameplay and depth were praised, with Ali Jones of ''[[PCGamesN]]'' stating in a preview that the game was a "cut above" other card games he had played before. He also added that it successfully captured elements from two different genres, creating something that he was "hugely excited to return to".<ref>{{cite web|last1=Jones|first1=Ali|title=Artifact isn't late to the CCG party, it's about to revolutionise card games|url=https://www.pcgamesn.com/artifact/artifact-review-pc|website=PCGamesN|date=March 9, 2018 |access-date=March 13, 2018|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180310010240/https://www.pcgamesn.com/artifact/artifact-review-pc|archive-date=March 10, 2018}}</ref> The game was also being compared to ''[[Hearthstone]]'', with Mike Minotti of ''[[Venture Beat]]'' considering ''Artifact'' as the more complex, in-depth option that has a chance of become the leading digital card game on the market.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Minotti|first1=Mike|title=Artifact hands-on: Valve's Dota 2-based card game sure isn't Hearthstone|url=https://venturebeat.com/2018/03/09/artifact-hands-on-hearthstone-this-aint/|website=Venture Beat|date=March 9, 2018|access-date=March 13, 2018|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180314043115/https://venturebeat.com/2018/03/09/artifact-hands-on-hearthstone-this-aint/|archive-date=March 14, 2018}}</ref> While also noting the game's complexity, Julian Benson of ''PCGamesN'' compared it more to ''[[Magic: The Gathering]]'' as its creator, Richard Garfield, served as the lead designer on the game.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Benson|first1=Julian|title=Gabe Newell: "Hearthstone's the benchmark online card game"|url=https://www.pcgamesn.com/artifact/artifact-vs-hearthstone|website=PCGamesN|date=March 9, 2018 |access-date=March 13, 2018|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180314043055/https://www.pcgamesn.com/artifact/artifact-vs-hearthstone|archive-date=March 14, 2018}}</ref>

Tim Clark of ''[[PC Gamer]]'' praised the art style and presentation, noting that all of the game's assets were new and not directly copied over from ''Dota 2''. Clark also stated that he could not wait to play more of the game, saying that he did not see it as a "cash grab" that others said it would be.<ref name="Gameplay notes" /> James Davenport of the same publication thought that the gameplay was akin to ''Magic: The Gathering'' meeting three simultaneous games of [[Uno (card game)|Uno]], and stated that while the game at first looked "extremely complex", it did not take him long to understand and begin playing.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Davenport |first1=James |title=Artifact is not nearly as hard to play as it looks |url=https://www.pcgamer.com/artifact-is-not-nearly-as-hard-to-play-as-it-looks/ |website=PC Gamer |date=September 2018 |access-date=September 3, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180902112948/https://www.pcgamer.com/artifact-is-not-nearly-as-hard-to-play-as-it-looks/ |archive-date=September 2, 2018 |url-status=live  }}</ref> Eric Van Allen of ''[[Polygon (website)|Polygon]]'' added that while the game demands investment to learn, it was "intensely rewarding" for those who stuck with it and did not mind its monetization model.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Van Allen |first1=Eric |title=Artifact review: Valve's card game is deep, but burdened by its marketplace |url=https://www.polygon.com/reviews/2018/11/28/18115031/artifact-review-dota-2-card-game |website=Polygon |date=November 28, 2018 |access-date=November 28, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181128192658/https://www.polygon.com/reviews/2018/11/28/18115031/artifact-review-dota-2-card-game |archive-date=November 28, 2018 |url-status=live  }}</ref>

=== Player response ===
Reception to the ''Artifact'' announcement at The International in 2017 was mixed, with the crowd voicing their disapproval.<ref name="Verge boo">{{cite web|last1=Savov|first1=Vlad|title=Valve is getting into card games and people are mad|url=https://www.theverge.com/tldr/2017/8/9/16118582/valve-artifact-card-game-dota-2-disappointment|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180309120402/https://www.theverge.com/tldr/2017/8/9/16118582/valve-artifact-card-game-dota-2-disappointment|archive-date=March 9, 2018|access-date=March 9, 2018|website=The Verge|date=August 9, 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last1=Workman|first1=Robert|title=This Reaction To Valve's New Game Is Just About Perfect|url=http://comicbook.com/gaming/2017/08/10/this-reaction-to-valve-s-new-game-is-just-about-perfect/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180309182928/http://comicbook.com/gaming/2017/08/10/this-reaction-to-valve-s-new-game-is-just-about-perfect/|archive-date=March 9, 2018|website=ComicBook.com |date=September 5, 2017 }}</ref> The trailer, uploaded to [[YouTube]], soon featured a high dislike-to-like ratio with commenters expressing their disappointment with Valve seemingly abandoning their other franchises, such as ''[[Half-Life (series)|Half-Life]]'', in favor of recent gaming trends.<ref name="Verge boo" /><ref>{{cite web|last1=Jackson|first1=Gita|title=The Internet Reacts To Valve's New Game Announcement|url=https://kotaku.com/the-internet-reacts-to-valve-s-new-game-announcement-1797680516|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180309182908/https://kotaku.com/the-internet-reacts-to-valve-s-new-game-announcement-1797680516|archive-date=March 9, 2018|access-date=March 9, 2018|website=Kotaku|date=August 9, 2017 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last1=Gilbert|first1=Ben|title=One of the biggest game companies in the world announced a new game, and reaction|url=http://www.businessinsider.com/valve-artifact-game-2017-8|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180310010023/http://www.businessinsider.com/valve-artifact-game-2017-8|archive-date=March [[monetization]] model; some players and critics called it "[[pay-to-win]]", as new cards could only be purchased and not traded from the Steam Marketplace, or gained as rewards in specific drafting game modes that require the purchase of a ticket to participate in.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Horti|first1=Samuel|title=Valve responds after Artifact community slams 'pay for everything' model|url=https://www.pcgamer.com/artifact-community-slams-pay-for-everything-monetisation-model/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181118230900/https://www.pcgamer.com/artifact-community-slams-pay-for-everything-monetisation-model/|archive-date=November 18, 2018|access-date=November 19, 2018|website=PC Gamer|date=November 18, 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last1=Jones|first1=Ali|title=Artifact launches to "mixed" Steam reviews complaining about pay-to-win|url=https://www.pcgamesn.com/artifact/artifact-user-reviews|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181129161802/https://www.pcgamesn.com/artifact/artifact-user-reviews|archive-date=November monetization structure is making Valve money and some gamers very angry|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/technology/2018/12/04/artifacts-monetization-structure-is-making-valve-money-some-gamers-very-angry/|access-date=December 5, 2018|newspaper=Washington ''Artifact''<nowiki/>'s concurrent player count dropped from 60,000 at launch to just over 1,500 within two months of its release, a 95% decline.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.businessinsider.com/valve-artifact-dota-card-game-a-flop-2019-1|title=The latest game from one of the most respected developers in the business is showing early signs of being a flop|last=Gilbert|first=Ben|website=Business Insider|access-date=February 13, 2019|archive-date=February 13, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190213054939/https://www.businessinsider.com/valve-artifact-dota-card-game-a-flop-2019-1|url-status=live}}</ref> By July 2019, ''Artifact'' had only around 100 concurrent players.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Stubbs|first=Mike|date=July 3, 2019|title=How Artifact became Valve's biggest failure|work=Eurogamer|url=https://www.eurogamer.net/articles/2019-07-03-how-artifact-became-valves-biggest-failure|access-date=September 1, 2019|archive-date=October 18, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191018040550/https://www.eurogamer.net/articles/2019-07-03-how-artifact-became-valves-biggest-failure|url-status=live}}</ref> In its first month of release, it averaged 8,300 viewers on the streaming service [[Twitch (service)|Twitch]]; by February 2020, it had lost 97% of this amount, and on April 8 viewers hit zero.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Artifact Twitch viewers hit the ultimate low: zero|url=http://www.vpesports.com/artifact/news/artifact-twitch-viewers-hit-zero|access-date=2021-03-04|website=VPEsports|language=en|archive-date=January 18, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210118142455/http://www.vpesports.com/artifact/news/artifact-twitch-viewers-hit-zero|url-status=live}}</ref> In response, [[internet troll]]s began using the ''Artifact'' Twitch category to stream pornography and other content that violated Twitch's terms of service, prompting Twitch to temporarily suspend new creators from streaming.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.theverge.com/2019/5/28/18643167/twitch-artifact-suspend-new-users-trolls-attack-valve | title = Twitch is temporarily suspending new creators from streaming after troll attack | first = Julia | last = Alexander | date = May 28, 2019 | access-date = May 28, 2019 | work = [[The Verge]] | archive-date = May 28, 2019 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20190528213635/https://www.theverge.com/2019/5/28/18643167/twitch-artifact-suspend-new-users-trolls-attack-valve | url-status = live }}</ref>

In March 2019, Valve said it was pausing its scheduled updates to the game to "re-examine" its decisions about its design, economy, social elements, and other issues.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|last=McWhertor|first=Michael|date=2019-03-29|title=Valve puts Artifact updates on hold to reexamine game's design, economy|url=https://www.polygon.com/2019/3/29/18287570/valve-artifact-statement-updates|access-date=2021-03-04|website=Polygon|language=en|archive-date=March 10, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210310063710/https://www.polygon.com/2019/3/29/18287570/valve-artifact-statement-updates|url-status=live}}</ref> In a statement on Valve's website, programmer Jeep Barnett said that ''Artifact'' represented the largest discrepancy between Valve's expectations for a game and the outcome.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|last=Kim|first=Matt|date=March 29, 2019|title=Valve Issues First Statement on Artifact in Months, Admits There Are "Deep-Rooted Issues" With Game|url=https://www.usgamer.net/articles/valve-issues-first-statement-on-artifact-in-months-admits-there-are-deep-rooted-issues-with-game|access-date=March 29, 2019|work=[[USGamer]]|archive-date=November 8, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191108221027/https://www.usgamer.net/articles/valve-issues-first-statement-on-artifact-in-months-admits-there-are-deep-rooted-issues-with-game|url-status=dead}}</ref> In March 2020, Newell said ''Artifact'' had been a "great disappointment", and that Valve planned to learn from its mistakes.<ref>{{Citation|title=Gabe Newell: ''Artifact'' Was a "Giant Disappointment"|date=March 18, 2020|url=https://www.ign.com/articles/gabe-newell-artifact-giant-disappointment-valve|language=en|access-date=2021-03-04|archive-date=March 19, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200319155343/https://www.ign.com/articles/gabe-newell-artifact-giant-disappointment-valve|url-status=live}}</ref> He told ''Edge'' that they were surprised by the response as they "thought that it was a really strong product"''.''<ref name=":2" />

Garfield felt ''Artifact'' had failed because it was [[review bomb]]ed early on, with players upset over the apparent [[pay to win|pay-to-win]] mechanics; this drove new players away, preventing the game economy from stabilizing at a point where the cost of building winning decks would have been on par with other digital card games, such as ''Hearthstone''.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.pcgamer.com/why-artifact-failed-to-take-off-according-to-designer-richard-garfield/ | title = Why Artifact failed to take off, according to designer Richard Garfield | first = Ian | last = https://web.archive.org/web/20190609182551/https://www.pcgamer.com/why-artifact-failed-to-take-off-according-to-designer-richard-garfield/ | url-status = live }}</ref><ref>{{cite He said that he and Elias were still optimistic about the game's future and would offer feedback and advice to Valve.<ref>{{cite web|last=MacGregor|first=Jody|date=March 8, 2019|title=Artifact '''''Chibi-Robo! Plug Into Adventure!'''''{{efn|{{nihongo|ちびロボ|lit. "Mini-Robo!"}} in Japanese}} is a [[Platform game|platform]]-[[Adventure game|adventure]] [[video game]] developed by [[Skip Ltd.]] and published by [[Nintendo]] for the [[GameCube]] console. It was released in Japan in 2005, and in North America and Europe the following year. Originally conceived as a [[point-and-click]] adventure game, it was put on developmental hold until Nintendo producer [[Shigeru Miyamoto]] gained interest in the title and overhauled its production.

The player takes on the role of the eponymous Chibi-Robo, a 10-centimeter-tall robot owned by the Sanderson family. Gameplay revolves around navigating a household and collecting "Happy Points" by completing various tasks from [[homemaking|housework]] to helping solve the dilemmas of the Sanderson family and the numerous living toys that inhabit their household. Every action consumes energy, requiring the player to recharge using electrical outlets.

''Chibi-Robo!'' was generally well received, with praise for the premise, the charming storyline, and sound design, but some gameplay mechanics and the quality of the graphics drew some criticism. Sales of ''Chibi-Robo!'' were modest. It spawned several sequels. For the [[Nintendo DS]], ''[[Chibi-Robo!: Park Patrol]]'' was released in 2007 and ''[[Chibi-Robo! (series)#Okaeri! Chibi-Robo! Happy Richie Ōsōji!|Okaeri! Chibi-Robo! Happy Richie Ōsōji!]]'' was released in 2009, the latter being a Japan-exclusive. For the [[Nintendo 3DS]], ''[[Chibi-Robo! (series)#Chibi-Robo! Photo Finder|Chibi-Robo! Photo Finder]]'' was released in Japan in 2013 and in North America in 2014, and ''[[Chibi-Robo! Zip Lash]]'' was released in 2015. The original ''Chibi-Robo!'' saw a Japanese re-release in 2009 for the [[Wii]] as part of the [[New Play Control!]] series and worldwide in 2025 on the [[Nintendo Switch 2]] via the GameCube [[Nintendo Classics]] service.

==Gameplay==
[[File:Chibi-Robo gameplay.jpg|left|thumb|Cleaning pawprints from the floor using the toothbrush is just one way for the player to earn Happy Points. The game's [[Head-up display|HUD]] shows the player's remaining time (upper left) and battery life (lower right).]]
''Chibi-Robo!'' is a [[platform game|platform]]-[[adventure game]] that puts the player in direct control of a tiny, battery-powered robot that does housework for humans. The objective of the game is to become the top-ranked "Super Chibi-Robo" in the world by accumulating Happy Points, a collectible gained by doing good deeds for the family and for various toys in the Sandersons' home.<ref name="npfeature"/><ref name="instructions"/><ref name="gspotrev"/><ref name="eurogrev"/><ref name="gspyrev">{{cite web | author=Williams | date=February 7, 2006 | title=Reviews: ''Chibi-Robo'' | url=http://cube.gamespy.com/gamecube/chibi-robo/686579p1.html | work=[[GameSpy]] | publisher=[[IGN]] | access-date=March 26, 2011 | archive-date=February 15, 2006 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060215104002/http://cube.gamespy.com/gamecube/chibi-robo/686579p1.html | url-status=live|first=Bryn}}</ref> In order to do this, the player must control Chibi-Robo and explore the Sandersons' home. The game has [[Open World|sandbox-style]] exploration when navigating the house. During exploration, Chibi-Robo can find a wide variety of things to collect, including "Moolah", the currency of ''Chibi-Robo!''. An important task in gaining Happy Points is to clean up messes around the house, such as disposing of trash or scrubbing dirty footprints.<ref name="instructions"/> The player can also interact with and help with the personal problems of the Sandersons and the toys. This ranges from solving a plot-driving crisis or completing a subquest of simply locating a lost object as a favor.<ref name="npfeature"/><ref name="gspotrev"/><ref name="eurogrev"/> With Chibi-Robo's assistant Telly Vision as his speaker, the player is often prompted to give either a positive or negative response to each question or request.<ref name="gspotrev"/> The player loses battery power with every step and action. If his battery is not charged before it empties, Chibi-Robo will collapse and re-emerge in the Chibi-House, having lost half of his Moolah.<ref name="gspotrev"/> Throughout the house are electrical outlets, which the player can plug into to recharge his battery or save his progress.<ref name="instructions"/><ref name="gspyrev"/> The player's exploration is limited by a timer representing a full day or full night. Once the timer expires, Chibi-Robo automatically returns to the Chibi-House.<ref name="eurogrev"/>

There are three collectibles in the game. One is the stickers, which can be obtained throughout the game, either by completing the game, completing quests, playing [[Minigame|mini-games]], or doing simple tasks for other [[non-player character]]s. The Second is the Frog Rings which can be collected and given to Jenny, the daughter of the Sanderson household, for Happy Points and a sticker. The third is the crayons found throughout the house which can be deposited in a crayon box for Happy Points.

At the start of both day and night, the player begins in the Chibi-House, where they can charge Chibi-Robo's battery, save at the [[AC power plugs and sockets|electrical outlet]], or connect to the Citrusoft "Chibi-[[personal computer|PC]]" to purchase a variety of items and power-ups with Moolah and use scrap metal to build "Utilibots", robotic helpers that ease the navigation of the Sandersons' home.<ref name="instructions" /><ref name="gspyrev" /> The gear available from Citrusoft includes the "Chibi-Copter", used to reach far-off points or fly down from a high place safely; the "Chibi-Blaster", used to eliminate obstacles and fend off the hostile Spydorz; and the "Chibi-Radar", used to detect hidden objects.<ref name="npfeature" /><ref name="gspotrev" /> There are several other items of the Sandersons' that Chibi-Robo can find and use. These include the toothbrush, used to clean up stains; the coffee mug, used for protection; the spoon, used to dig holes; and the squirter, used to hold fluids and squirt them.<ref name="npfeature" /><ref name="gspotrev" /> Chibi-Robo can also gain special costumes throughout the game, each of which has its own function.<ref name="instructions" /> For instance, if the player poses for Mr. Sanderson while wearing The Drake Redcrest costume, he will give Chibi-Robo Happy Points. As more Happy Points are acquired, the player's rank increases among all the Chibi-Robos in the world. At certain ranks, Citrusoft will send the player bonus batteries, allowing Chibi-Robo to roam longer without having to recharge until they earn the status of "Super Chibi-Robo", which earns the player unlimited battery life.<ref name="gspyrev" />

==Setting and synopsis==
===Setting and characters===
''Chibi-Robo!'' revolves around a tiny, highly advanced house-cleaning robot of the same name, created by a toy company called Citrusoft Robotics Inc.<ref name="skipinterview">{{cite web | author=Nintendo staff | script-title=ja:プラグをかついで プレイレポート | url=https://www.nintendo.co.jp/nom/0507/2_2/ | publisher=[[Nintendo]] | language=Japanese | access-date=March 26, 2011 | archive-date=October 26, 2012 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121026140230/http://www.nintendo.co.jp/nom/0507/2_2/ | url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="npfeature">{{cite magazine | magazine=[[Nintendo Power]] | publisher=[[Nintendo|Nintendo of America]] | location=Redmond Washington | title=Breaking the Mold: ''Chibi-Robo'' | issue=201 | pages=28–33 | author=Hoffman | date=March 2006 | issn=1041-9551|first=Chris}}</ref> The game takes place in a 1960s-style American home owned by the Sanderson family, consisting of George, an unemployed former toymaker for Citrusoft's rival, Macrowave Robotics Inc.; Helen, George's wife who is constantly stressed over how much money her husband spends on toys despite his unemployment; and Jenny, their eight-year-old daughter who is socially-withdrawn and behaves like a frog.<ref name="instructions">{{cite book | year=2006 | editor=Nintendo staff | title=Chibi-Robo!: Plug Into Adventure! ''instruction booklet'' | pages=6–22 | publisher=[[Nintendo|Nintendo of America Inc.]] | id=DL-DOL-GGTE-USA}}</ref> Chibi-Robo is packaged with a small "Chibi-House" and an assistant named Telly Vision who speaks on his behalf.<ref name="gspotrev">{{cite web |url=http://www.gamespot.com/gamecube/action/chibirobo/review.html |title=''Chibi-Robo!'' Review for GameCube |first=Greg |last=Mueller |date=February 8, 2006 |access-date=July 16, 2010 |work=[[GameSpot]] |publisher=[[CBS Interactive]] |archive-date=June 17, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100617031127/http://www.gamespot.com/gamecube/action/chibirobo/review.html |url-status=live}}</ref> During the night or when humans are not around in the Sandersons' house, several toys come to life:<ref name="eurogrev"/> a superhero action figure named Drake Redcrest, a toy caterpillar named Sophie, a group of egg-shaped army men called the Free Rangers, a wooden pirate named Plankbeard, a teddy bear named Sunshine, a toy fortune teller named The Great Peekoe, a brick-made T-rex named Dinah, a toy mummy named Mort, a toy princess named Princess Pitts, a toy potted flower named Funky Phil, and a black and white toy named Primopuel.<ref name="npfeature"/><ref name="gspotrev"/> Chibi-Robo also meets several animals and creatures consisting of two frogs named Freida and Fred, a plug-headed being named Mr. Prongs, a bluebird, a eggplant-like creature called Kid Eggplant, and the Sandersons' pet dog Tao.

===Synopsis===
On Jenny's eighth birthday, she is gifted a Chibi-Robo by George. Each of the one million Chibi-Robos in the world is supposed to collect "Happy Points" by doing good deeds for their owners and must occasionally charge their [[Battery (electricity)|batteries]] at electrical outlets; however, their mass consumption of electricity has resulted in an ongoing energy crisis.<ref name="npfeature"/><ref name="eurogrev">{{cite web | author=Kumar | date=March 15, 2006 | title=''Chibi-Robo!'' GameCube Review | url=http://www.eurogamer.net/articles/r_chibirobo_gc | website=[[Eurogamer]] | access-date=March 26, 2011 | archive-date=July 17, 2011 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110717165837/http://www.eurogamer.net/articles/r_chibirobo_gc | url-status=live|first=Mathew}}</ref> Chibi-Robo helps the Sandersons and the house's other inhabitants with various tasks, such as helping Sophie express her feelings towards Drake Redcrest, aiding the Free Rangers in their war against Tao after it is believed that he killed one of their men, finding bricks for Dinah's playset, finding Plankbeard's ship and providing him with a crew, finding frog rings for Jenny, helping Frieda find Fred somewhere in the house, finding George's wedding ring and helping him cook burgers, resolving Sunshine's addiction for nectar, playing music for Mr. Prongs, and helping Mort win Princess Pitts' heart. Chibi-Robo eventually finds a large robot in the basement with a missing leg called Giga-Robo, who was once a companion of the Sandersons', but had to be deactivated due to its high electricity consumption.<ref name="npfeature"/><ref>{{cite video game|title=Chibi-Robo! |developer=[[Skip Ltd.]]|publisher=[[Nintendo]]|date=February 8, 2006|platform=GameCube|quote='''Telly:''' He started a trend known as Giga Robo Fever a long time ago. But his energy consumption was too high and his popularity plummeted.}}</ref> Chibi-Robo attempts to revive Giga-Robo by fully charging its massive battery using the Giga-charger and makes it a goal to find Giga-Robo's missing leg, but is attacked by spider-like robots called Spydorz, which he defeats using his blaster weapon.

When George purchases yet another toy, Helen locks herself in her room and tells him that she wants a divorce, prompting the rest of the family to do housework in an attempt to make up for it.<ref>{{cite video game|title=Chibi-Robo! |developer=[[Skip Ltd.]]|publisher=[[Nintendo]]|date=February 8, 2006|platform=GameCube|quote='''Mrs. Sanderson:''' I'm sorry, but you've pushed me to the edge. The only option I've got left is... divorce.}}</ref> Meanwhile, Chibi-Robo finds a strange pattern in the backyard and uses his radar to contact an alien species. Once the aliens land and greet him, Chibi-Robo uses a time machine made by the visitors to go into the past to find a code to enter a safe in the master bedroom containing Giga-Robo's leg. He returns to the present to open the safe, but several larger Spydorz are released and capture the Sandersons. It is revealed that George originally created the Spydorz to be friends with the Chibi-Robos, but Macrowave reprogrammed them to be hostile, causing George to quit his job.<ref>{{cite video game|title=Chibi-Robo! |developer=[[Skip Ltd.]]|publisher=[[Nintendo]]|date=February 8, 2006|platform=GameCube|quote='''Mr. Sanderson:''' I designed the Spydorz to be your friends, Chibi-Robo. But then the company reprogrammed them to be hostile and cruel. And that's why I quit Macrowave Robotics Inc.!}}</ref> George upgrades Chibi-Robo's blaster, allowing the small robot to defeat the Queen Spydor, recover Giga-Robo's missing leg, and rescue the Sandersons. George apologizes for lying to Helen, and the two reconcile. Once Chibi-Robo fully recharges Giga-Robo's battery, reattaches his missing leg, and finds the passcode needed to turn him on, he reactivates Giga-Robo, and the aliens meet them in the backyard. The aliens explain that the toys are able to walk and talk due to a request from Giga-Robo to give them life and to give all Giga-Robos infinite battery power to prevent their energy consumption. The aliens could not do the latter at the time and returned to their own planet to obtain the item necessary to grant Giga-Robo's wish.<ref>{{cite video game|title=Chibi-Robo! |developer=[[Skip Ltd.]]|publisher=[[Nintendo]]|date=February 8, 2006|platform=GameCube|quote='''Aliens:''' Friend second wish... 'For Sandersons and Giga-Robos in the world... Give body that does not need energy.' But... no more balls of light in spaceship... No more balls of light in spaceship! We return to our home. And... we bring back ball of light again!}}</ref> They then give Giga-Robo this ability, who shares it with Chibi-Robo and the rest of the robots in the world as well, eliminating the energy problem. Sometime later, George gets a new job at Citrusoft.

==Development==
''Chibi-Robo!'' was developed by [[Skip Ltd.]]<ref name="npfeature"/> ''Chibi-Robo!'' was announced in early 2003 with publishing rights held by [[Bandai]]. Its original projected release date was June 2003 in Japan and spring 2004 in North America.<ref name="2003preview">{{cite web |author=IGN Staff |date=April 17, 2003 |title=''Chibi Robo'' - GameCube Preview |url=http://cube.ign.com/articles/394/394043p1.html |website=[[IGN]] |access-date=May 26, 2008 |archive-date=September 22, 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070922082703/http://cube.ign.com/articles/394/394043p1.html |url-status=live}}</ref> Unlike the released version of ''Chibi-Robo!'', the [[Software release life cycle#Beta|beta]] version entailed the player training Chibi-Robo to defend the home of his inventor from a pair of burglars. The gameplay was different as well; instead of a platform-adventure game, it played like a [[point-and-click]] adventure title, where the player was not in direct control of Chibi-Robo, but was rather conveying commands to him by clicking a cursor around the area.<ref name="skipinterview"/><ref name="2003preview"/> The protagonist was also to learn and develop depending on the choices the player made for him.<ref name="2003preview"/> This incarnation of ''Chibi-Robo!'' was ultimately put on "[[Development hell|indefinite hold]]" and disappeared from the media.<ref name="limbo">{{cite web |author=IGN Staff |date=February 19, 2004 |title=''Chibi Robo'' in Limbo |url=http://cube.ign.com/articles/493/493227p1.html |website=[[IGN]] |access-date=May 26, 2008 |archive-date=May 19, 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070519101445/http://cube.ign.com/articles/493/493227p1.html |url-status=live}}</ref> [[Shigeru Miyamoto]] was eventually introduced to the game by fellow [[Nintendo]] producer [[Kensuke Tanabe]].<ref name="npfeature"/> Miyamoto took a personal interest in the character of Chibi-Robo and signed on as the game's senior producer. The development of ''Chibi-Robo!'' was revamped with Nintendo acting as its new publisher.<ref name="npfeature"/><ref>{{cite web | author=Gantayat | date=October 29, 2004 | title=Nintendo Picks Up ''Chibi Robo!'' | url=http://cube.ign.com/articles/561/561720p1.html | website=[[IGN]] | access-date=March 26, 2011 | archive-date=September 21, 2007 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070921075104/http://cube.ign.com/articles/561/561720p1.html | url-status=live|first=Anoop}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | author=IGN Staff | date=November 29, 2004 | title=Nintendo Supports Cube | url=http://cube.ign.com/articles/568/568992p1.html | website=[[IGN]] | access-date=March 26, 2011 | archive-date=January 6, 2009 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090106061256/http://cube.ign.com/articles/568/568992p1.html | url-status=live}}</ref> ''Chibi-Robo!'' was in development for four years.<ref name="skipinterview"/>

Director [[Kenichi Nishi]] had previous development credits such as ''[[Chrono Trigger]]'', ''[[Moon: Remix RPG Adventure]]'' and ''[[Incredible Crisis]]''.<ref>{{cite web | author=Parkin | date=October 13, 2010 | title=JRPG Producer Looks To Twitter To Help Secure A Publisher | url=https://www.gamedeveloper.com/game-platforms/jrpg-producer-looks-to-twitter-to-help-secure-a-publisher | work=[[Gamasutra]] | publisher=[[UBM plc]] | access-date=March 26, 2011 | archive-date=August 3, 2017 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170803050031/http://www.gamasutra.com/view/news/30943/JRPG_Producer_Looks_To_Twitter_To_Help_Secure_A_Publisher.php | url-status=live|first=Simon}}</ref> Nishi's approach to game design, even with ''Chibi-Robo!'', was to always take a standard, orthodox method and "crash it, twist it, or create a totally different direction".<ref name="npfeature"/> The reason Nishi chose to make the majority of the cast toys is because humans are "too big to interact with [Chibi-Robo] and create all the drama" and that it added a sense of [[fantasy]] to the experience.<ref name="npfeature"/> The family dog Tao had appeared in Nishi's previous games: ''Moon: Remix RPG Adventure'' and ''[[L.O.L.: Lack of Love]]''. The director based the dog on his own pet because he felt that the "black-and-white color is very simple and universal".<ref name="GamesTm-Retro">{{cite journal |author=''GamesTM'' staff|journal=[[GamesTM]] |publisher=[[Imagine Publishing]] |title=Behind the Scenes ''LOL: Lack of Love'' |year=2010 |issue=3 |page=117 |series=The Ultimate Retro Companion |issn=1448-2606 |oclc=173412381}}</ref> Despite the game's overall happy attitude, the game designers put some emphasis on serious topics such as divorce, loneliness, pollution, and loss, in which Nishi said: "If we only concentrate on cheerful fun, we'll lose depth. There's nothing surprising for people if the game looks cheerful and the experience is cheerful. There are no surprises or unexpected things". Still, rather than use these topics as major themes for the player, Nishi felt it would be more effective to bring them in as "ordinary things to enhance the adventure of daily life".<ref name="npfeature"/>

The music and sound in ''Chibi-Robo!'' were composed by Hirofumi Taniguchi. He wanted to make unique sound patterns and [[Motif (music)|motif]]s for each character, and even used [[Vocal music|human voices]] to create the system sounds, such as on the menu selections.<ref name="npfeature"/> All of the noises made by Chibi-Robo's actions were [[Phrase (music)|phrased]]. Taniguchi used both [[Woodwind instrument|woodwind]] and [[Electronic music|electronic]] instruments for the character's actions, the former because "Chibi's actions are not ordinary robotlike actions" and the latter because he did not want to totally eliminate his mechanical characteristics.<ref name="npfeature"/> Different background music is played for the day and night cycles, but they lack [[melody]] because Chibi-Robo's footsteps create a melody at random. The [[tempo]] of his footsteps was designed to match the background music; if he picks up his plug to walk faster, the music speeds up.<ref name="npfeature"/> All of the game's music was compiled on the ''Chibi-Robo! Limited Soundtrack'', a [[Compact disc|CD]] released alongside an official 142-page guidebook and published by [[Shogakukan]] in Japan in August 2005.<ref>{{cite book|title=ちびロボ! (ワンダーライフスペシャル―任天堂公式ガイドブック) <nowiki>[単行本]</nowiki>| language=Japanese|id={{ASIN|4091062520|country=jp}}}}</ref>

''Chibi-Robo!'' has enjoyed a generally favorable critical reception.<ref name="metacritic"/> ''[[Official Nintendo Magazine]]'' ranked it the 88th best game available on Nintendo platforms. The staff felt that it was the GameCube's "last classic".<ref>{{cite web|title=Nintendo Feature: 100 Best Nintendo Games: Part One |url=http://www.officialnintendomagazine.co.uk/7188/features/100-best-nintendo-games-part-one/ |work=[[Official Nintendo Magazine]] |last=East |first=Tom |date=2009-02-17 |access-date=2013-12-05 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120414111615/http://www.officialnintendomagazine.co.uk/7188/features/100-best-nintendo-games-part-one/ |archive-date=2012-04-14}}</ref> Critics Greg Mueller of ''[[GameSpot]]'', Mathew Kumar of ''[[Eurogamer]]'', Bryn Williams of [[GameSpy]], Shane Satterfield of [[G4 (U.S. TV channel)|G4]], and [[Matt Casamassina]] of ''[[IGN]]'' all applauded the game's charming setting, compelling storyline, and complex characters.<ref name="gspotrev"/><ref name="eurogrev"/><ref name="gspyrev"/><ref name="g4rev"/><ref name="ignrev"/> Casamassina found that the fashion in which the main plot and objectives are sewn together is part of the reason the game is enjoyable.<ref name="ignrev"/> Mueller, Kumar, and Satterfield noted endearing, charismatic qualities among the various toy characters.<ref name="gspotrev"/><ref name="eurogrev"/><ref name="g4rev"/> Kumar heeded ''Chibi-Robo!'' as "honestly one of the most touching games I've played in ages" in which the player often becomes engrossed in "events that pan out like miniature plays, with [[love triangle]]s (nay, love dodecahedrons) between toys, and some scenes with a real pathos behind them".<ref name="eurogrev"/> Considering the joyous atmosphere of ''Chibi-Robo!'', Satterfield was pleasantly surprised at its inclusion of controversial topics like divorce and its possible distortion of a target audience.<ref name="g4rev"/> This attribute was criticized by Jinny Gudmundsen, a columnist for ''[[USA Today]]'', who thought that the interpersonal issues negate the game's overall charm and render it inappropriate for younger children.<ref>{{cite web | author=Gudmundsen | date=February 24, 2006 | title=Adult issues mar what could have been charming game | url=https://www.usatoday.com/tech/columnist/jinnygudmundsen/2006-02-24-chibi-robo_x.htm | work=[[USA Today]] | publisher=[[Gannett Company]] | access-date=April 2, 2011 | issn=0734-7456 | archive-date=April 23, 2009 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090423061000/http://www.usatoday.com/tech/columnist/jinnygudmundsen/2006-02-24-chibi-robo_x.htm | url-status=live|first=Jinny}}</ref> Writers for ''[[Computer Games Magazine]]'' praised ''Chibi-Robo'' by interpreting deep, symbolic meaning in its more subtle aspects. The publication found the game to use "overarching narrative arcs" and "stock melodramatic devices" among the Sandersons' dysfunctional interactions, "emotional crisis points, downtime, and rhythms and cycles of action" between its day and night events, and "evocative music" as a way for characters to communicate their feelings.<ref>{{cite magazine | magazine=[[Computer Games Magazine]] | author=''Computer Games Magazine'' staff | date=October 2006 | title=Saving the Family | url=http://www.cgonline.com/computer-games-magazine/article/saving_the_family | publisher=[[TheGlobe.com]] | issue=190 | issn=1095-1385 | access-date=2011-04-03 | archive-date=2011-09-27 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110927173455/http://www.cgonline.com/computer-games-magazine/article/saving_the_family | url-status=dead}}</ref>

Opinions on the gameplay of ''Chibi-Robo!'' have been mixed. Among the more positive reactions, Casamassina assessed the cleaning mechanics as "very fun and very rewarding", while Kumar compared the game to the ''[[Story of Seasons (series)|Story of Seasons]]'' series due to both entities convert seemingly boring tasks into something fun.<ref name="eurogrev"/><ref name="ignrev"/> James Mielke of ''[[1UP.com]]'' similarly enjoyed the "near-constant sense of discovery" and the tiny details included by Skip with earning Happy Points and Moolah.<ref name="1uprev"/> Casamassina, Mielke, and Williamson were satisfied that they had to frequently recharge Chibi-Robo, but Mueller was dismayed to have to stop one's current task in order to find an outlet.<ref name="gspotrev"/><ref name="eurogrev"/><ref name="gspyrev"/><ref name="ignrev"/> The GameSpot contributor was also aggravated with the mere five-minute intervals for the day and night cycles, which he considered a major interruption of the game's pacing.<ref name="gspyrev"/> Contrarily, Kumar felt the pacing was appropriate and Williamson viewed the feature as a "flexible [[difficulty level]] setting".<ref name="eurogrev"/><ref name="gspyrev"/> Satterfield proclaimed that although the gameplay is somewhat varied, most of it is constituted by the tedious location and collection of objects for the non-player characters.<ref name="g4rev"/> Jeremy Zoss of ''[[Game Informer]]'' was displeased with the game as whole and wrote that it was "not a platformer, but more of a 3D adventure game composed entirely of fetch-quests and repetitive menial labor".<ref name="girev"/>

The audio design of ''Chibi-Robo!'', particularly its integration of different instrumental tones for the hero's various actions, was lauded by the press.<ref name="gspotrev"/><ref name="1uprev"/><ref name="g4rev"/> Kumar felt that its utilization of sound could be "the seed of a new way of using music in games".<ref name="eurogrev"/> Casamassina commented: "Few developers would be brave enough to create a title whose main character generates varying musical notes whenever he takes a step, but this is exactly what Chibi does - and it's actually very whimsical and cute".<ref name="ignrev"/> Although many critics appreciated the bright and colorful features of the accompanying aesthetics, they also judged the graphical presentation as dated.<ref name="gspotrev"/><ref name="gspyrev"/><ref name="1uprev"/><ref name="girev"/> Casamassina encountered low-polygon 3D models and a below-average [[frame rate]]; Satterfield stated that the game operated at "[[Dreamcast]] level".<ref name="g4rev"/><ref name="ignrev"/> Other portions of ''Chibi-Robo!'' were assessed as unpolished as well. Several sources noted the game's default camera system to be unwieldy, cumbersome, or frustrating at times,<ref name="eurogrev"/><ref name="gspyrev"/><ref name="g4rev"/><ref name="ignrev"/> but Mueller noted that switching to the [[Video game graphics#Top-down perspective|top-down]] or [[Video game graphics#First-person perspective|first-person]] viewpoints and the ability to center the camera behind Chibi-Robo alleviates most of its problems.<ref name="gspotrev"/> Satterfield and Casamassina regarded the cutscenes as awkward and repetitive; the former of the two claimed that they "amount to ugly characters recycling the same animation routine over and over while gibberish comes from their gaping maws".<ref name="g4rev"/><ref name="ignrev"/> Kumar perceived the game's combat to be "messy", "uninteresting", and "entirely unnecessary".<ref name="eurogrev"/>

''Chibi-Robo!'' was not a significant commercial success.<ref name="graveyard"/><ref>{{cite magazine | author=''Edge'' Staff | date=September 18, 2008 | title=''Captain Rainbow'': Absurd Nintendo Nostalgia | url=http://www.edge-online.com/features/captain-rainbow-absurd-nintendo-nostalgia | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120616074155/http://www.edge-online.com/features/captain-rainbow-absurd-nintendo-nostalgia | url-status=dead | archive-date=June 16, 2012 | magazine=[[Edge (magazine)|Edge]] | publisher=[[Future plc]] | access-date=March 26, 2011}}</ref> According to [[Media Create]], the GameCube version was the fourth best-selling game in Japan for its week ending on June 26, 2005 with nearly 29,000 copies sold.<ref>{{cite web |first=David |last=Jenkins |date=July 1, 2005 |title=Japanese Sales Charts, Week Ending June 26th |url=https://www.gamedeveloper.com/game-platforms/japanese-sales-charts-week-ending-june-26th |work=[[Gamasutra]] |publisher=[[UBM plc]] |access-date=September 2, 2008 |archive-date=September 22, 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080922131855/http://www.gamasutra.com/php-bin/news_index.php?story=5832 |url-status=live}}</ref> The game managed to sell 97,879 units in Japan alone by the end of 2005.<ref>{{cite web | title=2005年テレビゲームソフト売り上げTOP500(ファミ通版) | url=http://geimin.net/da/db/2005_ne_fa/index.php | publisher=Geimin.net | language=Japanese | access-date=March 26, 2011 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141009011126/http://geimin.net/da/db/2003_ne_fa/index.php | archive-date=October 9, 2014 | url-status=dead | df=mdy-all|trans-title=2005 Top 500 Video Game Software Sales (Famitsu Edition)}}</ref> The Wii port of the game did not fare as well; it only sold 11,000 copies in Japan for the week ending on June 14, 2009 and a total of 38,573 copies throughout the remainder of that year.<ref>{{cite web |last=Graft |first=Kris |date=June 19, 2009 |title=Japanese Charts: Sega's Infinite Space Topples Kingdom Hearts DS |url=http://gamasutra.com/php-bin/news_index.php?story=24122 |work=[[Gamasutra]] |publisher=[[UBM plc]] |access-date=June 19, 2009 |archive-date=June 21, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090621213732/http://www.gamasutra.com/php-bin/news_index.php?story=24122 |url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | title=2009年テレビゲームソフト売り上げTOP1000(ファミ通版) | url=http://geimin.net/da/db/2009_ne_fa/index.php | publisher=Geimin.net | language=Japanese | access-date=March 26, 2011 | archive-date=June 27, 2015 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150627100212/http://geimin.net/da/db/2009_ne_fa/index.php | url-status=live|trans-title=2009 video game software sales TOP1000 (Famitsu version)}}</ref>

==Legacy==
''Chibi-Robo!'' received a sequel in 2007 for the [[Nintendo DS]] called ''[[Chibi-Robo!: Park Patrol]]'', which follows a different Chibi-Robo as it attempts to revitalize a park. Nintendo established a deal with [[Wal-Mart]] for the exclusive rights to sell it in the United States.<ref>{{cite web |first=Patrick |last=Klepek |date=October 4, 2007 |title=Why is ''Chibi-Robo DS'' Only at Wal-Mart? |url=http://www.1up.com/do/newsStory?cId=3163422 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110524023939/http://www.1up.com/news/chibi-robo-wal-mart |url-status=dead |archive-date=May 24, 2011 |work=[[1UP.com]] |publisher=[[Ziff Davis]] |access-date=March 26, 2008}}</ref> A second sequel for the DS, titled ''[[Chibi-Robo! (series)#Okaeri! Chibi-Robo! Happy Richie Ōsōji!|Okaeri! Chibi-Robo! Happy Richie Ōsōji!]]'', was released only in Japan in 2009. It involves yet another Chibi-Robo vacuuming dirt for money within the home of an adult Jenny.<ref>{{cite web |author= |date=June 30, 2009 |title=''Chibi-Robo'' Vacuums Riches On The DS |url=http://www.siliconera.com/2009/06/30/chibi-robo-vacuums-riches-on-the-ds/ |publisher=Siliconera |access-date=June 29, 2006 |archive-date=January 18, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100118064837/http://www.siliconera.com/2009/06/30/chibi-robo-vacuums-riches-on-the-ds/ |url-status=live}}</ref> The original ''Chibi-Robo!'' was re-released as part of [[New Play Control!]], a selection of [[Wii]] [[video game remake|remakes]] of GameCube games.<ref>{{cite web|first=John |last=Tanaka |date=October 2, 2008 |title=First Look: Wii de Asobu ''Pikmin'' |url=http://wii.ign.com/articles/915/915529p1.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081005070547/http://wii.ign.com/articles/915/915529p1.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=October 5, 2008 |website=[[IGN]] |access-date=October 5, 2008}}</ref> The remake features special [[Wii Remote]] controls for the game's tools. '''''Dredge''''' is a 2023 video game developed by Black Salt Games and published by [[Team17]] that combines genres of [[Fishing video game|fishing]], [[Survival game|survival]], and [[Horror game|horror]]. It follows a fisherman who faces [[Lovecraftian]] creatures as he fishes and explores an [[open world]] consisting of five [[archipelago]]s. As the game progresses, the player can upgrade the character's fishing equipment and abilities. It follows a [[day–night cycle]]; the day is serene, while the night contains the game's horror elements, such as supernatural events and sea monsters.

Black Salt Games conceived ''Dredge'' as a top-down [[turn-based game]]; that notion was scrapped during the prototype phase. Not wanting ''Dredge'' to be a [[jump scare]] horror game, they worked to create a [[psychological thriller]] atmosphere. Four of the five archipelagos are based on geological formations. After development was completed, they approached various publishers before settling on Team17. ''Dredge'' was released for [[Nintendo Switch]], [[PlayStation 4]], [[PlayStation 5]], [[Windows]], [[Xbox One]], and [[Xbox Series X/S]] on March 30, 2023, with versions for [[Android (operating system)|Android]] and [[iOS]] following on February 27, 2025. Two [[downloadable content|downloadable content pack]]s (DLCs), ''The Pale Reach'' and ''The Iron Rig'', were released in 2023 and 2024, respectively.

Critics positively received ''Dredge'', praising its gameplay, presentation, and exploration, while some complained that the fishing portions are repetitive. The game's story, horror elements, thriller undertones, and art style were also commended. Its DLCs were well received by critics. It was deemed one of the top video games of 2023 by several news outlets and was nominated for numerous awards.
