'''''Neverwinter Nights''''' is a [[role-playing video game]] developed by [[BioWare]]. [[Interplay Entertainment]] was originally set to publish the game, but financial difficulties led to it being taken over by [[Infogrames]], who released the game under their [[Atari]] range of titles. It is the first installment in the'' [[Neverwinter Nights]]'' series, and was released for [[Microsoft Windows]] on June 18, 2002. BioWare later released a [[Linux]] client in June 2003, requiring a purchased copy of the game to play.<ref name="linux client">{{cite web | url=http://nwn.bioware.com/downloads/linuxclient.html | author=BioWare | title=Neverwinter Nights For Linux | date=June 2003 | access-date=2010-03-17 | url-status=dead | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100311143315/http://nwn.bioware.com/downloads/linuxclient.html | archive-date=2010-03-11 | author-link=BioWare }}</ref> [[MacSoft]] released a [[Mac OS X]] port in August 2003.

''Neverwinter Nights'' is set in the fantasy world of the ''[[Forgotten Realms]]'' campaign setting, with the [[game mechanics]] based on the ''[[Dungeons & Dragons]]'' [[Dungeons & Dragons 3rd edition|3rd edition]] rules. The [[game engine]] was designed around an Internet-based model for running a [[massively multiplayer online game]] (MMOG), which would allow end users to host game servers. Up to 64 players could connect to a single server.<ref name="CGW-NWN">{{Cite magazine |last=Lombardi |first=Christ |date=July 2000 |title=Okay, roleplayers, let's play |url=https://archive.org/stream/Computer_Gaming_World_Issue_192#page/n75 |issue=192 |magazine=Computer Gaming World |pages=75–78}}</ref> The intent was to create a potentially infinite massively multiplayer game framework. This game was named after the original ''[[Neverwinter Nights (1991 video game)|Neverwinter Nights]]'' online game, the first graphical [[massively multiplayer online role-playing game]] (MMORPG),<ref name="59thEmmys">[http://www.mcvuk.com/press-releases/read/stormfront-studios-honored-at-59th-annual-emmy-technology-awards-for-creating-first-graphical-online-role-playing-game Stormfront Studios Honored At 59th Annual Emmy Technology Awards For Creating First Graphical Online Role-Playing Game] MCV, January 10, 2008</ref> which operated from 1991 to 1997 on [[AOL]].

The original release of ''Neverwinter Nights'' includes the game engine, a game campaign that can be played as single player or in multiplayer mode, and on Windows releases, the [[Aurora engine|Aurora]] toolset used for creating custom content that would run in the same engine. Three expansion packs were released for the game: ''[[Neverwinter Nights: Shadows of Undrentide|Shadows of Undrentide]]'' in June 2003; ''[[Neverwinter Nights: Hordes of the Underdark|Hordes of the Underdark]]'' in December 2003; and ''[[Neverwinter Nights: Kingmaker (expansion pack)|Kingmaker]]'' in November 2004. BioWare began selling premium modules through an online store in late 2004. The game's success led to a sequel, ''[[Neverwinter Nights 2]]'', released on October 31, 2006.

==Development and release==
{{expand section|date=November 2014}}
The game was developed by 65 people.<ref name="budget">{{cite web|first=Allan|last=Chambers|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/88434957/edmonton-journal/|title=Bioware's games hailed for innovations|newspaper=[[Edmonton Journal]]|page=19|date=July 27, 2002|accessdate=November 6, 2021|via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref> Development time was more than a year and the project had a multi-million dollar budget.<ref name="budget"/> The game was announced to use the Omen engine as a replacement for the Infinity engine which was not good enough for the new game.<ref name="engine">{{cite web|url=http://www.cnn.com/TECH/computing/9908/12/neverwinter.idg/|title=First look: Neverwinter Nights|newspaper=[[CNN]]|date=August 12, 1999|accessdate=April 13, 2022|via=[[CNN.com]]}}</ref>

BioWare intended to create a game system which emulated the interactions in a pen-and-paper version of ''Dungeons & Dragons'' including the role of [[Dungeon Master]]. They worked alongside the ''[[Advanced Dungeons & Dragons|AD&D]]'' to ensure the game framework was faithful to the tabletop game.<ref name="CGW-NWN"/>

A posting at the ''Neverwinter Nights 2'' Vault on June 4, 2008 contained information from what appeared to be original ''Neverwinter Nights'' documentation. At the BioWare forums, ''Neverwinter'' lead designer Rob Bartel confirmed that the "series of excerpts from the game's design doc" were not a hoax. When asked if the plans were altered due to time constraints, Bartel referenced various legal difficulties that the company was working through.<ref name="original campaign">{{cite web|url=http://nwn.bioware.com/forums/viewtopic.html?topic=633312&forum=43|title=Neverwinter Nights: NWN Original Plot Outline|date=2008-06-06|access-date=2010-03-17|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090525164258/http://nwn.bioware.com/forums/viewtopic.html?topic=633312&forum=43|archive-date=2009-05-25}}</ref>

The game was released for [[Windows]] in North America on June 18, 2002,<ref>{{Cite web |date=June 18, 2002 |title=June 18: ''Neverwinter Nights'' First Impressions at IGN PC |url=https://www.ign.com/articles/2002/06/18/june-18-neverwinter-nights-first-impressions-at-ign-pc |access-date=November 27, 2023 |website=[[IGN]] |language=en}}</ref> in Europe on June 28,<ref>{{Cite web |last=Gestalt |date=June 12, 2002 |title=A Neverwinter Night's Dream |url=https://www.eurogamer.net/article-46123 |access-date=November 27, 2023 |website=[[Eurogamer]]}}</ref> and in Australia on July 3.<ref>{{Cite web |date=June 28, 2002 |title=News on ''Neverwinter Nights'' Release in Australia & New Zealand |url=http://gamenation.com.au/news/?action=view&id=206 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20020730080620/http://gamenation.com.au/news/?action=view&id=206 |archive-date=July 30, 2002 |access-date=April 2, 2024 |website=Game Nation}}</ref> [[Sega]] released the game as its publisher on March 20, 2003.<ref>{{Cite web |title=ネヴァーウィンター・ナイツ 日本語版 |trans-title=''Neverwinter Nights'' Japanese version |url=http://sega.jp/pc/nwn/1st.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20041111051957/http://sega.jp/pc/nwn/1st.html |archive-date=November 11, 2004 |access-date=April 2, 2024 |website=[[Sega]]}}</ref> A [[Linux]] client for the game was made available on June 19, 2003.<ref>{{Cite web |date=June 19, 2003 |title=''Neverwinter Nights'' For Linux |url=http://www.bioware.com/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20030622190853/http://www.bioware.com/ |archive-date=June 22, 2003 |access-date=April 2, 2024 |website=[[BioWare]]}}</ref> A [[Mac OS X]] port published by [[MacSoft]] was released in North America on July 30, 2003, and in Europe later the same year.<ref name="mac">{{Cite web |last=Cohen |first=Peter |date=July 15, 2003 |title=MacSoft: ''Neverwinter Nights'' ships July 30 |url=https://www.macworld.com/article/167120/neverwinter-5.html |access-date=April 2, 2024 |website=[[Macworld]]}}</ref>

==Gameplay==
[[File:NWN showdown.jpg|thumb|A large end-game battle. The encounter is complete with dynamic graphical effects. In the lower left corner, the player console displays ''[[Dungeons & Dragons]]'' game mechanics behind the actions.]]

The original scenario supplied with ''Neverwinter Nights'' is the campaign. It comprises approximately sixty hours of [[gameplay]].<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.highbeam.com/doc/1G1-85656767.html | author=Low, Bob | title=Wholly Enjoyable!; The Caped Crusader Will Brighten up a Dark Night | work=Daily Record | location=Glasgow, Scotland | date=May 10, 2002 | access-date=| archive-date=2014-09-21 | via=HighBeam Research | url-access=subscription | url-status=usurped | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140921200831/http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1G1-85656767.html }}</ref> The gameplay centers on the development of a [[player character]] (PC) through adventuring, who ultimately becomes the hero of the story. The PC is tasked with defeating a powerful cult, collecting four reagents required to stop a plague, and thwarting an attack on the city of [[Neverwinter]], located along the [[Sword Coast]] of [[Faerûn]], in the [[Forgotten Realms]] campaign setting of ''[[Dungeons & Dragons]]''. The first and final chapters of the campaign deal with the city of Neverwinter itself, but the lengthy mid-story requires the player to venture into the surrounding countryside and travel northward to the city of [[Luskan]]. Along the way, many optional side [[quest (video gaming)|quest]]s are made available.

As in the ''Dungeons & Dragons'' tabletop game, the first thing a player must do is create a new character. The game provides a set of ready-made characters, or the player may create one from scratch.<ref name=martin>{{cite news | url=http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1N1-0FF67B2C7A7F253C.html | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140921200835/http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1N1-0FF67B2C7A7F253C.html | url-status=usurped | archive-date=September 21, 2014 | author=Martin, Kelly | title=Neverwinter Nights | work=[[Post-Tribune (Indiana newspaper)|Post-Tribune]] | location=Indiana | date=October 10, 2002 | via=[[HighBeam Research]] | url-access=subscription | access-date=February 6, 2013}}</ref> A series of panels are presented for selection of the character's gender, race, [[character class]], [[alignment (Dungeons & Dragons)|alignment]], [[ability score]]s (such as strength and intelligence), specialized abilities called skills and feats, in-game appearance, and name.<ref>{{cite news | url=http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1P1-73555512.html | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140921200821/http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1P1-73555512.html | url-status=usurped | archive-date=September 21, 2014 | title=Escape to Neverwinter | author=Siegel-Itzkovich, Judy | work=[[Jerusalem Post]] | date=April 4, 2003 | via=HighBeam Research | url-access=subscription | access-date=February 24, 2013}}</ref> This process grants significant allowance for customization; one can be, for example, an outdoorsman ([[Ranger (Dungeons & Dragons)|ranger]]) or a healer ([[Cleric (Dungeons & Dragons)|cleric]]), then choose skills and feats that would work well with that class in the game.

Following a small prelude, there are four chapters in the original game, with each chapter following part of the general storyline. Within each chapter, there are many quests, subquests, and mini-storylines provided to the player. Depending on the specific quests completed, and the unique items kept, some storylines are continued throughout the entire game, such as the Henchman's or [[Aribeth]]'s tales. Completing many of the side quests will give the player's character more experience and special items, making them improve more rapidly and continue to make the game easier as the player progresses. These improvements come in the form of levels earned through [[experience point]]s, with each level providing the protagonist with a set of enhancements as selected by the player.

The game's mechanics are based on the ''[[Dungeons & Dragons]]'' [[Dungeons & Dragons 3rd edition|3rd edition]] rule set;<ref name=chan/> the outcome of most actions, such as combat and skills usage, are randomly determined by [[dice]] rolls.<ref name=godinez>{{cite news | url=http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1G1-90174148.html | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140921200823/http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1G1-90174148.html | url-status=usurped | archive-date=September 21, 2014 | author=Godinez, Victor | title=Electronic Adventures: Sword and Sorcery Will Please Players | date=August 6, 2002 | work=[[Knight Ridder/Tribune News Service]] | via=HighBeam Research | url-access=subscription | access-date=March 4, 2013}}</ref>{{R|ref001}} For example, when a fighter attacks, the computer would digitally "roll" a 20-sided die (called a d20 in-game) to determine if he hits the target. On a success, another die is rolled to determine the damage dealt, with powerful weapons assigned to dice with a greater number of sides, due to their ability to do more damage. Although the outcome of nearly all actions is determined by dice rolls, the player does not see them, with the results calculated in the background. However, the player has the option to display the outcomes of these rolls. The player can control the game almost entirely via the mouse.<ref name=martin/>

===Multiplayer===
A robust multiplayer component separates ''Neverwinter Nights'' from previous ''Dungeons & Dragons'' games, as this allows players to play on many different servers hosting games. Depending on hardware and [[Bandwidth (computing)|bandwidth]], each server can support up to ninety-six players on the same server application, plus [[Dungeon Master]]s (DM) to run the games, if desired. ''Neverwinter Nights'' game modules are run in a variety of genres and themes, including [[persistent world]]s (which are similar to [[Multi-user dungeon|MUD]]), combat arenas ([[player versus player]] modules), whole servers dedicated to sexually oriented roleplay,
<ref>{{cite web | title = KK (Kinky Kingdom) | date = 2008-04-07 | url = http://nwvault.ign.com/View.php?view=Gameworld.Detail&id=1180 | access-date =2009-01-17 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | title = Islands of Desire | date = 2006-05-06 | url = http://nwvault.ign.com/View.php?view=Gameworld.Detail&id=925 | access-date =2009-01-17 }}</ref> and simple social gatherings similar to a [[chat room]]. BioWare requires that these persistent worlds be free of charge, primarily for reasons of copyright law.

Because ''Neverwinter Nights'' lacks a global chat function aside from the supported [[GameSpy]], players typically join [[pickup game]]s through the game's multiplayer interface, or schedule games in advance with friends. Matchmaking sites can facilitate scheduling of games, and the experience is much like traditional [[pen-and-paper]] [[role-playing game]]s. Persistent worlds do this work for them by inviting players to visit their website and continue to roleplay there.

An important feature of ''Neverwinter Nights'' is the Dungeon Master Client: a tool that allows an individual to take the role of the Dungeon Master, who guides the players through the story and has complete control of the server.<ref name=polak>{{cite news | url=http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1G1-90750143.html | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140921200828/http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1G1-90750143.html | url-status=usurped | archive-date=September 21, 2014 | author=Polak, Steve | title=Neverwinter Nights (PC) | work=[[PC World]] | location=Australia | date=September 1, 2002 | via=HighBeam Research | url-access=subscription | access-date=February 6, 2013}}</ref> Previous games such as ''[[Vampire: The Masquerade – Redemption]]'', based on the printed gamebooks by [[White Wolf Publishing]], utilized this feature to a limited extent.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.gamespot.com/vampire-the-masquerade-redemption-2000/reviews/vampire-the-masquerade-redemption-review-2585434 |author=Kasavin, Greg |author-link=Greg Kasavin |title=Vampire: The Masquerade – Redemption Review |website=[[GameSpot]] |page=2 |date=June 9, 2000 |access-date=February 6, 2013 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130622184641/http://www.gamespot.com/vampire-the-masquerade-redemption-2000/reviews/vampire-the-masquerade-redemption-review-2585434/ |archive-date=June 22, 2013 }}</ref> When it was released, ''Neverwinter Nights'' was viewed as the first successful implementation of the feature.<ref name=polak/> The DM Client allows players to participate in regular [[campaign (role-playing games)|campaign]]s, while also allowing persistent world servers to flourish by permitting the DMs of those servers to take control of [[non-player character]]s (NPCs) in mid-game for added realism and flexibility. The Dungeon Master Client also permits the user to spawn and control masses of monsters and NPCs much in the same way as units would be controlled in a [[real-time strategy]] game.

===Custom content===
''Neverwinter Nights'' ships with the [[Aurora toolset]], which allows players to create custom [[Module (role-playing games)|modules]] for the game.<ref name=Ramirez/> These modules may take the form of online [[Multiplayer video game|multiplayer]] worlds,<ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.highbeam.com/doc/1G1-90109276.html | author=Leek, Martyn | title=Game Reviews: Endless Fun with Classic Nights | work=[[Sunday Mercury]] | location=Birmingham, England | date=August 4, 2002 | access-date=| archive-date=2014-05-12 | via=HighBeam Research | url-access=subscription | url-status=usurped | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140512030827/http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1G1-90109276.html }}</ref> [[single player]] adventures, character trainers or [[technology demo]]s. Additionally, several third party utilities have further expanded the community's ability to create [[Mod (computer gaming)|custom content]] for the game. By the end of 2002, there were over 1,000 custom adventures available.<ref name=meadows>{{cite news | url=http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1G1-94965533.html | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140512030829/http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1G1-94965533.html | url-status=usurped | archive-date=May 12, 2014 | author=Meadows, Mark | title='Neverwinter' has Hookers, but no Heart of Gold | work=[[The Wisconsin State Journal]] | location=Madison, Wisconsin | date=December 5, 2002 | via=HighBeam Research | url-access=subscription | access-date=February 24, 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.gamedeveloper.com/design/postmortem-bioware-s-i-neverwinter-nights-i-|title=Postmortem: Bioware's ''Neverwinter Nights''|last=Greig|first=Scott|date=4 December 2002|work=[[Gamasutra]]|page=4|access-date=19 January 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121111000517/http://www.gamasutra.com/view/feature/131327/postmortem_biowares_neverwinter_.php?page=4|archive-date=11 November 2012|url-status=live|display-authors=etal}}</ref>

Custom content creators are known as builders in the ''Neverwinter Nights'' community. The Aurora toolset allows builders to create map areas using a [[Tile-based game|tile system]]; the appearance and surface textures of the area are defined by the area's selected tileset. Builders can overlay placeable objects onto areas, and use the built-in scripting language NWScript, which is based on the [[C (programming language)|C programming language]], to run [[cut scene]]s, quests, [[mini-game]]s and conversations.<ref name=meadows/> 

Third party utilities allow builders to create custom content for most aspects of the game, ranging from new playable races and character classes to new tilesets, monsters and equipment. Custom content is added to the game in the form of hakpaks. Builders have used the Aurora toolset in combination with hakpaks to create playing experiences beyond the scope of the original campaign. Additionally, the Aurora toolset has allowed for the creation of a number of ongoing [[persistent world]]s modules.

Despite the game's age, the ''Neverwinter Nights'' custom content community remains active. The community, mostly centered on the Neverwinter Vault, has created over 4,000 modules for the game, among them, many award-winning adventures and series such as ''Dreamcatcher''.<ref name="Adam Miller">{{cite web |url=http://adamandjamie.com/mod/nwn_campaign.aspx |title=Adam Miller's Game Mods for Neverwinter Nights and Dragon Age |date=June 6, 2008 |access-date=August 6, 2010 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100805055235/http://adamandjamie.com/mod/nwn_campaign.aspx |archive-date=August 5, 2010 }}</ref> The Aurora toolset is not available for the Linux and Macintosh versions of ''Neverwinter Nights''. The [[Open-source software|open source]] project neveredit aims to port the toolset features to these platforms. The game's module-making legacy was continued by ''[[Neverwinter Nights 2]]''.

==Plot==
The story begins with the [[player character]] (PC), the protagonist of the story, being sent to recover four creatures (dryad, intellect devourer, yuan-ti, and cockatrice) known collectively as the "Waterdhavian creatures" under the guidance of Lady [[Aribeth de Tylmarande]].<ref name=chan>{{cite news | url=http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1P1-82684762.html | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150924182353/http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1P1-82684762.html | url-status=usurped | archive-date=September 24, 2015 | author=Chan, Chris | title=Engaging in Never-ending Wars | work=[[New Straits Times]] | date=August 5, 2002 | via=HighBeam Research | url-access=subscription | access-date=February 13, 2013}}</ref> The Waterdhavian creatures are needed to make a cure for the Wailing Death, a plague that is sweeping the city of Neverwinter and forcing a quarantine.<ref name=Ramirez>{{cite news | author=Ramirez, Pedro III | title=Complex Game Is Worth the Effort | work=[[The Post-Standard]] | location=Syracuse, New York | date=September 18, 2002 }}</ref> With the help of Fenthick Moss, Aribeth's love interest, and Desther, Fenthick's friend, the PC is able to retrieve the creatures. As they collect the creatures, they are attacked by mysterious assassins from a cult that is behind the spreading of the plague.

As the cure is being made, Castle Neverwinter is attacked by the minions of Desther, who betrays the heroes. Desther takes the completed cure and escapes the castle, with the hero and Fenthick in pursuit. When they catch up to Desther, he surrenders after a short battle. Desther is sentenced to burn at the stake, and Fenthick, despite being unaware of Desther's true intentions, is sentenced to hang. 

The protagonist meets up with Aribeth and Neverwinter's spymaster, Aarin Gend, to begin searching for the cult responsible for the plague and the attack on Neverwinter. The PC retrieves the diaries of dead cultists and letters from a person named Maugrim Korothir, which convince Aribeth that the cult's headquarters are in [[Luskan]]. Aribeth goes ahead to Luskan, and the hero follows after speaking once more to Gend.

After arriving in Luskan, the protagonist hears rumors that Aribeth has defected and joined the cultists. These fears are confirmed when she is found meeting with Maugrim and Morag, Queen of the [[reptilian humanoid|reptilian Old Ones]]. They seek a group of magical relics called the Words of Power. The protagonist retrieves all of the Words of Power except for one held by the cult. The hero discovers that the Words open a portal to a pocket world inside the Source Stone, where Morag and the other Old Ones sealed themselves long ago to avoid extinction during a primordial ice age. The protagonist confronts Aribeth, and depending on how the meeting is handled, she either surrenders to the PC or they are forced to kill her. The hero battles Maugrim for the final Word, then uses the Words to enter the Source Stone and battle with Morag. After Morag's death, the protagonist escapes the Stone as the world inside it implodes.

==Reception==
===Sales===
For the launch of ''Neverwinter Nights'', publisher Infogrames shipped 1 million copies to stores, with half allocated to North America and the rest to international markets.<ref name=sales1 /> In an experimental move, the company priced the game at $55, an increase over the $50 typical of computer games at the time. [[CNN Money]] columnist Chris Morris reported that "gamers complained loudly about" this decision.<ref name=cnnsales>{{cite news | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20021228235642/http://money.cnn.com/2002/12/20/commentary/game_over/column_gaming/index.htm | url=http://money.cnn.com:80/2002/12/20/commentary/game_over/column_gaming/index.htm | title=Lawsuits, strippers and price hikes | newspaper=[[CNN Money]] | date=December 27, 2002 | author=Morris, Chris | archive-date=December 28, 2002 | url-status=dead | access-date=August 2, 2018 | df=mdy-all }}</ref> The game proceeded to sell 125,000 copies by June 27, after its release on the 18th.<ref name=sales1>{{cite press release | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20020701055909/http://www.infogrames.com/corp_pressreleases.php?op=story&sid=287 | url=http://www.infogrames.com/corp_pressreleases.php?op=story&sid=287 | title=Infogrames Closes Out Fiscal Year with Release of Major Titles Across All Platforms | date=June 27, 2002 | publisher=[[Infogrames]] | location=[[New York City|New York]] | archive-date=July 1, 2002 | url-status=dead }}</ref> It debuted at #1 on [[The NPD Group]]'s computer game sales chart during the June 16–22 period,<ref name=sales2>{{cite web | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20031207222838/http://www.gamespot.com/pc/rpg/neverwinternights/news_2873403.html | url=http://www.gamespot.com:80/pc/rpg/neverwinternights/news_2873403.html | title=''Neverwinter Nights'' tops the charts | author=Walker, Trey | work=[[GameSpot]] | date=July 3, 2002 | archive-date=December 7, 2003 | url-status=dead | access-date=August 2, 2018 | df=mdy-all }}</ref> and held the position for two weeks, before being displaced by ''[[Warcraft III: Reign of Chaos]]''.<ref name=sales3>{{cite web | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20040429223814/http://www.gamespot.com/pc/rpg/neverwinternights/news_2873902.html | url=http://www.gamespot.com:80/pc/rpg/neverwinternights/news_2873902.html | title=''Neverwinter Nights'' retains the lead | author=Walker, Trey | work=[[GameSpot]] | date=July 10, 2002 | archive-date=April 29, 2004 | url-status=dead | access-date=August 2, 2018 | df=mdy-all }}</ref><ref name=sales4>{{cite web | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20030402111204/http://www.gamespot.com/pc/rpg/neverwinternights/news_2874735.html | url=http://www.gamespot.com:80/pc/rpg/neverwinternights/news_2874735.html | title=''Warcraft III'' begins reign of sales | author=Walker, Trey | work=[[GameSpot]] | date=July 17, 2002 | archive-date=April 2, 2003 | url-status=dead | access-date=August 2, 2018 | df=mdy-all }}</ref> However, ''Neverwinter Nights'' continued to place in the chart's top 10 consistently for its first three months of release.<ref name=sales5>{{cite press release | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20030303091619/http://infogrames.com/corp_pressreleases.php?op=story&sid=324 | url=http://infogrames.com:80/corp_pressreleases.php?op=story&sid=324 | title=''Neverwinter Nights'' Interview | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20021020003557/http://pc.ign.com/articles/365/365613p1.html | url=http://pc.ign.com:80/articles/365/365613p1.html | revenues of $18 million.<ref name=cnnsales /> It was ultimately the region's 11th-best-selling computer game of 2002.<ref name=npd2003>{{cite report | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20030611054916/http://www.idsa.com/EF2003.pdf | url=http://www.idsa.com:80/EF2003.pdf | title=Essential Facts about the Computer and Video Game Industry; 2003 Sales, Demographics and Usage Data | date=May 14, 2003 | publisher=[[Interactive Digital Software Association]] | page=5 | archive-date=June 11, 2003 | url-status=dead | access-date=July 16, 2018 | df=mdy-all }}</ref>

Greg Zeschuk remarked in June 2003 that ''Neverwinter Nights'' had sold above 1 million copies, before the release of its first expansion pack.<ref name=undrentideint>{{cite web | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20030720053124/http://www.gamespy.com/interviews/june03/raygreg/index.shtml | url=http://www.gamespy.com:80/interviews/june03/raygreg/index.shtml | title=Talkin' ''Neverwinter'' with Ray and Greg | work=[[GameSpy]] | author=Padilla, Raymond | date=June 14, 2003 | archive-date=July 20, 2003 | url-status=dead | access-date=August 2, 2018 | df=mdy-all }}</ref> In the United States alone, the game sold 510,000 copies and earned $23.2 million by August 2006. At that time, ''[[Edge (magazine)|Edge]]'' declared it the country's 26th-best-selling computer game released since January 2000.<ref name=edgesales>{{cite magazine|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121017165955/http://www.edge-online.com/features/top-100-pc-games-21st-century/ |url=http://www.edge-online.com/features/top-100-pc-games-21st-century/ |title=The Top 100 PC Games of the 21st Century| author=''Edge'' Staff | date=August 25, 2006 |magazine=[[Edge (magazine)|Edge]] |archive-date=October 17, 2012 |url-status=dead }}</ref> It also received a "Silver" sales award from the [[Entertainment and Leisure Software Publishers Association]],<ref name=silverelspa>{{cite web |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090221154943/http://www.elspa.com/?i=3942 |url=http://www.elspa.com:80/?i=3942 |title=ELSPA Sales Awards: Silver |work=[[Entertainment and Leisure Software Publishers Association]] |archive-date=February 21, 2009 |url-status=dead }}</ref> which indicates sales of at least 100,000 copies in the United Kingdom.<ref name=gamasutrasales>{{cite web|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170918063107/https://www.gamasutra.com/view/news/112220/ELSPA_Wii_Fit_Mario_Kart_Reach_Diamond_Status_In_UK.php |url=https://www.gamasutra.com/view/news/112220/ELSPA_Wii_Fit_Mario_Kart_Reach_Diamond_Status_In_UK.php |title=ELSPA: ''Wii Fit'', ''Mario Kart'' Reach Diamond Status In UK | author=Caoili, Eric | date=November 26, 2008 |work=[[Gamasutra]] |archive-date=September 18, 2017 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Combined global sales of ''Neverwinter Nights'' and its expansion packs surpassed 2.6 million units by early 2005;<ref name=aboutbioware1>{{cite web | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050205222300/http://www.bioware.com/bioware_info/about/ | url=http://www.bioware.com:80/bioware_info/about/ | title=About BioWare | archive-date=February 5, 2005 | publisher=[[BioWare]] | access-date=September 11, 2011 | url-status=dead | df=mdy-all }}</ref> by August 2006, the games totaled 1.3 million sales in the United States alone.<ref name=edgesales /> Discounting its expansions, the original ''Neverwinter Nights'' ultimately sold 2.2 million copies, as of 2007.<ref name=latimessales>{{cite news | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081004230656/http://articles.latimes.com/2007/oct/12/business/fi-games12 | In general, ''Neverwinter Nights'' was met with positive reviews, receiving "universal acclaim" according to [[Metacritic]].<ref name="metacritic" /> [[GameSpot]] referred to it as "one of those exceedingly rare games that has a lot to offer virtually everyone, even if they aren't already into RPGs", and praised it for its campaign, its Aurora toolset, and its graphics.<ref name="gamespot" /> The publication later named it the best computer game of June 2002.<ref name=gotm>{{cite web | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20021204003624/http://gamespot.com/gamespot/features/pc/gotm/070502/index.html | url=http://gamespot.com/gamespot/features/pc/gotm/070502/index.html | title=PC Game of the Month, June 2002 | author=((The Editors of ''GameSpot PC'')) | date=July 5, 2002 | work=[[GameSpot]] | archive-date=December 4, 2002 | url-status=dead | access-date=December 8, 2020 }}</ref> ''[[PC Gamer]] US'' called it "a total package—a PC gaming classic for the ages", and said that its "storyline [is] as persuasive as any I’ve encountered in a fantasy roleplaying game".<ref name=pcgus>{{cite web | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071031030357/http://www.pcgamer.com/archives/2005/07/neverwinter_nig_2.html | url=http://www.pcgamer.com/archives/2005/07/neverwinter_nig_2.html | archive-date=October 31, 2007 | title=Neverwinter Nights | last=Smith | first=Rob | work=[[PC Gamer]] US | access-date=April 19, 2010 }}</ref> 

Chris Chan of ''[[New Straits Times]]'' said, "''Neverwinter Nights'' is every role-playing gamer's dream".<ref name=chan/> [[Allgame]] found that the game's story was "humdrum" and "mediocre".<ref name="allgame" /> Mark Meadows of ''[[The Wisconsin State Journal]]'' agreed, saying the game was too focused on technical details.<ref name=meadows/> Victor Godinez of ''[[Knight Ridder/Tribune News Service]]'' did not care for the turn-based combat system, preferring to have direct control. He also said the controls were difficult to use occasionally.<ref name=godinez/>

''[[GamePro]]'' noted the game's graphics as being "gorgeous" and its sound as "untouchable",<ref name="gamepro" /> and GameZone likewise praised its visuals, specifically mentioning its combat animation and spell effects as being well done.<ref name="gamezone" /> [[GameSpy]] was not as impressed by the graphics, saying "The biggest, and arguably the only, glaring flaw in the game, is its graphics. You can tell that this game has been in development for five years[...]"; however, they praised its voice acting and music.<ref name="gamespy" /> Godinez agreed, and also liked the game's audio, noting in particular the scraps of conversation that can be heard in the background throughout the city.<ref name=godinez/>

Allgame praised ''Neverwinter Night''{{'}}s DM tools, calling the game's level creation options "impressive" and the multiplayer options "great".<ref name="allgame" /> ''GamePro'' thought that ''Neverwinter Nights'' is the closest that any video game has come to accurately representing the full ''Dungeons & Dragons'' rules,<ref name="gamepro" /> a statement further reinforced by Greg Kasavin of [[GameSpot]], who said that "Neverwinter Nights isn't the first ''Dungeons & Dragons'' game for the computer to make use of the pen-and-paper game's 3rd Edition rules, but it's the first to implement them so well".<ref name="gamespot" /> 

GameZone said that the Aurora Toolset was one of the "best features" of the game.<ref name="gamezone" /> John Breeden II of ''[[The Washington Post]]'' said including the tool set was "smartest thing Bioware did".{{R|breeden}} He went on to say that giving such tools to the players became more commonplace, but was a bold move at the time of the game's release.<ref name=breeden/> Chan commented, "you could use the Aurora tools to create a dream world".<ref name=chan/>

Peter Suciu of ''[[Newsweek]]'' magazine called ''Neverwinter Nights'' "possibly the richest fantasy PC experience ever created."<ref>{{cite journal | url=https://www.highbeam.com/doc/1G1-90424394.html | author=Suciu, Peter | title=Games: Hooked On Saving The World | journal=[[Newsweek]] | date=August 19, 2002 | access-date= | archive-date=2014-06-14 | via=HighBeam Research | url-access=subscription | url-status=usurped | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140614172637/http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1G1-90424394.html }}</ref> According to GameSpy, "''Neverwinter'''s contribution to D&D gaming is always a hot topic and a source of argument."<ref name="rauschV">{{cite web | last=Rausch | first=Allen | date=2004-08-19 | url = http://pc.gamespy.com/articles/540/540375p3.html | title=A History of ''D&D'' Video Games - Part V | publisher = GameSpy | access-date = November 17, 2012 }}</ref>

===Awards===
During the [[6th Annual Interactive Achievement Awards]], ''Neverwinter Nights'' was awarded with "[[D.I.C.E. Award for Role-Playing Game of the Year|Computer Role-Playing Game of the Year]]" by the [[Academy of Interactive Arts & Sciences]] (AIAS); it also received a nomination for "Computer Game of the Year".<ref name=aias2002>{{cite web |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20040404185448/http://interactive.org/awards/IAA-6/winners.asp |url=http://interactive.org:80/awards/IAA-6/winners.asp |title=6th Annual Interactive Achievement Awards: Winners |publisher=[[Academy of Interactive Arts & Sciences]] |archive-date=April 4, 2004 |url-status=dead |df=mdy-all |access-date=March 28, 2018 }}</ref> The game also won role-playing game of the year awards from ''[[PC Gamer US]]'' and [[GameSpot]].<ref name=pcgamerusawards2003>{{cite journal |date=March 2003 | title=The Ninth Annual ''PC Gamer'' Awards | volume=10 | number=3 | pages=48–50, 54, 58, 60, 66, 68, 70 | journal=[[PC Gamer US]] | author=Smith, Rob }}</ref><ref name=gamespot2002>{{cite web|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20030207155400/http://gamespot.com/gamespot/features/all/bestof2002/ |url=http://gamespot.com/gamespot/features/all/bestof2002/ |title=GameSpot's Best and Worst of 2002 | author=GameSpot Staff | work=[[GameSpot]] |archive-date=February 7, 2003 |url-status=dead }}</ref> [[RPG Vault]] declared it "Product of the Year",<ref name=rpgvault2002>{{cite web | author=Staff | url=http://rpgvault.ign.com:80/articles/382/382567p1.html | title=2002 RPG Vault Awards | work=[[RPG Vault]] | date=January 13, 2003 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070918055234/http://rpgvault.ign.com/articles/382/382567p1.html | archive-date=September 18, 2007 | access-date=December 19, 2006 | url-status=dead | df=mdy-all }}</ref> while ''[[Computer Games Magazine]]'' ranked it the year's second-best computer game across all genres. The latter publication's editors wrote that the "single-player game is merely passable", but they highly praised ''Neverwinter Nights''{{'}} content-creation tools, and argued that the game is "what computer role-playing games should have been all along".<ref name=cgm12th>{{cite journal | author=Staff | journal=[[Computer Games Magazine]] | title=Best of the Year 2002; 12th Annual ''Computer Games'' Awards |date=March 2003 | issue=148 | pages=58–61 }}</ref>

The game won special awards for its technology from ''Computer Games'',<ref name=cgm12th /> the [[Game Developers Choice Awards]] (GDCA) and RPG Vault, the latter two for its network programming and Aurora Neverwinter Toolset, respectively.<ref name=rpgvault2002 /><ref name=gdca2002>{{cite web | url=http://www.gamechoiceawards.com/archive/gdca_3rd.html | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110703082229/http://www.gamechoiceawards.com/archive/gdca_3rd.html | archive-date=July 3, 2011 | title=Archive <nowiki>|</nowiki> 3rd Annual Game Developers Choice Awards | publisher=[[Game Developers Conference]] | url-status=live }}</ref> The Aurora Neverwinter Toolset was also a nominee in the AIAS's "[[D.I.C.E. Award for Strategy/Simulation Game of the Year|Computer Simulation Game of the Year]]" category.<ref name=aias2002 /> RPG Vault's staff hailed the tool as "an unprecedented combination of power, flexibility and ease of use."<ref name=rpgvault2002 />

''Neverwinter Nights'' received further nominations in the AIAS's special categories for "Outstanding Innovation in Computer Gaming" and "[[D.I.C.E. Award for Outstanding Achievement in Game Design|Outstanding Achievement in Game Design]]", and in RPG Vault's categories for music and writing, but lost these to other titles.<ref name=rpgvault2002 /><ref name=aias2002 /> However, it did win RPG Vault's "Outstanding Achievement in Community Building" prize.<ref name=rpgvault2002 />

''Neverwinter Nights'' was a runner-up for the "Role-Playing Game of the Year" awards of ''[[Computer Gaming World]]'', [[IGN]], [[GameSpy]] and RPG Vault, all of which went to ''[[The Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind]]''.<ref name=cgwpremier2002>{{cite magazine | author=Staff | magazine=[[Computer Gaming World]] | title=''Computer Gaming World''{{'}}s 2002 Games of the Year |date=April 2003 | issue=225 | pages=83–86, 88, 89, 92–97 }}</ref><ref name=rpgvault2002 /><ref name=gamespy2002>{{cite web |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080914023924/http://archive.gamespy.com/goty2002/pc/ |url=http://archive.gamespy.com:80/goty2002/pc/ |title=GameSpy 2002 Game of the Year PC |author=Staff |work=[[GameSpy]] |archive-date=September 14, 2008 |url-status=dead |df=mdy-all |access-date=August 2, 2018 }}</ref><ref name=ign2002>{{cite web | author=Butts, Steve | url=http://pc.ign.com:80/articles/382/382684p1.html | title=IGNPC's Best of 2002 Awards | work=[[IGN]] | date=January 14, 2003 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20030207123534/http://pc.ign.com/articles/382/382684p1.html | archive-date=February 7, 2003 | access-date=August 2, 2018 | url-status=dead | df=mdy-all }}</ref> The editors of ''Computer Gaming World'' wrote that ''Neverwinter Nights'' "gave gamers a fabulous toolset for creating their own adventures—too bad the single-player campaign prompted a staffwide shrugging of shoulders."<ref name=cgwpremier2002 /> It was also nominated as the overall best computer game of 2002 by GameSpot, ''PC Gamer US'' and the AIAS,<ref name=pcgamerusawards2003 /><ref name=aias2002 /><ref name=gamespot2002 /> and as the year's best game on any platform by the GDCA.<ref name=gdca2002 /> These prizes went variously to ''Warcraft III'', ''[[Battlefield 1942]]'' and ''[[Metroid Prime]]''.<ref name=pcgamerusawards2003 /><ref name=aias2002 /><ref name=gamespot2002 /><ref name=gdca2002 />

==Legacy==
IGN ranked ''Neverwinter Nights'' No. 4 on their list of "The Top 11 Dungeons & Dragons Games of All Time" in 2014.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.ign.com/articles/2014/02/05/the-top-11-dungeons-dragons-games-of-all-time|title=The Top 11 Dungeons & Dragons Games of All-Time|last=Johnson|first=Leif|date=2014-02-05|website=IGN|language=en-US|access-date=2018-01-04}}</ref> Ian Williams of ''[[Paste (magazine)|Paste]]'' rated the game #4 on his list of "The 10 Greatest Dungeons and Dragons Videogames" in 2015.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.pastemagazine.com/articles/2015/04/the-10-greatest-dungeons-and-dragons-videogames.html|title=The 10 Greatest Dungeons and Dragons Videogames|work=pastemagazine.com|access-date=2018-01-04|language=en}}</ref> The game has inspired a number of fan-made films made using [[machinima]] techniques of synchronizing video footage from a game to pre-recorded dialogue and other audio, such as ''[[BloodSpell]]'', and ''Neverending Nights''.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://nwn.bioware.com/players/profile_machinima_tutorial.html |title=Neverwinter Nights: Neverwinter Nights Machinima Tutorial<!-- Bot generated title --> |access-date=2006-01-05 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20051212205949/http://nwn.bioware.com/players/profile_machinima_tutorial.html |archive-date=2005-12-12 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://festival.machinima.org/modules.php?name=Content&pa=showpage&pid=5 |title=2005 Award Nominations and Selections |access-date=2009-05-25 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060427054638/http://festival.machinima.org/modules.php?name=Content&pa=showpage&pid=5 |archive-date=2006-04-27 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://nwvault.ign.com/fullstory.php?id=29182 |title=NWN Spotlight - Neverending Nights by FNBH Productions.|access-date=November 16, 2020 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110713005224/http://nwvault.ign.com/fullstory.php?id=29182 |archive-date=July 13, 2011 }}</ref>

Since the original release of ''Neverwinter Nights'', several in-game portraits have been modified in [[Patch (computing)|patches]] due to their having been copied from outside sources.{{citation needed|date=March 2013}} In another instance, the [[Canadian Red Cross]] complained to BioWare about the appearance of the Red Cross symbol on the in-game item "Healer's Kit", as part of a long-running attempt to discourage outside usage of the symbol. This resulted in the Red Cross symbol being removed from the Healer's Kit through patches.<ref>{{cite web | last =Doctorow | first =Cory | title =Canadian Red Cross wastes its money harassing video game makers | publisher =[[Boing Boing]] | date= 2006-02-09 | url =http://www.boingboing.net/2006/02/09/canadian-red-cross-w.html | access-date =2007-11-17 }}</ref>

''[[Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic (video game)|Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic]]'', a [[role-playing video game]] based in the ''[[Star Wars]]'' universe, was also released by BioWare using a modified version of the [[Aurora engine]] of ''Neverwinter Nights'', called the [[Odyssey Engine]]. The sequel, ''[[Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic II: The Sith Lords]]'', also used it. Because of this, modders have been able to modify these games using some ''Neverwinter Nights'' modding tools. ''[[The Witcher (video game)|The Witcher]]'', a role-playing video game by [[CD Projekt Red]], is also based on the Aurora engine of ''Neverwinter Nights''. BioWare used ''Neverwinter Nights'' and its toolset to develop prototypes and mock-ups of various areas and scenarios for ''[[Dragon Age: Origins]]''.<ref>{{cite video |people=Mark Darrath (executive producer of ''Dragon Age: Origins'') |date=2009 |title=Dragon Age: Origins Collector's Edition Bonus Disc: Origin of Dragon Age: Creating a Living World |medium=DVD |publisher= Electronic Arts |time= 07:38&mdash;08:06 }}</ref>

===Expansion packs and modules===
''Neverwinter Nights'' received an [[expansion pack]], ''[[Neverwinter Nights: Shadows of Undrentide]]'', in June 2003. Its story line concerns a student sent out to recover some stolen magical objects. The story begins in the [[Silver Marches]], moving toward the desert of Anauroch and the old Netherese city of Undrentide. A second expansion ''[[Neverwinter Nights: Hordes of the Underdark]]'' was released in December 2003. The story continued where ''Shadows of Undrentide'' ended, with a character of at least 15th level, and led into the vast subterranean world known as the [[Underdark]]. The first chapter of the story took place in the Undermountain dungeon beneath the city of [[Waterdeep (city)|Waterdeep]]. ''[[Neverwinter Nights: Kingmaker]]'' was released in November 2004, and features three premium modules: the award-winning ''Kingmaker'',<ref name="AoIAS RPG Award">{{cite web | title = Academy of Interactive Arts & Sciences 2005 'PC RPG of the Year' award | url = http://www.interactive.org/awards/award_category_details.asp?idAward=2005&idGameAwardType=29 | access-date =2012-10-15 }}</ref> ''Shadowguard'', and ''Witch's Wake''.

Atari and BioWare helped to promote and release free downloadable hakpaks, models, and tileset expansion packs, which greatly expanded the possibilities of mod-making.{{citation needed|date=October 2014}} The ''Players Resource Consortium'' (''PRC'') was released in early December 2003, and is a group of hakpaks adding classes, races, skills, and spells to the game.{{citation needed|date=October 2014}} The ''PRC'' has roughly three times the number of prestige classes the original game had.{{citation needed|date=October 2014}} It also adds dozens of epic spells, and many normal spells that make better use of BioWare's Aurora engine.{{citation needed|date=October 2014}} [[Psionics (role-playing games)|Psionic]] powers have also been included.{{citation needed|date=October 2014}} The ''Community Expansion Pack'' (''CEP''), originally released in March 2004 (last updated in January 2017), is based on the ''Neverwinter Nights'' community's fan-made material.{{R|nwvault_cep}} This freely downloadable expansion was compiled by members of the community. It combines a selection of previously released custom content into one group of hakpaks.{{R|nwvault_cep}}

In late 2004, BioWare launched its online store and started selling what it called "premium modules" as part of its digital distribution program. This initiative was led by BioWare's Live Team Lead Designer, Rob Bartel. These smaller-scale adventures introduced new storylines and gameplay, and include new music and art that BioWare integrated into later [[patch (computing)|patches]] to the core game. According to BioWare, the revenue generated by sales of the premium modules would be used to support their fan community and provide ongoing updates and improvements to the game. The modules that are sold in the BioWare store require an active Internet connection to play, even when played in single player mode. The modules in the ''Kingmaker'' expansion were stripped of this requirement, but are only available for Windows systems. The modules included with ''Neverwinter Nights Diamond Edition'' do not require Internet access to play. In August 2009, BioWare discontinued its selling of premium modules due to a request made by Atari.<ref name="discontinue premium mods">{{cite web|url=http://nwn.bioware.com/forums/viewtopic.html?topic=692018&forum=120|title=Neverwinter Nights: Can't Find The Premium Modules ...|date=2009-08-30|access-date=2010-03-17|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091113071204/http://nwn.bioware.com/forums/viewtopic.html?topic=692018&forum=120|archive-date=2009-11-13}}</ref> 

On June 16, 2011, the ''Neverwinter Nights'' [[digital rights management]] (DRM) authentication server was temporarily taken down as a reaction by [[Electronic Arts]] to the ''Neverwinter Nights'' store being hacked and customer data stolen.{{Citation needed|date=September 2011}} Premium modules which were purchased via BioWare's store could not be played during that time because they could not connect to the server to validate the purchase,<ref name="NOTICE: NWN Authentication Server Down">{{cite web|url=http://social.bioware.com/forum/1/topic/199/index/7715716/1|title=NOTICE: NWN Authentication Server Down ...|date=July 2011|access-date=2011-09-02}}{{dead link|date=December 2017 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> though DRM-free modules were unaffected. The modules ''Kingmaker'', ''Shadowguard'', and ''Witch's Wake'' were sold as part of the ''Diamond Edition'' package.<ref name=breeden/>

{{vanchor|Premium modules}} include ''[[Neverwinter Nights: Kingmaker (module)|Neverwinter Nights: Kingmaker]]'', BioWare's flagship premium module, which later received the [[Academy of Interactive Arts & Sciences]] "[[D.I.C.E. Award for Role-Playing Game of the Year|Computer Role-Playing Game of the Year]]" award.<ref name="AoIAS RPG Award"/> In the module's story, the hero must defeat the evil at the Keep of Cyan and win the throne. Others include ''[[Neverwinter Nights: ShadowGuard (module)|Neverwinter Nights: ShadowGuard]]'', created by community member Ben McJunkin; ''[[Neverwinter Nights: Witch's Wake]]'', a remastered version of a module by Rob Bartel; ''Neverwinter Nights: Pirates of the Sword Coast''; ''Neverwinter Nights: Infinite Dungeons'', a BioWare module taking place in the Undermountain area below [[Waterdeep (city)|Waterdeep]]; and ''Neverwinter Nights: Wyvern Crown of Cormyr'', which features fully ridable horses, flowing cloaks, tabards and long coats, a new [[Prestige class (Dungeons & Dragons)|prestige class]] (the Purple Dragon Knight), and extensive new art, creatures, and tilesets.

Premium modules were eventually discontinued. Three premium modules were known to be in development before cancellation. Two of them ended up being free downloads, while the third, a planned sequel to ''Witch's Wake'', was never released. ''Hex Coda'' by Stefan Gagne, the first cancelled premium module, was released to Neverwinter Vault in May 2005. The story was a mix of fantasy and science fiction and involved the protagonist dealing with the machinations of a multinational corporation called Cathedral. A sequel was in development, but was cancelled. 

In August 2006, Ossian Studios Inc., headed up by [[Alan Miranda]], a former producer at BioWare, released the second canceled premium module to the Vault: ''[[Darkness over Daggerford]]''. The story takes place in and around Daggerford and has been compared favorably to ''[[Baldur's Gate 2]]'' in terms of its scope. Characters start at the 8th level. The module includes a cinematic intro (like the main campaign) and a world map. ''Darkness over Daggerford'''s status as a quasi-official expansion pack was supported by the next release of the team, this time a fully official one: ''[[Neverwinter Nights 2: Mysteries of Westgate|Mysteries of Westgate]]'' for'' Neverwinter Nights 2''.

===Sequels===
A sequel to ''Neverwinter Nights'', ''[[Neverwinter Nights 2]]'', was developed by [[Obsidian Entertainment]], a company with a long history with BioWare. According to BioWare, the change of developer was due to BioWare's business with other titles, such as ''[[Mass Effect]]'' and ''[[Dragon Age: Origins]]''.{{Citation needed|date=September 2011}} ''Neverwinter Nights 2'' shipped in November 2006.

On August 23, 2010, [[Atari]] announced [[Cryptic Studios]] would be developing ''[[Neverwinter (video game)|Neverwinter]]'', an online role-playing game based on the book series of the same name by [[R.A. Salvatore]].<ref>{{cite magazine | last=Peckham | first=Matt | url=http://www.pcworld.com/article/203897/neverwinter_nights_reborn_as_online_roleplaying_game.html | title=Neverwinter Nights Reborn as Online Roleplaying Game | magazine=PCWorld | date=2010-08-23 | access-date=2011-11-24 | archive-date=2012-01-09 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120109033930/http://www.pcworld.com/article/203897/neverwinter_nights_reborn_as_online_roleplaying_game.html | url-status=dead }}</ref> It is based on [[Wizards of the Coast]]'s global property ''[[Dungeons & Dragons]]'' rules and feature the titular city [[Neverwinter]]. It was released in June 2013.

===Educational usage===
''Neverwinter Nights'' has been used by colleges and universities for a variety of educational purposes. It has been used at [[West Nottinghamshire College]] in the United Kingdom as a means of delivering key skills and of showing [[Information technology|IT]] designers how to understand the coding in the game.<ref>{{Cite news | title =Computer game to boost key skills | newspaper =[[BBC]] | date= 2007-01-07 | url =https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/uk_news/education/6254989.stm | access-date =2007-11-17 }}</ref><ref>{{cite news | url=https://www.highbeam.com/doc/1G1-152488363.html | author=Cole, Paul | title=Get the Sums Right or You Die | work=[[Sunday Mercury]] | location=Birmingham, England | date=October 8, 2006 | access-date=| archive-date=2014-09-21 | via=HighBeam Research | url-access=subscription | url-status=usurped | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140921200833/http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1G1-152488363.html }}</ref> The Synthetic Worlds Initiative at [[Indiana University]] has used it as a basis for the creation of ''[[Arden: The World of Shakespeare]]'', where Shakespeare's dramatic history of [[Richard III (play)|Richard III]] and [[Wars of the Roses|The War of the Roses]] can be interactively explored.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://swi.indiana.edu/ardenworld.htm |title=Arden: World Of William Shakespeare |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080828170612/http://swi.indiana.edu/ardenworld.htm |archive-date=2008-08-28 }}</ref> The game and the Aurora toolset were also used at [[Macquarie University]] in Australia.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.comp.mq.edu.au/units/info111/outline.htm| archive-url=https://archive.today/20110301074818/http://www.comp.mq.edu.au/units/info111/outline.htm| url-status=dead| archive-date=2011-03-01|title=INFO111/MAS111: Computer Games}}</ref> 

The [[University of Alberta]] has offered a video game design course which uses ''Neverwinter Nights'' and the Aurora Toolset as the platform for teaching and course projects.<ref>{{Cite news|title=The serious business of making the best games |newspaper=University of Alberta ExpressNews |date=2009-04-20 |url=http://www.expressnews.ualberta.ca/article.cfm?id=10115 |access-date=2010-03-22 }}{{dead link|date=November 2016 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> The [[University of Minnesota]] has used the game to teach journalism students how to gather facts and information for news events with a modified modern setting for the game that involves interviewing witnesses and doing library research;<ref>{{cite news | url=http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1P1-119504770.html | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150924172723/http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1P1-119504770.html | url-status=usurped | archive-date=September 24, 2015 | author=Svensson, Peter | title=Game Teaches Journalism Students Skills | agency=Associated Press | date=March 8, 2006 | via=HighBeam Research | url-access=subscription | work=AP Online | access-date=April 2, 2013}}</ref> in a modified game, students would work in pairs putting together a story about a train accident that causes a toxic chemical spill.<ref>{{cite news | url=http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1G1-144777022.html | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140921200836/http://www.highbeam.com/doc/1G1-144777022.html | url-status=usurped | archive-date=September 21, 2014 | author=Smetanka, Mary Jane | title=Teaching takes a virtual twist; High-tech computer games are adding interest and intensity to college coursework | work=[[Star Tribune]] | location=Minneapolis, Minnesota | date=April 21, 2006 | via=HighBeam Research | url-access=subscription | access-date=April 4, 2013}}</ref> ''Neverwinter Nights'' has also been used as an interface for some [[Moodle]] activity types.<ref>{{Cite news | author1=González, C. S. | author2=Blanco-Izquierdo, F. | title =Integrating an educational 3D game in Moodle | newspaper =[[Simulation & Gaming]] | date= 2008-07-01 | url =http://sag.sagepub.com/content/39/3/399.abstract | access-date =2016-02-07 }}</ref>
